The Cherwell and the Thames, which Oxford calls the Isis for part of its length, both slip through the town, and a short stroll takes you to meadows, punts and willow trees that feel miles from the traffic.

The university is the obvious story, with its first teaching recorded in the eleventh century and colleges added over the next several hundred years, but Oxford has another identity out in Cowley, a few kilometres east. That is where William Morris built cars in the early twentieth century, and the Mini is still made there today. The city sits between two worlds, scholars on one side and engineers on the other, and it is a rare place where you can see a medieval quad and a car plant in one afternoon.

Fuel is no problem anywhere around the edge of town, and the best advice is to fill up before you come in rather than hunt for a station among the one-way systems. Coffee is everywhere, from tiny independent counters to the covered market stalls. When you are ready to leave, the Cotswold edge begins within half an hour to the west and north, and that is where the riding turns lovely again: stone villages, rolling lanes and the kind of gentle hills that make a rider forget the traffic. Come on a weekday morning if you can, and leave before the school run.
t.betws y coed@53.1,-3.8:
Betws-y-Coed is where Snowdonia gets its coat on. The village sits at the meeting of three valleys, the Conwy, the Llugwy and the Lledr, in a wooded hollow ringed by steep hills, and it has been a base for walkers, painters and tourists since the Victorian era. Stone houses and outdoor shops line the main street, and cafés serve large mugs of tea to damp hikers. The resident population is small, and in summer the village hosts many times that number.

The road through it is the A5, built by Thomas Telford as the great Holyhead road, linking London with the ferry for Ireland, and the cast-iron Waterloo Bridge that carries it over the Conwy was completed in 1815, the year of the battle it is named for. The old stone bridge of Pont-y-Pair, in the middle of the village, spans the Llugwy among rocks and pools, and a short walk upstream leads to the Swallow Falls, a noisy cascade that has drawn visitors for two centuries.

For riders this is wonderful country. The A5 climbs west toward Capel Curig and the pass beneath the peaks of the Glyderau, a road of long, open bends and big mountain views, and the road north along the Conwy valley runs fast and easy toward Llanrwst and the coast. The forest of Gwydir covers the hills nearby, with spruce and larch, and the lanes that wind through it are narrow and green. Rain is frequent and heavy, and the roads are often wet, so mind your speed and watch for sheep. In summer the traffic is thick at weekends.

Fuel is the thing to plan: the village is small, and the larger towns are some way off, with Colwyn Bay about twenty kilometres away, so fill up in advance. There are good tea rooms and pubs, and a railway line to Llandudno. Come out of season for the best of it, in the calm of a misty autumn morning, with the trees turning red and the river high.
t.birmingham@52.5,-1.9:
Birmingham claims more miles of canal than Venice, a boast that is almost certainly true and that tells you something about the city. It grew in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as a place that made things, buttons, guns, jewellery, steam engines, and the canals were the lanes that carried the raw metal in and the finished goods out. The thinkers of the Lunar Society, among them Matthew Boulton, James Watt and Joseph Priestley, met here at full moon so they could walk home by its light, and their dinner conversations helped shape the age of industry.

With nearly a million people, Birmingham is the second city of England and it feels like it: large, fast, a little rough, and full of surprises. The old canal basins around Brindleyplace have been turned into cafés and restaurants, the Jewellery Quarter still has working goldsmiths, and the Bull Ring market, which dates back to the twelfth century, has been rebuilt in aluminium discs and glass. Cadbury's model village at Bournville, just south, remains one of the more civilised experiments in industrial housing, and the Balti houses of Sparkhill and Sparkbrook have made the city a destination for curry.

Riding out of Birmingham is an exercise in patience and map reading. The ring roads and flyovers are dense and unforgiving, and the spaghetti of the Gravelly Hill interchange, a tangle of ramps built in 1972, is famous even to people who have never driven in England. Use the smaller roads and avoid the rush hour if you can. Once you reach the edges, the landscape opens, with Shropshire hills to the west for the Ironbridge Gorge ride and the Peak District to the north-east for the Derwent Valley mills.

Fuel is on every corner, and parking is best done at an out-of-centre garage. The city is cooler and wetter than you might expect, so carry a waterproof. After dark, the canal lights and restaurants make for a lively evening, and the city does not feel in the least bit asleep.
t.york@54.0,-1.1:
York wears its history openly. The Romans founded Eboracum here in 71 AD, and in 306 the army proclaimed Constantine emperor within its walls. The Vikings turned it into Jorvik, a trading city on the Ouse, and the medieval merchants who followed left a tangle of narrow streets, among them the Shambles, where overhanging timber houses lean so close that the neighbours could shake hands across the lane. The Minster, England's largest Gothic cathedral north of the Alps, rises over it all with a vast stained-glass window that took a craftsman years to make.

York is a walled city of some 150,000 people, and the walls, which you can walk for about three kilometres, are the best way to see it. Chocolate was once its great industry, with Rowntree's and Terry's both based here, and on certain days the old factory smell hung over the streets. Today the Jorvik Viking Centre and the railway museum are the biggest draws, and the city is crowded with visitors in summer and at Christmas.

For a rider, the centre is a trap. Traffic is restricted in many streets, there are one-way systems and pedestrian zones, and parking is expensive. Park at the edge and walk. The river Ouse floods regularly, covering the lower quays, and the water can reach the doors of the riverside pubs, so check the weather in winter. Fuel is easy on the ring road.

The surrounding country is a delight. To the north lie the Howardian Hills and the Yorkshire Wolds to the east, and the wide Vale of York is a patchwork of fields and villages. The ride to Saltaire passes through the old mill towns of West Yorkshire, where Sir Titus Salt built a model village for his workers in the 1850s, and the contrast between the elegant medieval city and the stern industrial grid is striking. Come back to York at dusk, when the Minster is floodlit and the cobbles glisten, and a pint in a low-beamed pub is the best way to end the day.
t.bristol@51.5,-2.6:
Bristol sits at the head of the Severn estuary, which has the second-highest tidal range in the world, and its history is the history of ships. In 1497 John Cabot set sail from here in a small vessel called the Matthew and reached the coast of North America, and for centuries the merchants of the city grew rich on trade, much of it, as the city now admits, on the back of the slave trade. Isambard Kingdom Brunel left his mark: the Clifton Suspension Bridge, which crosses the Avon gorge in a single graceful span, opened in 1864 after his death, and the SS Great Britain, his great iron steamship, is now a museum in the dock where she was built.

With over 600,000 people, Bristol is the biggest city in the south-west, and it has a lively, slightly rebellious character. The harbourside is crowded with bars, galleries and street art, and the work of the local artist Banksy appears on walls around the city. Hills are the dominant feature, and the streets of Clifton and Totterdown climb steeply, with brightly painted houses stacked against the slopes.

Riding in is no hardship, but the centre can be slow, with buses, one-way systems and clean-air rules, so check the city's current restrictions before you go. Out on the edges, the old Severn crossings give access to Wales, and the tolls that once burdened them were scrapped in 2018, which helps if you are heading west for the Blaenavon ride. To the south the Mendips rise in green limestone ridges, with the Cheddar Gorge a good run, and the coast road toward Dorset and Devon opens up wide views of sea and downs.

Fuel is easy, parking is manageable in the outer suburbs, and the city is full of places to eat, from fish and chips on the quay to a long Sunday lunch in a village pub. Mild, damp weather is normal, so pack a waterproof. A good day in Bristol ends at the water, with the ships moored, the lights on and the tide coming up the river.
t.london@51.5,-0.1:
London is the one place on the map where the best advice is to leave the bike at the edge. The centre around Charing Cross and Trafalgar Square is a maze of one-way streets, bus lanes, taxis and tourists, and parking is limited and expensive. The city also has a congestion charge and a low-emission zone, whose rules for motorcycles have changed over the years, so check the current conditions for your own machine before you ride in. For a start and finish, a quiet side street or a secure garage on the outskirts is a better plan.

What you are stopping for here is history on a large scale. St Martin-in-the-Fields, a handsome eighteenth-century church with a tall steeple and a classical portico, stands at the north-east corner of Trafalgar Square, and its crypt hosts a café, a gallery and a brass-rubbing centre. It is famous for its lunchtime concerts and for its work with homeless people. Across the road, Nelson's Column rises over the square, with its bronze lions, and the National Gallery stretches along the north side.

The city has some 7.5 million people, and it is never quite finished with itself. Roman Londinium was a muddy trading post on the Thames, and the medieval city grew into a great port, burning down in 1666 and rebuilding in brick and stone. Westminster, a short walk south, holds the Palace of Parliament and the Abbey, where English monarchs have been crowned for nearly a thousand years. The riding here is entirely about getting out: the A3, A4 and A40 lead to quiet lanes in Surrey, the Chilterns and Kent, and a very early start on a Sunday morning makes it easy.

Fuel is available, but it is among the most expensive in the country, so top up on the outskirts. For a drink, a pub in the side streets off Whitehall, with its brass and etched glass, is as London as it gets. And when the light fades, the square is full of buskers, pigeons and people, and the lamps along the Mall glow.
t.hurricane ridge@48.0,-123.5:
Hurricane Ridge is the high balcony of the Olympic Mountains, about sixteen miles of climbing from the sea at Port Angeles, reaching roughly 1,600 metres at the visitor centre. The road leaves the town, passes the national park entrance at Heart o' the Hills, and then winds up through Douglas fir and silver fir, with the forest thinning and the views opening out until the trees give way to alpine meadow. At the top, the whole range spreads out in front of you, jagged and white, with Mount Olympus sitting among the glaciers.

The riding is memorable but demanding. The road climbs steadily, and corners tighten as the grade steepens, with steep drops on the outside in places and few guardrails. Speed limits are low, and the national park rules apply: the road is also used by buses, campers and cyclists, so patience is part of the equipment. The best time is a clear morning in summer, when the light is sharp and the cloud has not yet formed on the peaks. Weather changes fast up here; it can be warm at the bottom and near freezing, windy and foggy at the top, so bring layers. The name itself comes from the gales that sweep the ridge.

Wildlife wanders the meadows, with black-tailed deer often grazing beside the car park and marmots whistling from the rocks. The Olympic marmot lives nowhere else in the world. In late spring and early summer, wildflowers carpet the slopes, and in winter the ridge becomes a small ski area, which means the road may close at times or require tyre chains. Check the park's road status before you go.

Fill the tank and eat properly in Port Angeles, about seventeen kilometres away, and bring water. The descent is a long one and hard on brakes, so use engine braking. Come back down in the late afternoon, when the Strait of Juan de Fuca glows below and the mountains of Vancouver Island float on the horizon.
t.port angeles@48.1,-123.4:
Port Angeles sits low on the northern edge of the Olympic Peninsula, facing the Strait of Juan de Fuca and, across the water, Vancouver Island. It is a working harbour town of some nineteen thousand people, with a long curved sandspit called Ediz Hook sheltering the port, a ferry that sails daily to Victoria in British Columbia, and a downtown of brick storefronts, bookshops and seafood spots. It is also the main gateway to Olympic National Park, which means it has what the rest of the peninsula lacks: choice.

For a rider doing the loop around the Olympic Peninsula, this is the logical place to fuel, eat and reorganise. The supermarkets, hardware stores and motels are all here, and so are the practical things nobody lists in guidebooks, like laundromats and a place to buy a spare tube. The national park visitor centre is on the edge of town and can tell you about road conditions on the Hurricane Ridge road, which closes in bad weather. Highway 101 runs right through, east toward Sequim and west toward Lake Crescent, so you are well placed.

The landscape here is a rain-shadow oddity. The Olympic Mountains block most of the Pacific moisture, so Port Angeles and neighbouring Sequim are much drier than the rainforests on the coast side. The town gets a fraction of the rain that falls at Forks, only fifty-odd miles away. The upshot is that the best riding weather is often right here, while the west side is under cloud. The sea air is cool, and fog can drift in during the summer mornings, burning off by midday.

Historically, the town grew around timber, fishing and shipping, and Coast Guard and naval history have left a mark. The waterfront is pleasant for a wander, with views over the strait to the Canadian mountains, and the fish and chips on the pier are a local ritual. Traffic on the main road gets heavy on summer weekends, when ferry arrivals and visitors to the park stack up. Start early, and use the town as a base before heading into the quiet forests to the west.
t.lake crescent@48.1,-123.8:
Lake Crescent is the kind of lake that makes you slow down without being asked. It fills a deep glacial trough in the north of Olympic National Park, roughly six hundred feet at its deepest, and the water is so clear and blue that on a calm day it looks lit from below. Steep forested ridges drop straight into it, with Storm King rising above the south shore. Port Angeles lies about twenty-seven kilometres east, and that is where you find fuel and a proper meal.

Highway 101 follows the lake's southern edge in a series of curves that hug the shoreline, with the forest pressing close on the uphill side and the water glittering through trees on the other. It is a narrow road with no real shoulders and a firm speed limit, shared with logging trucks, motorhomes and the occasional cyclist, so this is a ride to take at a gentle pace, watching the road and enjoying the scenery in the straights. In the morning the lake is often glassy and the light comes in at a low angle; by midday the shoreline fills with visitors.

The lake has a history of its own. Lake Crescent Lodge, a cluster of wooden buildings on the south shore, dates from the early twentieth century, and Franklin Roosevelt stayed in the area in 1937 on the trip that helped shape the national park. The lake is also home to a trout found nowhere else, the Beardslee, a quirk of isolation after the glaciers retreated. A short walk from the road leads to Marymere Falls through old-growth forest of fir, hemlock and cedar draped with moss.

Weather here is changeable. The park sits on the edge of one of the wettest regions in the lower forty-eight, and rain can arrive in minutes, making the road slick, especially under the trees where leaves and needles gather. A fleece and a rain shell make sense even in summer. The best months are July to September, though weekends are busy. Take your time, stop at a turn-out, and let the lake have your attention.
t.astoria@46.2,-123.8:
Astoria sits at the very mouth of the Columbia River, the last town of Oregon before the water spreads out into the Pacific, and it has the weathered, salt-cured look of a place that has spent two centuries facing wind. About ten thousand people live here, on steep streets of Victorian houses that climb a hill above the docks. It is the oldest American settlement west of the Rockies, founded in 1811 as a fur-trading post by John Jacob Astor's company, and Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1805 to 1806 camped nearby at Fort Clatsop, where a replica now stands.

The river and the bar are the stars. The Columbia meets the Pacific here in a stretch of shifting sandbars and violent weather that has wrecked hundreds of ships, earning the name Graveyard of the Pacific, and the Columbia River bar pilots still guide big freighters across it. The Astoria-Megler Bridge, a four-mile steel truss opened in 1966, carries Highway 101 across the river's mouth to Washington, and riding it, with the huge estuary below and the wind hammering, is a major event. The Astoria Column, a painted tower on a hilltop, offers a long view over the river, the bridge and the ocean when the clouds allow.

For the rider, Astoria is a lively place to rest. There is fuel, breakfast and plenty of seafood, and the waterfront has brewpubs, converted canneries and old piers where sea lions bark and bask. Fans of eighties film will recognise places from The Goonies, which was shot in the town. Weather is the major variable. Rain is frequent, fog rolls in, and the wind off the sea is cold even in summer, so proper rain gear is not optional.

Highway 101 runs south from here along the Oregon coast, with plenty of tight curves, sudden views and, in the wet, slick patches. The best time for the coast is late summer and early autumn, when skies clear and traffic thins. Winter storms bring spectacular waves but also fallen trees and slides. If you reach Astoria at the end of a day, find a table by the river and watch the light drain from the water.
t.seattle@47.6,-122.3:
Seattle runs on water. The city is squeezed between Puget Sound on the west and Lake Washington on the east, and is cut through by canals and bridges, so that every day involves a shore of some kind. Elliott Bay holds the working waterfront, with the ferry terminal at Colman Dock and the old piers, and ferries still carry commuters and tourists to Bainbridge Island and Bremerton, past a skyline that looks best from the deck.

The Space Needle, built for the 1962 World's Fair, is the symbol, and Pike Place Market, open since 1907, is the heart. Fishmongers throw salmon, flower sellers fill the aisles, and the first Starbucks opened nearby in 1971. Coffee culture is serious here, so the stop for a good espresso is no problem at all. On a clear day, Mount Rainier appears to the south as a huge white dome, seeming almost too large to be real, and the Olympic Mountains form a jagged wall to the west across the Sound.

The ride toward the Olympics starts with the ferry, which is part of the fun. You queue with the bike at the terminal, ride aboard, and cross the water in about half an hour, with gulls hanging off the stern. Beyond, the roads of the Kitsap and Olympic Peninsulas run through dark forest of Douglas fir and cedar, with curving, well-kept highways and moderate traffic. Rain is common from October to April, and the roads can be greasy, with moss and wet leaves. Summer is generally dry and bright, the best time for riding.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of more than six hundred thousand. Parking in the centre is expensive, so look for a lot with an attendant or use the ferry terminal area. Ferry lines can be long on summer weekends, so arrive early. Seattle drivers are generally courteous but freeway traffic jams are legendary, and the best hours for riding out of town are early morning or mid-day.
t.olympic national park@47.7,-123.4:
It lies in the park's interior, in the folded, glaciated heart of the range where no road goes, so a motorcyclist will only ever see the mountains from the edges. The Olympics rise straight out of Puget Sound and the Pacific, reaching nearly 2,400 metres at Mount Olympus, and they catch so much moisture from the ocean that their western valleys are among the wettest places in the continental United States.

That rain is the secret of the Hoh Rainforest, where Sitka spruce and western hemlock grow huge, draped with moss and ferns, and where several metres of rain fall in a typical year. The whole park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it protects both the high country and a long strip of wild coast. Roosevelt elk, named for the president who set aside this land, browse in the valleys, and black bears and marmots roam the meadows. Wolves are gone but the cougars remain.

For riding, the roads follow the outside. US 101 loops around the peninsula and gives long, gentle, forested curves with views of Lake Crescent, a deep glacial lake of astonishing blue. From Port Angeles, a steep road climbs seventeen miles to Hurricane Ridge, at about 1,600 metres, with wide views over snowy peaks, though fog and snow can close it. Roads leading to the Hoh and Quinault valleys are narrower and run through dark tunnels of trees.

Fuel is limited. The towns of Port Angeles, Sequim and Forks have stations, and the east side has services at Hoodsport and Shelton, but there is nothing at all deep in the park. Rain can come in any season, and temperatures at the ridge are much lower than on the coast, so pack layers. Ferry lines add time to the trip in summer, and the best weather runs from July to September. Take your time on the forest roads, because wet moss and fallen needles make the surface slick.
t.peak district@51.8,-0.5:
Dunstable Downs is the high point of this corner of England, and gliders use the ridge's updrafts nearly every fine day. It is the highest ground in Bedfordshire, and from the top the plain stretches north towards the Midlands.

The ride that ended here started in the Peak District, so the downs feel like a gentle echo of the hills. Roads along the escarpment are twisty and open, with sharp bends where they climb or drop, and the views on a clear day are wide. The surface is generally good, but busy roads like the A5 and M1 run close by. On a sunny weekend the car park at the top fills with kite-flyers and walkers, so mornings and weekdays are quieter. Whipsnade Zoo, on the same ridge, has a huge chalk lion carved into the hillside, visible for miles.

Markyate sits on Watling Street, the Roman road that became the A5, and the town grew as a stopping place for coaches and travellers. Its long high street is lined with old inns and houses, and the name of the street has been in use since Roman times. Nearby, chalk grassland on the downs is rich in wild flowers, including orchids and rare butterflies such as the chalkhill blue, which fly in July and August.

Fuel and food are easy at Dunstable, with large stations and supermarkets, and Markyate has a few shops and a pub. A visitor centre at the top of the downs has a cafe with a terrace and a view that suits a tired rider.

Stay a little while to watch the gliders turn above the slope. It is an easy way to enjoy the end of a long ride.
t.north wessex@51.5,-0.6:
Runnymede is a few minutes away, and it carries more weight than any other meadow in England. King John sealed Magna Carta there in June 1215, and a memorial stands on the riverbank, with another to John F. Kennedy on a hillside above.

It is a good place to finish a ride that crossed the Wessex Downs. The roads here are flat and busy, with traffic lights and roundabouts, and the surface is generally good, though patched in places. But Windsor Great Park, just south, has long straight avenues and quiet lanes, with ancient oaks and herds of deer, and the Long Walk, which runs three miles from the castle to the Copper Horse statue, is one of the finest avenues in the country. Vehicles are not allowed on the Long Walk, so park and walk.

The river is the real feature. The Thames here is wide and slow, with meadows, locks and boat houses, and swans and geese gather along the banks. Datchet has a pretty green, a village pub and a long bridge over the river, and Old Windsor has an old priory site and a church with a tower. The castle, which has been a royal residence for almost a thousand years, is the largest inhabited castle in the world, and its walls dominate the skyline for miles around.

Fuel is easy at Windsor and Old Windsor, with stations and supermarkets, and the streets of Windsor have cafes and pubs for every taste. A pint by the river, with the castle across the water, is a fine ending to a day.

Heathrow's flight path is nearby, so expect aircraft overhead, but the quiet of the meadow is a surprising contrast.
t.essex saltmarsh@51.6,-0.6:
Amersham is two towns in one. The old town, on the hill, has a broad high street of timbered inns and Georgian houses, while the newer town, down by the railway, grew up around the Metropolitan line, which ends here.

After a ride through Essex saltmarsh and Suffolk villages, this is a very different kind of finish. The roads here are narrow, steep and winding, with sunken lanes between high hedges, and the surface is often damp and covered with leaves in the woods. Traffic is light on the lanes and heavy on the main routes into London. In autumn the beeches turn copper, and the colours are outstanding, though wet leaves are slippery. The Chess valley, running south-west from Chesham, has a stream and watercress beds, and its lanes are among the prettiest in the area.

Amersham's history includes a dark chapter. In the early sixteenth century, a group of local Lollards, early dissenters, were burned for heresy, and a memorial on the hill commemorates the Amersham Martyrs. The town was also a popular filming location, with its old streets and inns appearing in several films and television series. Seer Green, a smaller village, has a quiet green and an old church.

Fuel and food are easy at Amersham, with stations, supermarkets and many cafes and pubs, especially on the old high street. A pub with a log fire is a good place to end a day in cold weather, and a picnic in the woods is good in summer. Red kites, reintroduced to the Chilterns in the 1990s, wheel above the fields and are an almost certain sight.

Look up as you park the bike. The kites are the best part of the arrival.
t.stow on the wold@51.9,-1.7:
Stow-on-the-Wold sits high. At roughly two hundred and fifty metres, it is the highest town in the Cotswolds, and the wind across its market square is famously keen. Old roads meet here, including the Roman Fosse Way, which runs along the edge of the town, and the place has been a market since the Middle Ages.

The ride's earlier legs crossed Essex and Suffolk, so the Cotswolds are a very different sort of country. The honey-coloured limestone of the buildings is the first thing you notice, and the lanes around Stow are lined with drystone walls and grassy verges. The roads are narrow and quiet, with gentle bends and short hills, and the surface is mostly good, though cracked in places. In summer, the lanes fill with visitors, so try to come early in the morning or late in the evening, and in winter, ice can linger in the shadows.

The wool trade made Stow rich, and the enormous market square, big enough to hold thousands of sheep, is a reminder. The church of St Edward has a north door framed by two ancient yew trees, which is said to have inspired Tolkien, though the claim is not certain. The last battle of the first English Civil War was fought nearby in 1646, when the Royalists were defeated, and many prisoners were held in the church. Two horse fairs are still held every year, in May and October, and draw large crowds.

Fuel is a point to consider: Stow is small, with about two thousand people, so fill the tank in a bigger town before you arrive. The town has many tea rooms, antique shops and pubs, and the cheese and chutney shops are good for snacks. A bench in the square is the ideal place to eat.

Walk round the square, read the old stones, and enjoy the hush that falls when the coaches leave.
t.barnstaple@51.1,-4.1:
Barnstaple lies at the head of the Taw estuary, and it claims to be one of the oldest boroughs in England, with a charter said to date from the tenth century. It is the largest town in North Devon, and it is the natural start for the Atlantic Highway.

The A39, named the Atlantic Highway, runs west and south-west along the coast, passing through Bideford, Clovelly, Hartland and the Cornish border, with long climbs, tight bends and sudden views of the Atlantic. The road is good in places, rough in others, and often narrow, with high Devon hedges that hide oncoming traffic. In summer, the roads fill with holiday traffic, and the best time to ride is early in the morning or in the quieter shoulder seasons. Rain and sea fog are common, and the wind off the Atlantic can be strong on the exposed sections.

The landscape around Barnstaple is rich in story. Henry Williamson wrote Tarka the Otter here, and the Tarka Trail, a long walking and cycling route, follows the old railway along the river. Braunton Burrows, a huge dune system near the estuary, is a nature reserve with rare plants and a biosphere status. To the east lies Exmoor, with its wild red deer and open moor, which makes a fine detour.

Fuel and food are easy in Barnstaple, with large stations, supermarkets and many cafes, and it is wise to fill up here, as stations become less frequent west of Bideford. The quayside has pubs and restaurants with views over the river.

Set off early. The coast ahead rewards an unhurried pace, and the first light on the estuary is a very good start.
t.fraser canyon@49.8,-121.4:
When the Fraser River squeezes through the Coast Mountains between Hope and Lytton, it makes a canyon so narrow and steep that the railways, the highway and the river have to share it. This is the end of the ride, and it is a worthy one. The road clings to cliffs above the water, plunges through tunnels, and crosses the river on bridges with views straight down.

The canyon has a history of gold and hardship. In 1858, tens of thousands of prospectors came up the river after gold was found there, and the colony of British Columbia was created partly to control them. Miners built trails along the cliffs, and later the Cariboo Wagon Road was blasted into the walls, reaching Barkerville and the goldfields far to the north. The two transcontinental railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, followed in the early twentieth century, one on each side of the river, and you can sometimes see long freight trains crawling through the tunnels on the far bank.

At Hell's Gate, a few kilometres south of Boston Bar, the river is forced into a channel only thirty-five metres wide, and the whole flow, which can be huge in the spring melt, thunders through it. An airtram carries visitors across the gorge. The narrows once blocked the passage of salmon, when a rockslide during railway construction in 1914 made it impassable, and fishways were built to help them. The salmon runs still pass through in late summer and autumn.

The highway has seven tunnels between Yale and Boston Bar, some of them narrow, with low ceilings, so check for dripping water and slippery patches inside. Rockfalls and landslides are a known risk, particularly in the wet season, and the road can close at short notice, so check DriveBC before you go. Summers are hot in the canyon, particularly near Lytton, which has set records for heat, and winter brings snow and ice. Fuel is found in Boston Bar and in Hope to the south, with Lytton to the north. The village has a few cafes and motels, and the view of the river from the road is worth a pause.
t.mount st@47.2,-122.2:
Bonney Lake sits on a plateau east of Puget Sound, at the edge of the suburban sprawl that spreads out from Tacoma and Seattle, and on a clear day Mount Rainier fills the horizon as a vast white wall. The mountain, at over four thousand metres, is such a presence that it seems closer than it is, and locals check it each morning the way other people check the weather. It is a very large volcano, officially active, and the city is built in the path of its mudflows, a fact that the county takes seriously.

The town itself is modern and unassuming, with shopping centres, subdivisions and a fine lake, but its location is useful. A short ride east on State Route 410 takes you to Enumclaw and then up the White River valley to the Crystal Mountain turn-off and Chinook Pass, one of the best mountain roads in Washington, which winds through old-growth forest to the foot of Rainier's slopes and over a pass at about sixteen hundred and seventy metres. The pass is closed by snow in winter, usually from November to May. Closer to town, the plateau roads around Lake Tapps and Sumner have a pleasant rural feel, with farmland and views of the mountain between the trees.

After a day in the volcanic landscape of Mount St. Helens, the wide, quiet roads of the plateau make a gentle finish. The traffic on SR 410 can be heavy at commuting hours, with long lines of cars heading to and from the Tacoma and Seattle suburbs, so avoid the late-afternoon crush if you can. Watch for deer and for wet roads under the firs, particularly in autumn.

Bonney Lake has about twenty thousand people, with petrol stations, supermarkets and plenty of chain restaurants, and Sumner, nearby, has a small, pleasant main street with cafés. There is no shortage of services, so there is no need to fret over range.

On a clear evening, stop at a viewpoint and watch the alpenglow on Rainier. It turns pink and then fades to blue, and the mountain's presence is oddly calming.
t.chuckanut drive@47.3,-121.9:
Black Diamond is a coal town that outlived its coal. In the 1880s, a coal company opened mines on this ridge in the foothills south-east of Seattle, and for decades the town sent coal by railway to ships in Seattle and San Francisco. Miners from Wales, Italy, Slovenia and many other countries lived in company houses, and a nearby ghost town, Franklin, was abandoned after a disaster in 1894. The mines closed in the early twentieth century, and today the town is a quiet place of old frame buildings, a railroad museum and a famous bakery.

The bakery is the main attraction for riders. Black Diamond Bakery has been baking bread in a wood-fired oven since 1902, and the smell of fresh loaves and cinnamon rolls drifts down Railroad Avenue on weekend mornings, drawing a steady stream of cyclists and motorcyclists. It is one of those stops where a pastry and a coffee feel earned, and the line moves faster than you might expect. Opening hours vary, so look before you plan around it.

The roads around Black Diamond are the draw. Highway 169 runs through the Green River Gorge, a steep wooded canyon with a good surface and bends that suit a relaxed rider, and the back roads around Ravensdale and Covington wind through forest and farmland. Enumclaw, twelve kilometres east, is the gateway to Mount Rainier and the high country on Route 410. Traffic is moderate except at commuting hours, and deer and logging trucks are the main hazards.

Black Diamond has just over four thousand people, with a small supermarket, a few places to eat and a petrol station, and Enumclaw, with more than eleven thousand, has bigger shops and every service you might need. There is no problem with fuel anywhere around here.

The old Chuckanut Drive, the ride's namesake, is far to the north near Bellingham, and that is a very different scene of cliff roads above Samish Bay. This corner is a gentler, more domestic ending, with the smell of bread in the air.
t.sunrise road@46.9,-121.6:
Sunrise is the highest point in Mount Rainier National Park that you can reach by road, about 6,400 feet above the sea, and the view from the car park is the one that makes people stop mid-sentence. From here the mountain, a volcano of 14,411 feet that is the highest in the Cascade Range, stands only a few miles away across a bowl of meadows and moraines, with the Emmons Glacier, the biggest in the contiguous United States by area, spilling down its flank. On a clear day it is almost too large to take in.

The road to get there is the White River Road, branching from State Route 410, which itself climbs through fir and hemlock forest to Chinook Pass, at about 5,400 feet. The final switchbacks to Sunrise are steep and tight, climbing about three thousand feet in a few miles, with big drops at the edge and the mountain appearing and vanishing between the trees. The surface is generally good, but frost heaves and patches do appear, and fog and cloud can hide the view completely, so go on a clear day. The road is only open in the snow-free season, usually from early July until October, and it can close at short notice in early storms. A park entrance fee applies.

At the top, wildflowers fill the meadows in July and August, with lupine, paintbrush and avalanche lilies, and marmots whistle from the rocks. Mountain goats may be seen on the cliffs, and the weather is cool and breezy even in summer, so a warm layer is a good idea. Trails lead out from the car park to viewpoints. At this height you may feel the thinner air.

A visitor centre and snack bar operate in summer, with limited hours. The best light is in the morning, and the crowds arrive by noon, so an early start pays. In autumn the huckleberry leaves turn red across the slopes, and the first snow dusts the peak. Check the National Park Service website for road conditions before setting out.
t.packwood food@46.6,-121.7:
Packwood is a small town on the south side of Mount Rainier, on US 12 in the Cowlitz Valley, about twenty miles west of the White Pass summit, and it has long been a place where people stop for something to eat. The population is only a few hundred, but the town has a handful of cafes, a general store and a gas station, and in a stretch of road with very little else, that counts as a metropolis. It is known locally for its flea market, held in summer, which has grown into a large gathering of vendors and visitors.

The valley is forested and steep, with the Cowlitz River running over boulders and the snowy bulk of the Goat Rocks Wilderness to the east. Rainier itself is hidden behind ridges from town, but a road runs north to the park's Ohanapecosh entrance, through old-growth forest of Douglas fir and western red cedar, some of the tallest trees in the park. The state highways around here are well surfaced, with smooth bends and a limit that fits the terrain, and they are very good for riding, especially in the early morning when the mist hangs over the river.

US 12 over White Pass, at about 4,500 feet, is one of the quieter crossings of the Cascades, and the road from Packwood winds up through forest to the ski area at the summit and then drops into the dry country of the east side. Rain falls here heavily on the west side, and the change on the other side is dramatic, with ponderosa pine and sage replacing the cedar and moss. Take rain gear, as showers are frequent even in summer, and expect cold on the pass.

Summer is the main season, when the road is dry and the passes are open, and the autumn colours of the vine maple are a bonus.
t.mount rainier viewpoint@46.9,-121.8:
Mount Rainier is not a mountain that you view casually. At 14,411 feet it rises more than two miles above the lowlands of Puget Sound, a huge, ice-capped volcano with some twenty-five named glaciers, visible on a clear day from Seattle, Tacoma and as far away as Portland. The Puyallup and Nisqually people called it Tahoma or Tacoma, and the name Rainier was given by Captain George Vancouver in 1792, in honour of a friend in the navy. It is considered an active volcano, and the scientists who study it keep a close watch, because the ice and mud on its flanks could flow in great lahars down the valleys to the suburbs below.

On a clear day the white dome appears above the green hills, and the sight can be startling when you come around a bend. The weather in the Cascades is a gamble, and the mountain is often hidden by cloud for days, so a clear morning is worth taking, especially in summer and early autumn.

The roads of the foothills are quiet, narrow and forested, with moderate bends, and pavement that varies from smooth to patched. Moss and fir needles can make the surface slick, and the damp lingers under the canopy. Logging trucks use some of the roads, so give them room. The nearest fuel is at Eatonville, about thirty-eight kilometres away, a small town with a pioneer feel, and at larger towns toward Tacoma, so check your tank. Cell coverage can be patchy.

Spring and autumn are rainy, and the best time for a view is July to September. In winter, snow closes the high roads, and the white cone dominates the horizon. Wildlife includes deer, elk and black bears, and in the old forest you may hear the call of a pileated woodpecker. Pack water and a layer, since the air cools quickly in the evening.
t.snoqualmie and yakima canyon@47.5,-121.9:
Snoqualmie Falls drops two hundred and sixty-eight feet over a granite ledge, about a hundred feet farther than Niagara, and it sounds like a train. The Snoqualmie River pours into the gorge in a column of white, and a pale mist rises from the pool below, drifting over the viewing platform. For the Snoqualmie people, the falls are sacred, a place where the mist rising from the water connects the earth to the sky, and they still hold ceremonies there. The Salish Lodge, a handsome hotel perched at the lip, has become a landmark in its own right, and its restaurant has long been popular for breakfast, though bookings help.

The town of Snoqualmie, with thirteen thousand people, is close to the falls and has a bit of the logging-town charm that it was founded on. Next door at North Bend, a few miles up the valley, Twede's Cafe and the surrounding hills were used for the filming of Twin Peaks, the cult television series, and fans still come to find the diner and the cherry pie, and Mount Si, the jagged peak behind the town, looks every bit the part.

For a rider, this is the doorstep of the Cascades. Interstate 90 runs up the valley to Snoqualmie Pass, about three thousand feet, and the older roads on the valley floor offer a quieter way with long curves and forest. The surface is mostly good, but rain makes it slick, and traffic builds on weekends when hikers head for Mount Si and the trails. Look out for cyclists in the valley, and for fog in the morning.

The town has fuel stations, supermarkets and many places to eat, and the area around the falls has a large car park and a short walk to the viewing platform. A trail leads to the base of the falls, about half a mile, and is steep on the way back. The falls are at their best in winter and spring, when the river is full, and in summer they thin to a pale veil. Rain is likely, so take waterproofs. In winter, ice sometimes forms on the cliffs beside the falls, and the whole scene is silent and white.
t.snoqualmie and@47.4,-122.4:
Vashon Island is reached only by water, which has kept it quieter, greener and somewhat more eccentric than the mainland. Orchards, small farms, craft studios and a few galleries make up most of the economy, and locals take pride in a certain independent streak.

The island has long been known for its fruit, and strawberries in particular were a major crop in the early twentieth century, when Japanese American farmers supplied much of the Seattle market. Their families were removed from the island and interned during the Second World War, a painful chapter that the community remembers. Every July, the Strawberry Festival fills the main street with a parade, music and pie.

The riding is the reason to come. Vashon Highway and the lesser roads loop around the island, climbing and falling through forest and farmland with a chain of gentle bends, little traffic and good views of water through the trees. The surface is mostly smooth, but there are occasional patches of gravel, and the narrow roads can be slippery after rain. Deer are common, particularly at dusk, and local drivers tend to go slowly. Point Robinson, on Maury Island, has a small lighthouse on a spit of land with a view across to Mount Rainier and Seattle's skyline.

Ferries run from Fauntleroy in West Seattle and from Southworth on the Kitsap side, and there is also a passenger ferry from downtown. Vehicle ferries can have long queues in summer and on weekends, so check the schedule and allow time. Bikes usually go aboard at the front.

Vashon town has about ten thousand people across the island, with a petrol station, a small supermarket, bakeries and a few cafés. There is not much fuel elsewhere on the island, so fill up in town before a long loop. On a quiet weekday, the whole island has the feel of a place that has chosen to be slow.
t.cascade loop@47.8,-122.3:
Kenmore sits at the top of Lake Washington, where the Sammamish River slips in and the long freshwater lake that defines eastern Seattle finally runs out of room. For a rider coming back from the North Cascades Highway, this is the last relaxed corner before the city.

The lake is the main character. Lake Washington was lowered by about nine feet around 1916, when the Ship Canal and the Hiram Chittenden Locks linked it with Puget Sound, and the change left the old shoreline high and dry and turned the water from a fresh, slow lake into a busy boating channel. At Kenmore, the Kenmore Air Harbor is a base for seaplanes that fly to the San Juan Islands and British Columbia, and you can watch them land and take off on the lake. Locals say the sound of a floatplane is the soundtrack of summer.

The Burke-Gilman Trail, an old railroad right of way, runs along the shore, and on a fine weekend it is packed with cyclists, runners and families, making the roads near it busy. Bothell, just beyond, has a restored old town and a river path. On the north side of the lake, the roads that climb through Lake Forest Park have tight bends under tall firs, though the speed limits are low and the neighbours are watchful.

The key issue for a rider is traffic. State Route 522 is one of the busiest roads in the north end, and at commuting hours it moves slowly, so avoid it between about four and six in the afternoon. Highway 9, to the east, is a quieter way to head north to Snohomish and Monroe, with farm views and a mix of curves and straights.

The area has all the services you need, with petrol stations and supermarkets on every main road. Lake Forest Park's Town Center has coffee shops and a good bookstore, and Kenmore has several restaurants on the waterfront.

Park for a minute at Log Boom Park and watch the water. In the evening, the light across the lake can be golden.
t.kootenay rockies@49.1,-123.2:
It is a landscape that looks empty and is not: each tide carries it from shining water to glistening mud and back, and every square metre is grazed by birds.

The Fraser delta lies on one of the major bird migration routes of the Americas, and the flats and marshes here, including the nearby Reifel Bird Sanctuary, support hundreds of thousands of birds in winter and spring. Western sandpipers arrive in huge flocks in April and May, feeding on the biofilm that coats the mud, and at certain times of year the whole shore seems to ripple with their flight. Bald eagles, peregrine falcons and short-eared owls hunt over the grass. Seals haul out on sandbanks, and at the right season, salmon pass through on their way upriver.

Steveston, the old fishing village at the south-west corner of Richmond, is the nearest settlement and the best place to get your bearings. It was once one of the busiest salmon canning centres in the world, home to dozens of canneries and a large Japanese Canadian fishing community, which was forcibly removed in 1942. The Gulf of Georgia Cannery, now a national historic site, preserves the machinery and stories of that period. The boardwalk along the working harbour is lined with fish stalls where you can buy prawns or salmon straight off the boat, and the fish and chips are widely praised.

The ride along the river dyke from Steveston to Garry Point is flat and quiet, with a path used by cyclists and walkers, and the main roads of Richmond are straight and busy. Traffic on Steveston Highway slows to a crawl at commuting hours. A day starting at the Kootenays, in the high interior, is a long way from here, but the Fraser Valley freeway brings you down to the sea in a few hours.

Richmond has more than enough fuel, restaurants and shops. Garry Point Park is a good place to fly a kite or watch the sunset over the Strait, with a great view of the mountains of Vancouver Island on a clear evening.
t.hastings cliffs@51.1,-0.2:
The land here rolls in long ridges of sandstone, with deep ghylls, the local word for a wooded stream valley, cut between them. It is pretty, in an unshowy way: small fields, oak woods, white-painted weatherboard on the farm buildings, and every junction signed for somewhere with an unlikely name.

The thing that most people notice is the Ouse Valley Viaduct near Balcombe, which carries the London to Brighton railway across the river on thirty-seven arches of pale brick. It was opened in the early 1840s, and its stone balustrades and pavilions were designed to make it look less like an industrial thing and more like a feature in a park. You can see it from a footpath and a couple of lanes, and it is worth a minute even if you do not care about railways. Nearby, Nymans garden at Handcross is a National Trust property with a ruined house and a very good collection of plants, and it makes a decent excuse for a stop if the rain starts.

The riding is fun in the old, unsophisticated way. The B2036 and the lanes between Balcombe, Staplefield and Cuckfield offer tight bends, patchy surfaces and a lot of mud after rain, so keep your speed honest and watch for horse riders. The A23 runs close to the east and carries the main London to Brighton traffic, which is a reminder of how near the capital is, and on a Sunday afternoon its southbound lanes can be solid. The nearest big shops and fuel stations are at Maidenbower and Crawley a few miles north, and Handcross has a village pub and a garage within reach. If you plan to run low, do not trust a village.

As a place on a route home, this is a good one to have at the end: gentle, wooded, close to the motorway but far enough from it to keep a sense of the countryside for a little longer.
t.burford stone street@51.8,-1.6:
Burford's High Street drops down a hill so steeply that you can see the roofs below you before you see the street, and it ends in a medieval stone bridge over the River Windrush. That one view is the whole reason to stop. The town grew rich on Cotswold wool in the Middle Ages, and the honey-coloured limestone houses with their tilted stone-tiled roofs, the big church and the arched doorways all date from that prosperity. Later it became a coaching stop between Oxford and the west, and some of the old inns still serve travellers.

History comes in a harder form too. In 1649, at the height of the Civil War's political chaos, Cromwell's troops crushed a mutiny of Levellers, the radical soldiers who wanted a wider vote and fairer laws, and locked several hundred of them in Burford church. Three leaders were shot against its wall the next morning, and the town still marks the day each May. Nothing in the quiet street prepares you for it. A few miles east, the ruins of Minster Lovell Hall stand on the riverbank, and the village of Swinbrook, where the Mitford sisters grew up, is also nearby.

The riding around here is gentle and good for a slow day. The A361 and the lanes along the Windrush valley run through small stone villages, past fields bounded by dry-stone walls and sheep in neat blocks. Surfaces are generally fine, though a lot of lorries use the A40 close by. Traffic in the street itself is slow on weekends, with coaches and visitors on foot, and parking a bike on the High Street is easy if you tuck it in among the cars. Go early and the town is almost empty, with the smell of baking drifting out of the bakery doors.

Burford is a small place of barely twelve hundred people, so for fuel, plan on Carterton, about six kilometres away, which is a proper town of sixteen thousand with supermarkets and filling stations. For food you are well served. There are tea rooms, pubs with log fires and a couple of delis, all of which cater to the sort of walkers and riders who arrive tired and wet in autumn.
t.broadway tower ridge@52.0,-1.8:
A Cotswold escarpment does not announce itself from the Vale of Evesham side; you simply turn a corner at Broadway and the road tilts upward, steeply, toward a tower on the skyline. Broadway Tower is a folly, built in 1798 for the Earl of Coventry on one of the highest points of the Cotswolds, at about three hundred and twelve metres. It was designed to look like a small castle and to be seen from the earl's estate far to the west, and the legend says that on a clear day you can see sixteen counties from the top.

The climb up Fish Hill is a proper test for a loaded bike, with a steady gradient, a couple of hairpin-like bends and a wide view back over the vale as you gain height. At the top, the tower sits in a country park, with grass, sheep and a car park, and the wind is nearly always blowing. Autumn and winter mornings can bring mist in the vale below while the ridge stays clear, and the sunrises are memorable. Weekends bring crowds, so if you want the view with some peace, go early on a weekday.

The story of the tower includes an interesting piece of Victorian history. William Morris, the designer and founder of the Arts and Crafts movement, rented the tower as a retreat in the 1880s, and it became a gathering place for artists and writers. The honey-coloured Cotswold limestone, formed in warm seas about a hundred and seventy million years ago, is the material of the villages below, and it glows gold in low sun, especially in Broadway and Chipping Campden.

Broadway, about two and a half kilometres away, has a good choice of tea rooms, pubs and shops along a wide green-lined high street, and it makes a handsome place for a break, though it is busy in summer. Chipping Campden is smaller but just as lovely. Fuel is not abundant in the villages, so plan around Evesham, about eleven kilometres away, which is a proper town of over twenty thousand people. Bring a windproof layer, since the ridge always seems to be colder than the valley.
t.south downs@51.7,-0.1:
Waltham Cross takes its name from one of the most moving things a medieval king ever built. When Queen Eleanor of Castile died in 1290, her husband Edward I had her body carried from Lincolnshire to London, and at each place the funeral procession stopped overnight he put up a stone cross. Only three of the twelve survive, and the one at Waltham Cross, with its carved figures of the queen and its pinnacles, is the most complete. It stands in the middle of the high street, among bus stops and cafés, and most people walk past it.

The town sits on the River Lea and the old Roman road, Ermine Street, on the line where Hertfordshire meets Essex and Greater London. Close by, in Waltham Abbey, are the ruins of a church said to have been where King Harold was buried after Hastings, and the Royal Gunpowder Mills, which for centuries produced explosives for the Navy and the army and are now open as a museum and nature reserve. The M25 crosses overhead at a busy junction, so the noise is constant. Further north the Lea Valley has reservoirs and wide marshes, with herons and kingfishers.

For a rider this is an edge place. It is where the suburbs finish and you can head north into the Hertfordshire lanes or east into the quiet Essex farmland around Epping, and equally the point where the fast roads, the A10 and the M25, take over for the journey home. The streets in the centre are mostly one-way, often congested, and not much fun. The reward is behind you: the cut-through lanes toward Cheshunt, Goffs Oak and Theobalds Park are short and shady, and on a weekday morning they are good practice for a slow, steady pace.

A couple of kilometres away you are in Enfield, with about a hundred thousand people, so fuel and food are everywhere. In Waltham Cross itself there are a number of cafés, takeaways and a big supermarket with a fuel station, and the pubs along the high street serve a Sunday lunch to bikers and cyclists alike. It is not a place for contemplation, but the cross is worth thirty seconds and a photo.
t.bude@50.8,-4.5:
Bude is where the long Atlantic Highway comes to a stop against the sea. The town sits at the top of north Cornwall, on a coast of black, folded cliffs and long sandy beaches, with big Atlantic swells rolling in and surfers in the water at almost every hour of daylight. It is not a pretty harbour town in the manner of south Cornwall; it is a windy, bright, slightly salty place, with a canal, a sea pool and a handful of old streets behind the beach.

The sea pool at Summerleaze beach is a good example of the town's character. It is a large tidal pool built in the 1930s into the rocks and filled by the sea at high tide, giving a place for safe swimming in clear water, and it is free. The old Bude Canal, which was built in the early nineteenth century to carry sea sand inland for farmers, ends at the sea lock beside the beach, and it is a handsome piece of industrial heritage. Beyond the town, the cliffs hold the dishes of a military communications station, which stands out strangely against the coast.

The ride in along the A39 is a moderate affair, with some fast open sections, plenty of roundabouts and a good chance of holiday traffic, particularly in July and August. The finest riding is on the lanes to the south and north, where the coastal roads wind through hedge-lined valleys to tiny harbours and clifftop viewpoints. Be careful on those lanes: they are narrow, with high Cornish hedges and blind bends, and sand and gravel often lie on the surface after a storm.

Bude has about seven thousand people and every service you might need, with fuel on the approach roads, a supermarket and plenty of cafés, pasty shops and fish-and-chip bars. Parking near the beach can be tight in summer, but the town has pay car parks within a short walk. The weather changes fast on this coast, with fog, wind and sudden showers, so carry waterproofs, and enjoy the end of the road with a cup of tea facing the waves.
t.box hill rider@51.3,-0.3:
Box Hill is the Surrey Hills' best-known bump, and it earns its fame. The hill rises sharply from the valley of the River Mole to a crest of chalk grassland and ancient box trees, from which the land falls away in a wide view toward the South Downs. It is a National Trust property, and it has been a favourite day out for Londoners since the railway came to Dorking in the nineteenth century. The poet John Keats finished part of Endymion in the inn below the hill, and Jane Austen set a famous picnic scene on its slopes in Emma.

The road up is the Zig Zag, a series of well-graded hairpins that climb the north face, and it is well known among riders and even more among cyclists, who test themselves against it all year round. It was part of the road race route at the 2012 Olympics, which brought a new wave of visitors. The corners are wide and the surface generally good, but they are busy at weekends, with groups of riders and cyclists, so ride carefully and do not overtake on the bends. The cafe at the top is a well-known meeting point.

The nature here is distinctive. Box Hill is one of the few places in Britain where native box grows wild, along with yew and juniper, and the chalk grassland supports orchids and butterflies in early summer. The air is clean and the light on the slopes is soft in the morning. In autumn the beech woods turn gold, and the view over the Weald is at its best after rain, when the haze lifts.

Dorking, about two and a half kilometres away, has about seventeen thousand people and has stations, supermarkets and a good range of cafés, so that is where to fuel. Great Bookham is another option. At the hill itself, the National Trust has a visitor centre and a cafe, but the car park fills early on fine days. If you plan to start here, arrive before nine o'clock on a weekend, when the road is quiet and the riders are only beginning to appear.
t.ditchling beacon@50.9,-0.1:
Ditchling Beacon is the highest point on the South Downs in East Sussex, at 248 metres, and the way up from the north is steep enough to make a loaded bike grumble. The lane leaves the village of Ditchling and climbs the scarp in a series of narrow bends, with a gradient that is a serious test for cyclists, who treat it as a rite of passage, since the London to Brighton charity ride famously ends with this climb. A motorcycle takes it in its stride, but there is little room to pass, so patience is needed.

At the top, the land opens into a wide, open grass hilltop with a view that justifies the climb. To the north lies the Weald, a green, wooded plain stretching away to the horizon, and to the south the Downs roll toward Brighton and the sea, a pale glimmer on clear days. The summit carries the earthworks of an Iron Age hill fort, a ring of banks and ditches built more than two thousand years ago, and the whole hilltop is a nature reserve of chalk grassland, rich in wild flowers and butterflies in summer.

The wind is the thing to watch. The Beacon is exposed, and a stiff breeze coming off the Channel can be strong and cold, even in summer, so bring a windproof layer and keep a firm grip when getting on and off the bike at the car park. Weekends are busy with walkers, cyclists and dog owners, and the car park fills early on fine days. Mornings are quieter, and sunsets from the top are worth waiting for.

Nearby Ditchling is a village of about fifteen hundred people, with old flint cottages, a museum and a couple of pubs, and it was once home to a community of artists and craftspeople. It is a good place for coffee or a bite, but fuel is limited. Hassocks, about five kilometres away, is a small town with a station and shops, while Brighton, a short ride south, offers everything. Fill up in one of those before you tackle the Downs, because the roads beyond are quiet and the pumps are far apart.
t.box@51.3,-0.3:
Box Hill is the great chalk lump south of Leatherhead, where the River Mole cuts through the North Downs and leaves a steep slope of box trees, yews and wildflower grassland on one side. The box trees give the hill its name, and it is one of the few places in Britain where they grow wild. The National Trust looks after much of it. Down by the river at Burford Bridge, the poet John Keats finished his poem Endymion in 1817, and Jane Austen set the famously awkward picnic in Emma on the hill.

Riders know it for the zig-zag road, a set of nine or so hairpins that climbs the northern slope in a long series of bends. It was a part of the 2012 Olympic cycling road race, and ever since it has been busy with cyclists, especially at weekends, so ride it with respect. The road is smooth and well graded, the bends are open enough to see through, and the view from the top car park over the Weald is wide and calm. It is a good road to ride slowly and well, and it rewards a smooth line more than speed.

The café at the top has been a meeting place for bikers for decades, and on Sunday mornings dozens of machines line up there, from vintage Triumphs to modern sports bikes. It is a good place to look at other people's bikes, drink tea and trade stories. Police patrols and speed checks are common, and noise complaints from residents have led to a firmer line on loud exhausts, so keep it civil. Wet leaves in autumn can make the bends greasy.

Dorking, about three kilometres away, has fuel stations, supermarkets and pubs, and Great Bookham has a few more. If you want a quiet visit, come on a weekday or at dawn, when the mist lies in the valley below and the box trees smell sharp and green. Put your bike on its stand, walk a few hundred yards on the path along the ridge, and you will feel a long way from London.
t.new@51.3,-0.2:
Ewell and Cheam are two of the old villages that London swallowed in the twentieth century, on the border between Surrey and the capital, with Nonsuch Park between them. That park holds the secret. In 1538 Henry VIII began building a palace here, meant to be so grand there would be none like it, and he named it Nonsuch. It was never finished in his lifetime and was demolished in the 1680s after Charles II gave it to a mistress who sold the materials to pay her gambling debts. The site was lost for centuries and was found again by archaeologists in the 1950s, and the park remains as a wide expanse of grass and trees, with the old mansion house of a later era at its edge.

Ewell itself is older. The Hogsmill river rises from springs in the village, and its clear water was enough to power mills for centuries. The village has a few timbered cottages and a pond, and the parish church tower is a medieval survivor. Nearby is the great racecourse on Epsom Downs, where the Derby has been run since 1780, and its grandstand is visible from the surrounding roads.

For a rider, this is the last leg. The A24 and A217 lead north through a long run of suburban streets to the city, and the lanes toward Banstead and Tadworth offer a little more interest, with brief runs of hedgerow and open downs. Crowds appear on Derby day in early June, when the roads are closed or heavily congested around the racecourse, so check first. Otherwise it is steady, calm riding with little excitement.

With forty thousand people in Ewell alone, plus Cheam and Sutton close by, everything is easy. Filling stations stand along the A240 and the Ewell bypass, and there are plenty of cafés in the village and in the big shopping streets. A bike can be parked in Nonsuch Park for a modest fee, and a short walk across the grass is a decent way to loosen up before the final push home.
t.manchester@53.5,-2.2:
Manchester invented a good part of the modern world and then spent a century being too busy to brag about it. The first passenger railway station anywhere, Liverpool Road, opened here in 1830, the Bridgewater Canal brought coal into the city, and the mills of Cottonopolis spun and wove so much cloth that the damp red-brick warehouses became the model for industrial cities from Osaka to Massachusetts. The Cooperative movement began a few miles north in Rochdale, and the splitting of the atom was first achieved at the university here. Karl Marx's friend Friedrich Engels ran a mill in the city and wrote about its slums.

It is a tough, funny, welcoming place, and the old mills along the canals now hold flats, bars and offices. The Northern Quarter has independent record shops and the kind of cafés where the barista also plays in a band. The rain is real, but the stereotype is a little unfair; a fine Sunday morning here, with sunlight on the canal basins at Castlefield, is as good as anywhere. Football is a religion, with two enormous clubs on the east and west sides, so do not talk about it unless you mean it.

For a rider, though, the point of Manchester is what lies east. Within forty minutes you can be on the Pennines. The A57 Snake Pass climbs from Glossop to about 500 metres across wild moorland and drops into the Derwent valley, and the A537 over the Cat and Fiddle is another famous, exposed road with a long record of crashes and a firm speed limit. Beyond them lie Buxton, Castleton and the Peak District, with limestone dales, reservoirs and a thousand sheep. Moorland weather changes in minutes, and ice can linger on the high roads into April, so dress for a different season than the city's.

Leaving the city takes patience, because the M60 ring road and the radial roads fill at rush hour. The sensible plan is to go early on a weekend. Fuel and food are everywhere, with filling stations on every main road and more cafés than you could try in a year. Look for secure bike parking near the centre; the city has designated motorcycle bays, and many hotels will let you leave a bike inside a gated yard.
t.bath@51.4,-2.4:
The Romans came to Bath because of the water. Hot springs rise here at roughly forty-six degrees, and the legions built a sacred pool and a bathing complex around them in the first century, dedicating the place to a local goddess whom they merged with Minerva and calling it Aquae Sulis. The great bath is still there, green and steaming, below a Victorian terrace of statues. Over a thousand years later the Georgians remade the city in pale golden stone, the architect John Wood and his son building the Circus and the sweeping Royal Crescent, so that the place looks like a stage set for a Jane Austen novel. Austen herself lived here for several years and was not entirely happy about it.

Bath sits in the steep valley of the Avon, with hills rising on all sides, and the stone itself is dug from the local limestone, which glows in low sun. Pulteney Bridge, with shops built along both sides like Florence's Ponte Vecchio, crosses the river by the weir. The city is small and very walkable, but it is a magnet for visitors, so the centre is crowded and slow most days.

As a place to ride from, it is wonderful. Within a few minutes you are out onto the Cotswold edge or south through the Limpley Stoke valley, a deep wooded gorge where the canal and the railway run beside the river. Bradford on Avon is a few miles away, with its tiny Saxon church, and beyond lie the Mendip Hills, Cheddar Gorge and the Somerset Levels. The A36 along the valley is a good road, but it is busy with lorries. The better riding is on the B-roads that climb the hills and run along the ridge tops, with lovely views down into the valley and a mix of tight bends and fast, open sections.

Traffic inside the city is a headache. The ring road is clogged at rush hour, and parking in the centre is expensive, though motorcycles are often better treated than cars. Fuel stations stand on the outskirts, around Lower Weston and along the A4, and the centre has plenty of cafés, bakeries and the famous Sally Lunn buns, which are a decent way to start a ride.
t.troutdale@45.5,-122.4:
Samuel Lancaster, the engineer who built the Historic Columbia River Highway between 1913 and 1922, wanted a road that would show off the gorge instead of conquering it, and Troutdale is where it begins. The town sits where the Sandy River meets the Columbia, on the eastern edge of the Portland area, with a tidy main street, an old railroad depot and a hotel that began life as a poor farm. For a rider the gateway is easy: you leave the suburban edges, cross the river, and within a few miles the road starts to climb.

The highway was the first planned scenic road in the country, designed with stone guardrails, arched bridges and viaducts that fit the cliffs. At Crown Point, about 700 feet above the Columbia, Vista House, an octagonal stone building from 1918, serves as an observatory and rest stop, with a view up the gorge that explains why people drive here from across the world. Beyond it, the road threads past waterfalls, among them Latourell, Bridal Veil, Wahkeena and the biggest of all, Multnomah Falls, which drops 620 feet in two tiers and attracts huge crowds. During busy seasons, access to the waterfall corridor can require timed permits, so check before you go.

The road is narrow, curvy and quite slow, with tight bends under the rock and damp patches in the shade, and the sections in the woods can be covered with moss and leaves. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends, so a weekday morning is much better. Mist and fog hang in the gorge in spring and autumn, and the wind that whips through the gorge can surprise you at exposed viewpoints. The Columbia River Gorge is a transition zone, with wet, mossy forest in the west and dry grassland in the east, and the change over a short distance is remarkable.

Troutdale has around sixteen thousand people, with fuel, cafes and bakeries, and the nearby Gresham and Portland have everything else. Pick up supplies before you go, since there are limited stops along the old road, and stop for a pastry in one of the villages. Spring, with waterfalls at full flow, and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.hood river@45.7,-121.5:
Wind is the reason Hood River became what it is. Where the Columbia River Gorge narrows between the cool, wet west and the dry eastern plateau, the air funnels through with such force that windsurfers and kiteboarders gather by the hundreds, and the town has grown into a capital of outdoor sports. On a summer afternoon the river is dotted with colourful sails, and the bridge across to Washington State hums in the wind. Behind the town, Mount Hood rises to 11,249 feet, snow-covered through most of the year, and in front of it lies a valley full of orchards.

The Hood River Valley is one of the major fruit-growing areas of the Pacific Northwest, famous for its pears and apples, and in spring the blossom covers the slopes in white. A loop of farm stands, cideries and wineries, usually called the Fruit Loop, takes you along small roads through the orchards with Mount Hood hanging over the scene. The valley has a gentle rhythm, with undulating road, small bridges, packed farm stands and signs for u-pick cherries in June. In autumn the harvest brings pumpkins and fresh cider.

The Historic Columbia River Highway ends here after climbing out of Troutdale, and some of its most beautiful stretches lie east of the town, including a section of restored road between Hood River and Mosier, with two old tunnels cut through the cliffs that now carry bikes and walkers instead of cars. For motorcycles, the better route east follows the road along the cliffs, with long views and strong winds. Take care of crosswinds, particularly on the bridge and in the open sections.

Hood River has about seven thousand people, so fuel, repairs and good food are easy. Local breweries are plentiful, and the downtown, set on a steep hill above the river, has coffee shops and bakeries. Late April has blossom, summer has the sails and the heat, and September is warm and quieter. Highway 35 runs south toward Mount Hood, with pine forest, snow-covered peaks and, in winter, ice, so check conditions.
t.chinook pass@46.9,-121.5:
At 1,656 metres, Chinook Pass is a gate into Mount Rainier country, and the mountain makes itself known well before you arrive. State Route 410 climbs from the Enumclaw plateau through dark Douglas fir and hemlock, past the little settlements of Greenwater and the access road to Crystal Mountain, and then breaks out into subalpine meadows where the great white cone appears over the shoulder of the road. Rainier stands 14,410 feet, and on a clear morning it looks close enough to touch.

The pass was a trade and travel route long before cars, used by Native peoples crossing the Cascades between the coast and the interior, and the modern road was carved out in the 1930s. At the summit the Pacific Crest Trail crosses over the highway on a planted land bridge, so you may see backpackers in the middle of their months-long walk from Mexico to Canada, blinking at the traffic. Tipsoo Lake, just beside the road, is a small, still tarn framed by firs and flowers, and has the best easy photograph of the whole crossing.

The riding is lovely, with long, easy bends rather than hairpins, wide enough for a relaxed rhythm and with a smooth surface. Weather swings fast. A sunny afternoon in Enumclaw can turn to cold drizzle at the pass, and in spring and autumn snow comes down onto the tarmac. The road is shut in winter once snow builds up, usually from late autumn until late spring, so check the state transport page before planning. Late July to September is the safe window, and early autumn adds red huckleberry and mountain ash on the slopes.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. Nothing on the pass sells it, and the last dependable stations are in Enumclaw to the west or in Naches and Yakima to the east. Bring water, expect cool air, and treat the summit as the place to pull over and listen. You will hear marmots whistle among the rocks, and ravens, and perhaps nothing at all.
t.victoria@48.4,-123.4:
Victoria sits at the southern tip of Vancouver Island, the capital of British Columbia and the very British city that nobody expects on the Pacific coast. The Inner Harbour is the center of it, with the Parliament Buildings outlined in lights at night and the grand old Fairmont Empress hotel facing across the water, and ferries, seaplanes and little harbor taxis crowd the dock. The Hudson's Bay Company built a fort here in 1843, and the town grew from it, with a Chinatown that is among the oldest in Canada.

The weather is mild, the mildest in Canada, with flowers blooming early in the year and Beacon Hill Park a mass of color in spring. The city is known for afternoon tea, pubs, bookshops and a gentle pace of life, and it has a lively, walkable downtown. Mile Zero of the Trans-Canada Highway lies at the edge of the park, where the road begins its long way east across the country. Butchart Gardens, a spectacular garden in a former quarry, is a short drive north.

The Pacific Marine Circle Route starts here. The loop follows Highway 14 west through Sooke, along a coast of rocky coves and driftwood beaches, to Port Renfrew, then crosses the island through Lake Cowichan and returns south on the Trans-Canada over the Malahat, a steep, winding highway with big views over Saanich Inlet. Along the way, the forest is huge, with old cedar and Douglas fir, and the rain, when it comes, is persistent. The roads have gentle curves with some tight bends, and the surface is generally good, though logging trucks and tourist traffic are common.

Victoria has all the services: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, though downtown parking is tight. The ferry terminal at Swartz Bay, about thirty kilometers north, links to the mainland. The best months are June to September, with dry, mild weather, though fog on the coast is common in summer mornings. Winter is wet and gray, and the west coast road can be slick with rain and fallen needles. Watch for deer, which are bold and plentiful here, and for cyclists on the narrow shoulders.
t.buxton@53.3,-1.9:
Buxton is England's highest market town, give or take a rival's claim, perched at about three hundred meters in the hills of the Peak District, and it has the cool, brisk air to prove it.
