The Romans knew the place for its warm spring, which rises from deep in the limestone at a constant temperature of about twenty-eight degrees, and named it Aquae Arnemetiae. In the eighteenth century the Duke of Devonshire turned it into a fashionable spa, building the great Crescent in the 1780s, a curved Georgian terrace modeled on Bath.

The town is full of well-kept Georgian and Victorian architecture. The Opera House, a gilded theater from 1903 by Frank Matcham, hosts an annual festival, and the Pavilion Gardens, with their glass pavilion, make a pleasant park. St Ann's Well, a public fountain outside the Crescent, lets you fill a bottle with the warm, soft spring water, and Buxton Water is bottled and sold across the country.

For motorcyclists, Buxton has a mixed reputation, because it is the gateway to some famous, and notorious, roads. The A537 over the Cat and Fiddle, a high moorland road toward Macclesfield, is a fast and exciting run with sweeping bends and big views, but it has a long history of accidents and is heavily policed, with reduced limits and cameras. The A515 and A53 lead through limestone dales and over open moor, with stone walls, sheep and sudden views, and the White Peak lanes are narrower and quieter. The weather is the issue: Buxton is damp, misty and cold even in summer, and the moors are exposed.

Buxton has fuel, supermarkets, pubs and cafes, and it is a convenient stop. Chapel-en-le-Frith, nearby, has more. The best months are May to September, though morning fog and sudden rain are common, and winter ice on the moor roads can be dangerous. Weekends are busy with bikers, cyclists and walkers, so weekdays are quieter.
t.pickering@54.3,-0.8:
Pickering lies at the southern edge of the North York Moors, and it is the town where the moor begins. A castle of Norman origin stands on a mound above the market place, with a ruined keep and walls that once held kings, and in the parish church, medieval wall paintings of saints and scenes from the Bible, found again under whitewash in the nineteenth century, cover the nave. The streets are lined with warm honey-colored stone, and the market, held weekly, has been going for centuries.

The North Yorkshire Moors Railway, a heritage steam line, runs from Pickering through the moor to Whitby, via Goathland, and the station, with its old signs and gas lamps, is a favorite for photographers. The line was built by George Stephenson in the 1830s, and on summer days the whistles of steam locomotives echo along the valley. Thornton Dale, a village a few miles east, is often called the prettiest in Yorkshire, with a stream running through, thatched cottages and flower beds.

The A169 north from Pickering is the classic road onto the moors, and a good ride. It climbs steeply out of the town, past the great hollow of the Hole of Horcum, a huge natural amphitheater said in legend to have been scooped out by the giant Wade, then runs across high, open moorland with heather, sheep and views toward the golf-ball domes of Fylingdales radar station, before dropping to Whitby on the coast. Bends are open and moderate, and the surface is generally good, but the moor is exposed, with strong winds and sudden fog. In August the heather blooms purple.

Pickering has fuel, supermarkets, pubs, cafes and hotels, and it is the best base for the southern moors. Kirkbymoorside, to the west, has a market too. The best months are May to September, with August for heather, though the moor weather can turn cold and wet at any time. Winter snow can close the high road. Sheep wander across the road, so keep your speed in check, and give walkers and cyclists room on the lanes.
t.cheltenham@51.9,-2.1:
Cheltenham is a spa town of the Regency age, all pale stucco, iron balconies and tree-lined avenues, and it wears its elegance lightly. A mineral spring was found here in the early eighteenth century, and when King George III visited in 1788 the town became fashionable overnight, with grand terraces and a promenade lined with trees built to match. The Pittville Pump Room, a Greek-style building of 1830, still offers a glass of the water for the brave.

The town's best-known event is the Cheltenham Festival, four days of horse racing in March at Prestbury Park, with the Gold Cup the highlight, drawing crowds from across the country and, especially, Ireland. The composer Gustav Holst, who wrote The Planets, was born here in 1874, and his birthplace is a small museum. Edward Wilson, who died with Captain Scott on the return from the South Pole, also came from Cheltenham. The government's communications headquarters, GCHQ, sits in a ring-shaped building on the edge of town, a secretive presence.

For riders, Cheltenham is the western gateway to the Cotswolds, the limestone hills that rise abruptly to the east in an escarpment. The roads climb from the town to Cleeve Hill, the highest point of the Cotswolds at about 330 meters, with views across the Severn Vale toward Wales. Beyond, narrow lanes wander through honey-colored villages such as Winchcombe, Stanway and Broadway, past stone walls, sheep pastures and manor houses. The surface is generally good, but the lanes are narrow and busy with tourists, cyclists and tractors, so patience is essential, and summer weekends are slow.

Cheltenham has every service, with fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, though town traffic can be heavy at rush hour. Charlton Kings and Shurdington, nearby, are smaller. The best months are May and September, with warm days and fewer crowds, and October brings golden foliage on the beech woods. Winter is damp and cold, with the odd frost on the hill roads. Watch for horse boxes and farm vehicles in the lanes.
t.caernarfon@53.1,-4.3:
The first thing you see in Caernarfon is the castle, and it is meant to be. Edward I began building it in 1283 after conquering the Welsh princes, and he designed it to impress as well as to defend, with polygonal towers and bands of different coloured stone in imitation of the walls of Constantinople. It was the seat of English power in north Wales, and in 1284 Edward's son, later Edward II, was born here and became the first English Prince of Wales, a title since given to the heir to the throne. The castle, along with Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the sheer scale of it, rising above the Menai Strait, is staggering.

But Caernarfon is not simply a museum. It is a living Welsh town of nearly ten thousand people, where Welsh is spoken in the shops and cafés as the first language, and the atmosphere is friendly and unpretentious. The old town inside the walls has narrow lanes, pubs and small shops, and the quay on the Seiont is a pleasant place to sit. Fuel, supermarkets and anything else you need are easy to find, and the town makes a good base for exploring Snowdonia. A narrow-gauge railway, the Welsh Highland, runs from here to Porthmadog through the mountains.

The ride from Caernarfon through the Llanberis Pass is among the best in Wales. The road runs southeast along the shore of Llyn Padarn, past the old slate quarries at Llanberis, whose huge terraced steps mark the mountain across the lake, and then climbs into the pass itself, a steep-sided glacial valley with a river and walls of boulders. Snowdon, at 1,085 metres the highest peak in Wales, rises to one side. The road narrows as it climbs to Pen-y-Pass, with tight bends and rock on both sides, and it is spectacular, but it can be crowded with walkers, cyclists and cars in summer.

The weather in Snowdonia is changeable and often wet, with low cloud and sudden showers even in July, so wet-weather gear is essential. The surface can be greasy, and sheep wander across the road without warning. Early morning is the best time, when the light is clear and the traffic is thin. Have a good breakfast before you leave, and keep an eye on the clouds.
t.llanberis@53.1,-4.1:
Llanberis is the town at the foot of Snowdon, and it carries slate in its bones. Behind it, the huge terraced scar of the Dinorwic quarry climbs the mountainside in steps, a reminder that for most of the nineteenth century this was an industrial valley, with thousands of quarrymen blasting and splitting rock that roofed half of Britain. The quarry closed in 1969, and the old workshops beside Llyn Padarn are now the National Slate Museum, with working water wheels and a foundry. Inside the mountain across the lake, a vast hidden power station, Dinorwig, known as the Electric Mountain, can supply Britain's grid at short notice.

The town itself is a long, straggling street of grey stone, with outdoor shops, cafés and chip shops catering to walkers, climbers and families heading for the summit. The Snowdon Mountain Railway, a rack-and-pinion line opened in 1896, climbs from here to just below the top of Wales's highest mountain, at 1,085 metres, and in summer its little steam and diesel trains chuff past the end of the high street. On a quiet morning the lake, with the ruined tower of Dolbadarn Castle, built by Welsh princes in the thirteenth century, makes a fine photograph.

For riders, Llanberis is the starting point for the Llanberis Pass, one of the best mountain roads in Wales. The A4086 climbs east out of the town, following a glacial valley between the Glyderau and Snowdon, with rock walls rising on either side and boulders scattered across the valley floor. The road is narrow and winding, with tight corners and sheer drops in places, and the surface is generally good, but the weather is the key. Rain is common, cloud sits on the tops, and the wind can be strong. On a clear day, the views are magnificent, but even in summer, bring waterproofs. Weekends and bank holidays are very busy, with walkers' cars parked along the verges.

Nature here is Welsh mountain nature: sheep on the road, red kites in the sky, ravens on the cliffs, and a smell of wet slate and bracken. The Snowdon lily, a rare arctic-alpine plant, grows on a few high rocks. Welsh is widely spoken in the town, and you will hear it in shops and cafés.

Llanberis has what a rider needs. There are cafés, pubs and shops, and a fuel station in the valley is possible, but it is safer to fill up in Caernarfon, about ten kilometres to the west, or Bangor. Parking is available by the lake. A bacon sandwich and strong tea in a walkers' café is the right way to start the day.
t.pen y pass@53.1,-4.0:
At 359 metres, Pen-y-Pass is not high by any alpine standard, but it is the highest point on the A4086, and it feels like the doorway to something big. The road tops out here between the shoulders of Snowdon and the Glyderau, with the cliffs of Crib Goch and Lliwedd on one side and the long glacial trough of the Llanberis Pass falling away on the other. Mist often fills the gap, and on a day of low cloud it can feel like the top of the world. When the sun comes out, the contrast is astonishing, with the green valley stretching down to the lakes.

It is also the starting point for the best-known paths up Snowdon. The Pyg Track and the Miners' Track both begin here, and on a summer morning the car park, one of the most expensive and crowded in Wales, fills before eight. The old Gorphwysfa Hotel, now a youth hostel, was where early climbers gathered at the end of the nineteenth century, and nearby, the Pen-y-Gwryd Hotel was where the 1953 Everest expedition team trained before their successful ascent. Their signatures are still on the ceiling of the bar.

The ride up from Llanberis is a sequence of tight bends and sheer rock, with the road narrowing in places to barely two cars wide. The surface is good, but there are cattle grids, sheep, cyclists and walkers' cars stopping suddenly, so it is no place for speed. On the east side, the road drops toward Capel Curig past the Pen-y-Gwryd hotel, and from here you can continue along the A5 or turn south through Beddgelert. Weather is important. Cloud can fall quickly, and winter ice is a real risk, so check conditions before you set out.

The mountains above hold plenty of natural interest. Cwm Glas, a hanging valley, has some of the best examples of glacial features in Britain, and the rocks are rich in fossils. Alpine plants cling to the high crags, and choughs, the red-legged crows, nest on the cliffs.

Parking at the pass is limited, and a park-and-ride bus runs from Nant Peris in summer to relieve the crowding, so a bike makes things easier. Fuel is not available here. Llanberis, about six kilometres down the hill, has services of a sort, and Bangor, a bigger town, is further away, so keep an eye on the tank. The café at the pass is handy for tea and a bacon roll in season.
t.beddgelert@53.0,-4.1:
Beddgelert is a village of grey stone cottages at the meeting of two rivers, the Glaslyn and the Colwyn, surrounded by steep green mountains, and it is famous for a dog. The legend says that Llywelyn the Great, a thirteenth-century Welsh prince, left his baby son in the care of his hound Gelert, and returned to find the cradle overturned, the dog covered in blood and the child nowhere to be seen. Believing the dog had killed him, he drew his sword, and only after the dog was dead did he hear the baby crying and find a dead wolf nearby. He is said to have buried Gelert with great sorrow, and the village's name means Gelert's grave.

The story is almost certainly a later invention, probably popularised in the eighteenth century by a local innkeeper who wanted to attract visitors, which, if true, is a good piece of marketing. Still, a stone marks the supposed grave, in a meadow beside the river, and it is a pleasant ten-minute walk. The village itself has a tidy stone bridge, tea rooms, outdoor shops and pubs, and it fills with hikers on summer weekends. Walks start from the village up Snowdon and into the Aberglaslyn Pass, a rocky gorge just south of the village where the river tumbles over boulders.

The ride that ends here, from Llanberis over Pen-y-Pass, follows the A498 down through the Nantgwynant valley, past the lakes of Llyn Gwynant and Llyn Dinas, with Snowdon's flanks above you. The road is good, with gentle bends and wonderful views, and it descends gradually into the village. The Welsh Highland Railway also runs to Beddgelert, and a steam train puffing through the valley is a fine sight. The Sygun Copper Mine, a Victorian copper mine now open to visitors, lies a short distance away.

Parking in the village is limited and fills quickly in summer, so arrive early. Rain is frequent, and the damp air smells of bracken and wet slate. After a long ride, a pot of tea and a slice of bara brith, Welsh fruit bread, by the river is a pleasure.
t.tintagel@50.7,-4.7:
Tintagel has been selling King Arthur for a long time. The twelfth-century writer Geoffrey of Monmouth first placed Arthur's conception here, in his History of the Kings of Britain, and the legend grew from there, helped by a Victorian love of chivalry and a ruined castle on a dramatic headland. Archaeologists have since found that the site was an important trading post in the fifth and sixth centuries, when imported Mediterranean pottery and glass came in by sea, so something notable did happen here, but whether it involved a king named Arthur is another matter. Cornwall, characteristically, has chosen to believe.

The castle ruins, run by English Heritage, stand on a rocky island joined to the mainland by a narrow neck, and in 2019 a new footbridge, with a gap in the middle that gives the impression of a narrow slot between two cliffs, replaced the old stone steps. The site is dramatic: stone walls clinging to the edge of a cliff, a sea cave below known as Merlin's Cave, and the Atlantic crashing in. Up in the village, the Old Post Office, a fourteenth-century manor house with a slate roof that sags with age, is cared for by the National Trust, and the street is lined with shops selling swords, crystals and mead, in a cheerfully kitsch way.

Riding here means the A39, known as the Atlantic Highway, which runs along the north Cornish coast. It is more of a cruise than a thrill. The road is generally good, with long straights and gentle bends over open moorland, but it can be slow, with caravans, tractors and holiday traffic in summer. The better sport is on the lanes, which are narrow, hedged and winding, with blind corners and a good deal of mud and gravel, so approach with caution. The weather here is Atlantic: wind, mist and sudden rain can arrive at any time of year, but a clear evening on the cliffs is one of the glories of Cornwall.

Nearby, the slate quarry at Delabole has been worked for six hundred years and is among the largest in England, and next to it stands one of Britain's first onshore wind farms, from 1991. The coast is a protected landscape, with sea cliffs, wild flowers and seabirds such as fulmars, kittiwakes and choughs, which are Cornwall's emblem.

Tintagel village has pubs, tearooms and pasty shops, a few small hotels, and a car park near the castle. For fuel, Wadebridge, about seventeen kilometres to the south, is the best option, though there is a small garage at Camelford, near the main road, so plan your fill-up. A hot pasty eaten on the cliffs, preferably out of the wind, is the traditional pleasure.
t.padstow@50.5,-4.9:
Padstow has two reputations, and they get along rather well: it is an old working fishing port on the Camel estuary, and it is the town that Rick Stein turned into a food destination. His seafood restaurant opened in the 1970s and drew so many diners that the place became known to locals, half in jest, as Padstein. Today the harbour is packed with restaurants, delis, bakeries and pasty shops, and on a summer day the quay is a crowd of holidaymakers eating crab sandwiches and ice cream in the sun, while the gulls plot the theft of their chips.

Beneath the polish, the town has a deeper tradition. On May Day, Padstow hosts the 'Obby 'Oss festival, an ancient ritual in which two dancers in black or red costumes and huge hooped masks whirl through the streets accompanied by drums, accordions and singing. It is one of the oldest surviving folk customs in Britain, and its origin is lost in time. The town fills with people, and the streets hum with music from dawn until dusk.

The Camel Trail, an old railway line converted into a path for walkers and cyclists, runs from here upriver to Wadebridge and beyond, past mudflats, salt marsh and woods. Across the estuary, the village of Rock is linked by a small passenger ferry, and the sand dunes and the deceptive Doom Bar sandbank at the river mouth, named after the many ships it has wrecked, have given the name to a famous local beer.

For riders, the approach is along the A389 from Wadebridge or from the A39 on the coast, and the road is not particularly demanding, though in summer it is slow with holiday traffic. The streets of Padstow itself are narrow and crowded, with parking difficult, so the best option is to leave the bike in the large car park at the edge of town and walk. Spring and autumn are the best times, with fewer people and good light, though wind and rain are possible at any time. In winter the town is quiet, and some restaurants close.

The coast beyond is a delight, with sandy beaches, such as Harlyn Bay and Trevone, and cliff paths where thrift and sea campion bloom in spring. Fuel is not sold in the middle of town, so Wadebridge, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest big settlement, with stations and supermarkets. A proper Cornish pasty, with beef, potato, swede and onion, crimped at the side, is the lunch to look for, though fish and chips on the quay is hard to resist.
t.eskdale@54.4,-3.3:
Eskdale is the quiet, long valley on the western edge of the Lake District, running from the high fells down to the Irish Sea, and it is the sort of place where the road narrows, the sheep multiply and the mountains seem to lean in. At the top end stand the peaks of the Scafell range, including Scafell Pike at 978 metres, the highest in England, and below them the green valley floor is dotted with stone farms, drystone walls and small woods. The hamlet of Boot has a pub, a watermill and a station, and the setting is extraordinarily pretty.

The station belongs to the Ravenglass and Eskdale Railway, a fifteen-inch gauge steam line known affectionately as La'al Ratty, which runs for about eleven kilometres from the coast at Ravenglass up the valley to Dalegarth. It was built in the 1870s to carry iron ore and later converted to carry passengers, and today the little locomotives pull open carriages through woods and fields. Riding beside the track with a train chuffing alongside is a nice experience. Ravenglass has a Roman bath house and Muncaster Castle, with its owl centre and gardens, near the coast.

The real draw for motorcyclists is what lies to the east. The road climbs out of Eskdale over the Hardknott Pass, one of the steepest roads in England, with a gradient signed at one in three on its tightest hairpins. The road is narrow, single-track in places, with passing bays, and it requires a steady hand and a clear head. At the top, at about 390 metres, the remains of a Roman fort, Mediobogdum, stand on a ledge with a view across the valley, built in the second century to guard the route to the coast. Beyond, the road continues over the Wrynose Pass to Little Langdale.

Fuel is not available in Eskdale, and the nearest options are Egremont, seventeen kilometres away, and Seascale, so arrive with a full tank. The passes can be dangerous in ice, snow or heavy rain, and they are frequently closed in winter. Come in late spring or early autumn, early in the day, to avoid the crowds. Wear a layer even in summer, because the weather here changes fast and cloud can drop onto the road. The silence at the top, with only wind and sheep, is something to remember.
t.hardknott pass@54.4,-3.2:
Hardknott Pass has a reputation among British riders that is partly earned and partly exaggerated, but the earned part is considerable. The road climbs from the Eskdale side in a series of short, sharp hairpins with gradients of up to one in three, among the steepest on any public road in England, and the surface is narrow, rough and often slick, with no barriers on the outside of the bends. At the summit, 393 metres above sea level, the road crosses a high saddle between the valleys of the Esk and the Duddon, and then drops again, nearly as steeply, to Cockley Beck. Take it slowly, in first gear, with both hands on the bars and a good look ahead.

Beyond the challenge, the pass has a fascinating history. Just below the summit on the Eskdale side stand the remains of Hardknott Roman Fort, called Mediobogdum by the Romans, built in the second century to guard the road from Ravenglass on the coast to Ambleside. The fort commanded one of the loneliest postings in the empire, and on a clear day you can walk around the foundations of the granary, the commander's house and the bath house, with a spectacular view to the Scafell range. It is easy to imagine a legionary from the Mediterranean, standing here in the rain, wondering what he had done wrong.

The Lake District here is at its roughest and most remote. Bare crags, bracken and heather cover the slopes, and the lakes are far below, out of sight. Herdwick sheep, the tough, grey-faced breed of the Lakes, graze the hillsides and wander across the road without concern. The weather matters: low cloud and mist can reduce visibility to a few metres, rain makes the surface treacherous, and in winter, ice and snow close the road. It is best done in dry, clear conditions, in spring or early autumn, and many riders prefer to approach from the west, climbing the steeper hairpins rather than descending them, though opinions vary.

There are no facilities on the pass. Fuel is available in Ambleside, about twenty kilometres to the east, and at villages on the coast such as Seascale, and the Woolpack Inn at Eskdale and the café at Boot may serve food, though opening hours vary. Carry a warm layer and a drink, and make sure your clutch and brakes are in good order before you go. The pass is not for large vehicles or caravans, and drivers who ignore the warnings often cause long delays, so be prepared to wait.
t.wrynose pass@54.4,-3.1:
If Hardknott is the show-off, Wrynose is its older, grumpier sibling. The two passes are usually ridden together, linking Ambleside and Langdale in the east with Eskdale and the Cumbrian coast in the west, but Wrynose comes first for those heading from the east, and it sets the tone. The road is single-track for much of its length, narrow, with passing places, rough edges and a gradient of one in four on some of the hairpins. At the top, at about 393 metres, there is a bare saddle of grass and boulders, and a modest stone marker in the road called the Three Shire Stone.

The stone stands where three old counties met, Cumberland, Westmorland and Lancashire, and it has stood here since 1816. Today all three lie inside the modern county of Cumbria, but the stone remains, and children like to stand with one foot in each former county. The high ground around is known as Wrynose Bottom, and there is a ford where the River Duddon rises, a short walk away. Fell ponies and sheep graze freely, and they pay little attention to bikes.

The ride from Little Langdale is a fine one, climbing through stone-walled fields, past slate quarries and then onto open fell. The road is narrow and the surface variable, with loose gravel at the sides and potholes after winter, and visibility around the bends is poor, so ride within your limits and be ready to stop. Cars and walkers come in the other direction, and in summer, the pass can be busy with coaches and cyclists, though the road is not suitable for large vehicles. Cloud is common, and rain makes the rock slippery. The best times are a dry spring day or an autumn morning, when the bracken is bronze and the air is clear.

Wrynose Pass is beautiful in an austere way, and it gives access to some of the great walks of the Lake District, including the climb of Pike of Blisco. In the valleys, you pass dry-stone walls, small farms and old slate workings, a reminder that this was industrial country as well as pastoral. The Duddon Valley, which Wordsworth wrote sonnets about, runs from the foot of the pass.

Windermere, about fourteen kilometres away, and Ambleside, a little nearer, have fuel stations and cafés. Check your fuel and carry water. If you plan to ride both Wrynose and Hardknott in one go, allow plenty of time and expect delays.
t.little langdale@54.4,-3.0:
Little Langdale is a small, secretive valley in the central Lake District, with a hamlet of slate-roofed farms, a tarn and a stream, and it feels as if the rest of the world had been forgotten. The valley lies at the foot of the Wrynose Pass, and the road you ride in on climbs from the head of the valley to the pass, past a stone known as the Three Shires Stone, where the old counties of Cumberland, Westmorland and Lancashire once met. The stone is a simple marker, but standing at a point where three historic counties joined is a pleasing small thrill.

The Wrynose Pass is narrower than Hardknott, with steep gradients and tight, blind bends, and the Little Langdale side drops at around one in four. The road runs in a single track for much of its length, with passing places, and meeting a car head-on at a bend is a daily event, so use patience and good manners. The surface is generally good but can be wet and gritty, and it is not a road to rush. In winter, ice and snow can make it dangerous, and the pass is sometimes closed.

The landscape is classic Lakeland, with grey-green fells, drystone walls and Herdwick sheep, the hardy local breed with grey wool and white faces, which Beatrix Potter, a farmer as well as an author, helped to preserve. The slate that roofs the houses was quarried in the hills, and old quarries and tunnels honeycomb the area, with the remains of a few workings visible near the road. A packhorse bridge, Slater Bridge, crosses the river Brathay on a path, a graceful old structure of slabs, and it is a gentle walk from the hamlet. The Langdale Pikes rise above to the north.

A pub in the hamlet serves food and local beer, popular with walkers and riders, and the garden looks over the fells. Weather can change in minutes, so carry waterproofs, and note that the roads can be slow in summer with walkers and cyclists. When you finish, the soft light on the tarn in the evening makes it hard to leave.
t.mount rainier sunrise junction@46.9,-121:
This is the place where Highway 410 and the road to Sunrise part company, and it is worth knowing about because the turning leads to the highest point you can reach by road on Mount Rainier. The junction lies near the White River entrance on the park's north-east side, in a valley of old-growth fir and cedar, with the White River running cold and milky beside the road, and the mountain hidden behind the ridges until you climb out of the trees.

The Sunrise road is a spectacular, tidy piece of mountain engineering. It climbs about fifteen miles in a series of switchbacks and gentle bends to a height of around 6,400 feet, where Rainier stands directly in front of you, 4,392 metres of ice and rock. The Emmons Glacier, the largest in the lower forty-eight by area, is spread across the mountain's north-east face. The road is generally open only from early July until September or October, and snow can fall at any time at the top. Wildflower season in late July and August brings meadows full of lupin and paintbrush, and marmots whistle from the rocks.

Highway 410 itself, the Chinook Pass Scenic Byway, is a joy. It leads south-east from Enumclaw along the Greenwater and White rivers, climbing toward Chinook Pass at 5,430 feet, with a sequence of flowing bends under big timber. The road is closed in winter, normally from about November until late May, and the pass often sees cloud and drizzle even in July. There are few places to stop or turn, so be wary of traffic behind you, and be aware of the cold wetness of the forest roads, where moss and shade keep the surface damp.

There is a park entry fee payable at the White River entrance, and a limited timed-entry system has sometimes been in place for Sunrise in recent summers, so check ahead. Enumclaw, to the west, is the last big town with petrol, and the small communities on Highway 410 have limited and sometimes seasonal supplies, so fill up before you leave. Bring warm clothing even in August, because Sunrise can feel like early spring.
t.naches@46.7,-120.7:
Naches is a very small orchard town in the Yakima valley, at the place where the Naches River comes down out of the Cascades, and it is the dry-side end of the Chinook Pass road. The change from west to east is dramatic. On the Seattle side the slopes are wrapped in dripping fir and cedar, and over the crest the forest thins into ponderosa pine and then sagebrush, with sun, orchards and irrigated fields. Naches is where the green gives way to gold.

The valley produces much of America's apple crop, and also pears, cherries, hops and wine grapes, thanks to water from the mountains and a dry, sunny climate. Fruit stands appear along the road in late summer, selling peaches, apricots and cider, and in autumn the air smells of apples and wood smoke. The cascades act as a barrier to rain, so the east side gets only a fraction of the precipitation that falls on the west. The change in climate is something you can feel in a single afternoon.

Chinook Pass Scenic Byway, State Route 410, climbs along the river and crosses the Cascade crest at about fifty-four hundred feet, running along the edge of Mount Rainier National Park. Rainier itself, at over fourteen thousand feet, dominates the western horizon, a huge, glacier-covered volcano. The road is good, with smooth bends, forest and big views, and the descent east follows the river past cliffs of basalt. The pass is closed in winter, usually from November to late May, because of heavy snow, so check conditions.

You can find basic services in Naches, though the larger town of Selah, about fifteen kilometres away, or Yakima, offers more fuel and food. Fill the tank before the climb, since stations are scarce on the pass. A roadside fruit stand is a great reward after a day's ride. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, with cold rain or even snow in summer, so bring a waterproof. In September and October, golden larch and red vine maple add colour to the slopes, and the light is warm.
t.sedro woolley@48.5,-122.2:
Sedro-Woolley is two towns that stuck together. Sedro and Woolley were separate rivals on the Skagit River until they merged in 1898, and the double-barrelled name, with its hyphen, has stayed ever since. It is a working town of about eleven thousand people on the flat, green floodplain of the Skagit valley, in north-western Washington, with farms, sawmills, a timber heritage and a loggers' festival in July. For riders it is the start of the North Cascades Highway, and the last easy place to buy supplies.

The valley around it is famous for its fields. In April, commercial tulip and daffodil fields blossom in broad stripes of red, yellow and pink, drawing crowds. In winter, thousands of bald eagles gather along the upper river to feed on spawning salmon, and the stretch between Rockport and Marblemount is a favourite for birdwatchers. Dairy farms, berry patches and potato fields fill the rest of the valley, and the climate is mild, damp and green.

State Route 20 runs east from here along the Skagit River, climbing gradually past the old lumber town of Concrete, then into the mountains, where it passes the turquoise lakes behind Seattle City Light's dams at Diablo and Ross. The highway was only completed in 1972, after decades of debate, and it crosses the Cascade crest at Washington Pass, at about fifty-four hundred feet. The road is superb, with long, flowing bends, clean tarmac and spectacular scenery, though it is closed by snow every winter, usually from November until April or May.

Fuel is available in Sedro-Woolley, and it is wise to fill up here or at Marblemount, the last town before a long stretch with no services, about seventy miles to Winthrop. Rain is common on the west side, even in summer, so take waterproofs, and it can be cold on the pass. Wildfire smoke in late summer sometimes obscures the views. September, when the weather is often settled, the huckleberries are ripe and the larches begin to turn gold, is a good time for the trip.
t.diablo lake@48.7,-121.1:
Diablo Lake is the colour that nobody believes in photographs. The water is a milky, luminous turquoise, as though someone has dissolved a gemstone in it, and it is not a trick of the light. Glaciers on the surrounding peaks grind the rock beneath them into a fine powder, rock flour, which washes down in meltwater and stays suspended in the lake, scattering blue and green light back to the surface. The effect is strongest in late summer, when the melt is at its peak and the sun is high.

The lake is a reservoir, formed by Diablo Dam on the Skagit River, built by Seattle City Light in the late 1920s to produce electricity for the city. The company ran the project, building a company town at Newhalem and an incline railway to haul equipment up the mountain, and it still runs tours of the dams. The construction was a tremendous effort in this rugged, steep valley. Above the lake, the Skagit climbs further to Ross Lake, an even more remote body of water that reaches north to the Canadian border.

State Route 20, the North Cascades Highway, was finished in 1972 after decades of argument, and it passes the lake at an overlook that is among the most popular stops on the route. The road here is easy: a wide, smooth, well-engineered highway climbing in sweeping bends through forest, with great views of jagged peaks, hanging glaciers and cascades of water down the cliffs. It is a motorcyclist's road, and a slow one thanks to the speed limit and the number of stopping places. The pass is closed in winter by snow, usually from about November until April or May, and conditions can change quickly in the mountains. Rain is common on the western side, and cool mist drifts up the valley in the morning.

Marblemount, on the west side, is the last place with petrol, and Winthrop on the east has the next, a gap of around ninety miles, so fill up before you start. Newhalem has a small store and a visitor centre, and a campground sits nearby. Take warm clothing, and watch for deer and the occasional bear.
t.washington pass@48.5,-120.6:
At 1,669 metres, Washington Pass is the highest point on the North Cascades Highway, and from the overlook just beside the road you look straight across at a wall of grey granite that seems to have been designed by a rock climber. Liberty Bell Mountain stands out as a smooth, blunt dome, with the sharp spires of the Early Winters group beside it, and the whole group rises above a basin of scree, larch and bare rock. The overlook is reached by a short, paved path from the car park, with a viewing platform above a cliff, and it is one of the best easy views in the state.

The highway was opened in 1972, after a long and expensive campaign, and it is still one of the most spectacular roads in the Pacific Northwest. East of the pass, it descends in a series of tight bends, hairpins and long, open bends toward the Methow Valley, through forests of Douglas fir and ponderosa pine, with signs of earlier wildfires. The road surface is excellent, the radius of the bends is generous, and the gradients are manageable. On a clear day, with the sun on the peaks and the road empty, it is a rider's dream. Weather can be savage: snow can fall in any month, and the highway is closed for the winter, typically from November to April.

The best moment of the year is the last week of September or the first of October, when the larches turn gold. These deciduous conifers cover the high slopes, and their needles turn a brilliant yellow-orange before falling, in a display that draws crowds. It is also cold, with frost on the road in the morning and wind on the ridge, so dress accordingly. Early summer brings wildflowers and waterfalls, and mosquitoes.

Mazama, down the eastern side, has a small store, and Winthrop, a western-themed town in the Methow Valley, has petrol, cafes and a bakery. On the west side, Marblemount is the last stop. Fill up at either, and carry food and water. Remember that cell reception is poor, and the weather can change in a flash.
t.winthrop@48.5,-120.2:
Winthrop has dressed up as the Wild West, and it does so with enthusiasm. The town sits where the Chewuch and Methow rivers meet, in a sunny valley on the dry eastern side of the North Cascades, and its main street is lined with wooden false fronts, boardwalks and hitching posts. In the 1970s, with the new highway about to bring tourists from Seattle, local businesses agreed on an Old West theme, and the plan worked. Today there are saloons, a general store, a small museum in an old log cabin, and at weekends a cowboy hat is not out of place.

The real history is also colourful. The area was a gold and silver prospecting zone in the 1880s, and the town was named after the writer Theodore Winthrop, whose book on the Pacific Northwest had been popular. Cattle ranchers, orchardists and homesteaders followed. It is a small place, with about five hundred people, but the Methow Valley is well known for its sunny climate, with warm summers and cold, dry winters that make it one of the best places in the country for cross-country skiing.

The ride in from the west is a classic. After Washington Pass, the North Cascades Highway drops steeply down the eastern slope, through hairpins and long bends, with granite spires above and forests of larch and pine below, then follows the Methow River into the valley. The change from the wet west side to the dry east is dramatic, and the temperature can rise by ten degrees within a few miles. Autumn is magical, when the larches turn bright gold in October, among the evergreens, and the light is clear.

Winthrop has fuel stations, cafes, bakeries and a few hotels, and it is a very pleasant place to end the day, with a cold beer on a porch. Services are limited farther back along the highway, so fill the tank here before turning around. Summer can be hot, with temperatures in the thirties Celsius, and wildfires have affected the valley in recent years, so check the news. Watch for deer and cattle on the road, especially at dusk, and for cyclists on the pass.
t.government camp@45.3,-121.8:
Government Camp takes its name from an episode of frontier misfortune. In the autumn of 1849, a detachment of Mounted Riflemen heading west over the Barlow Road found the going so hard that they left their wagons at a spot near here and carried on without them. The place became known as the government camp, and the name stuck, a small piece of American history on a modern resort village at the foot of Mount Hood.

Today the town is a ski community strung along US 26, at roughly twelve hundred metres. In winter the streets fill with skiers, and in summer with hikers, mountain bikers, and riders heading up to Timberline. The buildings are alpine in feel, with timber and steep roofs, and the mountain looms behind them with its glaciers and its summit often in cloud. The air is cool and smells of fir, even in July.

The ride here is a long, pleasant climb. US 26 comes up from the Portland side through the forest, with steady grades and sweeping, forgiving bends, and the road is well maintained and generally quick. It is a busy highway, so you will often be sharing it with trucks, campervans, and weekend traffic. Beyond the village, the Timberline road branches off and climbs more steeply, and the Mount Hood Scenic Byway continues down the east side toward Hood River. Snow can arrive early and linger late, so the high section is best ridden from late spring through autumn, and ice is possible well into the warm months at night.

Services are practical. There are lodging, cafes, and a few small shops, and the town is used to hungry and cold visitors. Fuel is more doubtful, and the safe bet is to fill the tank down the hill, around Mount Hood Village and the Sandy area, before the climb. Eighteen kilometres of road separate Government Camp from the nearest bigger settlement, which is not much until you are on a bike with an empty tank. The mountain weather changes fast, so carry a rain layer even on a bright morning, and enjoy a hot drink while you wait for the clouds to move off the peak.
t.timberline lodge@45.3,-121.7:
The road up to Timberline Lodge is six miles of climbing from Government Camp, and at the top there is a building that looks as if it has grown out of the mountain. The lodge was built in the late 1930s as a Works Progress Administration project during the Depression, and craftspeople carved its timbers, wove its rugs, forged its ironwork, and painted its murals by hand. President Franklin Roosevelt dedicated it in 1937. The exterior was later used to represent the hotel in the film version of The Shining, though the interiors were done elsewhere.

The location is at about six thousand feet on the south side of Mount Hood, which is Oregon's highest peak, an enormous glaciated volcano that dominates the horizon for a hundred miles. At the lodge you are right beneath it, with the snowfields above and the forest below, and the view south over the Cascades on a clear day is outstanding. Skiers use the lifts in winter and even in early summer, and the Pacific Crest Trail passes close by, so you may see long-distance hikers coming through with weathered faces and big packs.

The riding is a pleasure: a well-surfaced road with steady climbing, tight, flowing turns, and ever-widening views as the trees thin. It is a National Forest road with a fee in some seasons, and traffic can be heavy on sunny weekends. Snow closes or restricts it for much of the winter, and the road can have ice and snow into late spring, so check conditions. At the top, the air is thin and cold even in July, and the wind can be sharp, so keep a warm layer to hand.

The lodge itself is a good place for a hot drink and a look at the carvings, even for those who are not staying, and the public areas are open to visitors. Time your visit for late morning or midafternoon, when the cloud tends to lift, and give the descent the attention it deserves. Brakes work hard on the way down, and it is easy to arrive at Government Camp with a smell of hot pads.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum in wall mile 6:
The western end of Hadrian's Wall runs right through Carlisle, and the stretch counted as wall mile 66 lies on the edge of the city, close to where the wall crossed the River Eden. The Roman town of Luguvalium grew up here, and the fort at Stanwix, across the river, housed a cavalry regiment and was the largest on the wall. Very little of the stone wall survives in the city, much of it having been robbed for buildings, but the line of the wall and vallum can be traced in places, and the Tullie House museum tells the story of Roman Carlisle with excellent displays.

Carlisle has always been a frontier city. After the Romans left, it changed hands between England and Scotland several times, and the red sandstone castle, begun under William Rufus in the late eleventh century, has seen sieges, rebellions and imprisoned royalty, including Mary, Queen of Scots. The cathedral, also red sandstone, is one of the smallest in England. The border country to the north was the land of the reivers, families who raided across the border for cattle and plunder for centuries.

The city, with nearly eighty thousand people, has everything you need: fuel, shops, restaurants and accommodation. Traffic can be heavy, especially at rush hour, and there are speed cameras on the main roads. Park near the castle and walk; the centre is compact, and the old market cross, the cathedral and the museum are all a few minutes apart.

For riders, Carlisle is a gateway. To the south lies the Lake District, with its famous passes, Hardknott and Wrynose, steep and narrow, and Kirkstone and Honister, more forgiving. To the north and east, the roads into the Scottish Borders and along the wall offer quieter riding across moors and through river valleys. West, the Solway coast leads to the end of the wall at Bowness-on-Solway, a flat, quiet road with big skies and views across the firth to Scotland.
t.campfield@54.9,-3.3:
Out on the Solway coast west of Carlisle, the land flattens into salt marsh, peat bog and wide tidal sands, and the sky takes over. Campfield Marsh, near Bowness-on-Solway, is a nature reserve run by the RSPB, a mix of salt marsh, wet grassland and raised bog, and in winter it fills with tens of thousands of geese, barnacle and pink-footed, arriving from the Arctic, along with waders that feed on the mud at low tide. Across the firth, the town of Annan and the Scottish hills are visible on a clear day.

Bowness-on-Solway marks the western end of Hadrian's Wall, where the fort of Maia stood, and the frontier continued along the coast with a chain of milefortlets and towers. The wall's line here is barely visible, and the village is small and quiet, with a pub and a few houses, many built with Roman stones. The Hadrian's Wall Path ends here, and walkers often celebrate in the pub.

The Solway coast is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and it feels remote despite being so close to Carlisle. The tides are fast and dangerous, and the sands can trap the unwary, so stick to the roads and paths. The coast road is narrow and flat, sometimes flooded at very high tides, with views over the marshes and the firth. Watch out for cattle and sheep on the road, which is unfenced in places.

The nearest towns with fuel and supplies are Silloth, a Victorian seaside resort to the south-west, Wigton, and Carlisle. Annan, across the water, is closer as the crow flies but a long ride around the head of the firth. Summer has its own charm, with natterjack toads calling at night and the bog covered in cotton grass. Come in autumn or winter for the geese, early in the morning or at dusk, when the skeins fly overhead, calling.
East of Carlisle, between the villages of Brampton and Wetheral, the countryside rolls gently towards the Pennines, with green fields, hedges and patches of woodland. Somewhere in these fields lie the faint traces of Watchclose, a Roman temporary camp, one of many marching camps built by soldiers on campaign or during the construction of Hadrian's Wall. These camps were enclosed by a ditch and bank and used for a night or a season, and today they are often visible only from the air or as slight undulations in the grass. Watchclose is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The wall itself runs a few kilometres to the north, through some of its most interesting western stretches. Birdoswald fort, perched above a gorge of the river Irthing, has well-preserved walls and gates, and a long section of the wall runs east from there. Lanercost Priory, a short ride from Brampton, is a beautiful ruined Augustinian abbey built partly with stone taken from the wall, and Edward I stayed there during his campaigns against the Scots. Carlisle, the border city, has a medieval castle and cathedral and a museum with a fine Roman collection.

The riding in this area is pleasant, with narrow lanes winding through farmland and villages, and the A69 offering a faster route between Carlisle and Newcastle. North of the wall, quieter roads lead into the hills and forests of Kielder, and south, the A686 climbs over the Pennines to Alston, one of the finest motorcycle roads in England, with long climbs, sweeping bends and spectacular views. Weather here can be wet and windy, even in summer, and mist and rain can descend quickly on the hills.

Brampton, a small market town with a few thousand inhabitants, has fuel, shops and pubs, and Carlisle has everything you need. Try a Cumberland sausage, a long coiled sausage seasoned with pepper, or a slice of Cumbrian ham with eggs, and finish with sticky toffee pudding, said to have been created in the Lake District not far away.
t.jodrell bank observatory@53.2,-2.3:
You see the dish long before you arrive. The Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank rises out of the flat Cheshire farmland like something from a science fiction film, a white steel bowl seventy six metres across, tilting slowly to follow its targets across the sky. When it was completed in 1957 it was the largest steerable radio telescope in the world, and one of its first tasks was tracking the rocket that carried Sputnik into orbit. The observatory, founded by Bernard Lovell after the Second World War, has been at the forefront of radio astronomy ever since, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2019 for its role in the development of the science.

The visitor centre explains the work of the observatory and offers a close view of the telescope, as well as gardens, an arboretum and a cafe. It is a fascinating place, even for those with only a passing interest in astronomy, and the sheer scale of the telescope is impressive up close. Visitors are asked to switch off mobile phones near the dish because they can interfere with the sensitive instruments.

The riding around Jodrell Bank is gentle and pleasant, with quiet lanes winding through the Cheshire countryside, past farms, woods and small villages. The roads are generally good but narrow, with hedges on both sides and occasional mud from farm vehicles. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, especially around the towns and the motorway junctions. The landscape is flat to gently rolling, with the hills of the Peak District rising to the east, and they offer more challenging and dramatic riding if you want to extend the day. The Cat and Fiddle road, running from Macclesfield towards Buxton, is famous among riders, though it is heavily policed and has average speed cameras.

Holmes Chapel, about five kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, shops and pubs, while Goostrey and Chelford are smaller villages with basic services. The weather in this part of England is mild but often damp, and the flat land is exposed to the wind. Clear nights are rarer than you would hope, but on the right evening the stars are surprisingly bright here, and it is easy to understand why the scientists chose this spot, far from city lights and radio noise.
t.lyme regis to west bay@50.7,-2.8:
The cliffs between Lyme Regis and West Bay are falling into the sea, and that is precisely why people come. This stretch of the Dorset coast is part of the Jurassic Coast, England's first natural World Heritage Site, and its soft clay and limestone cliffs constantly release fossils from the Jurassic seas of around two hundred million years ago. Ammonites, belemnites and the bones of marine reptiles wash out onto the beaches after every storm, and at Charmouth you will see families combing the shingle with hammers and bags at low tide.

The most famous fossil hunter of them all was Mary Anning, a working-class woman from Lyme Regis who, in the early nineteenth century, found the first complete ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons on these shores, and helped to change the scientific understanding of prehistoric life. Her story is told in the Lyme Regis museum, built on the site of her family home. Between Charmouth and West Bay rises Golden Cap, the highest point on the south coast of England, its top capped with golden sandstone that glows in the evening sun.

The main road along this coast, the A35, runs a little inland, climbing and descending through the hills with long views over the sea and countryside. It is a fine road to ride, with good surfaces and flowing bends, but it can be busy in summer with holiday traffic and caravans. The smaller roads down to the coast are narrow and steep, often single track with passing places, and they lead to small villages, beaches and car parks. Parking a bike is usually easier than parking a car, which is one advantage in high season.

Bridport, about six kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel, shops, a lively street market, and a long history of rope and net making. The phrase Bridport dagger was once grim slang for the hangman's rope. West Bay, the town's harbour, has golden cliffs that became familiar to television viewers as the backdrop of a crime drama, and stalls selling fish and chips and crab sandwiches. The weather on this coast is mild but changeable, and the cliffs are unstable, so keep away from the edges and the base, especially after heavy rain.
t.palisade ditches@54.9,-3.4:
Hadrian's Wall did not simply stop at the edge of the Solway. Beyond its western end at Bowness, the Romans continued the frontier down the Cumbrian coast with a chain of milefortlets and towers, and in places with ditches and palisades, to watch over the shoreline and guard against raids across the firth from what is now south west Scotland. The palisade ditches near Silloth are part of that coastal system, faint traces in the flat land behind the dunes, and they are a reminder that the Roman frontier was a complex network that stretched far beyond the famous stone wall.

The Solway coast is a strange and beautiful place, with wide, shallow sands, salt marshes and dunes, and huge skies over the water. Across the firth rises the dark bulk of Criffel in Scotland, and on clear evenings the sunsets here are spectacular, with the sea turning gold and pink. The area is a protected landscape, rich in birdlife, including vast flocks of geese in winter, and it is one of the few places in Britain where the rare natterjack toad still breeds, its loud rasping call carrying across the dunes on spring nights.

Silloth itself is a Victorian port and seaside town, built in the nineteenth century when the railway arrived, with a grid of wide streets, a long green along the seafront, and a working dock. It has a slightly faded charm, with cafes, chip shops and a few pubs, and it is a pleasant place to stop for a break. It has the basics for a town of its size, and Wigton and Aspatria are inland options if you need more.

The riding along the Solway is gentle and flat, with quiet roads winding through farmland and along the coast. The coast road north from Silloth to Bowness and on towards Carlisle passes through small villages and marshes, with views across the firth and the occasional flooded section at very high tides, so check tide times before setting off. The wind can be fierce, coming straight in off the sea. For a more dramatic ride, head south towards the Lake District, whose fells rise on the horizon and offer some of the best riding in England.
t.avebury and associated monuments@51.4,-1:
Avebury is the place where a village grew up inside a stone circle. The henge, a huge circular bank and ditch enclosing the largest stone circle in Britain, was built around four and a half thousand years ago, and the village, with its church, its manor house and its pub, sits partly within it, with a road running right through the middle. You can walk among the stones, touch them, sit beside them, and watch the sheep grazing around them, which is a very different experience from the controlled visits at Stonehenge, its more famous partner on the World Heritage list.

The monuments around Avebury form one of the richest prehistoric landscapes in Europe. Silbury Hill, the largest man-made mound in prehistoric Europe, rises beside the A4, a grassy cone whose purpose remains a mystery. West Kennet Long Barrow, a chambered tomb older than the stone circle, lies on a ridge to the south and can be reached by a short walk. The Kennet Avenue, a double line of standing stones, runs from the circle towards another site on Overton Hill, where the ancient trackway known as the Ridgeway begins its long journey across southern England.

Many of the stones you see today were reerected in the 1930s by Alexander Keiller, an archaeologist and heir to a marmalade fortune, who bought much of the village and excavated the site. Others had been toppled and buried in the Middle Ages, possibly as a result of the church's disapproval, or broken up for building stone. The museum in the village tells the story.

The riding here is through the rolling chalk downs of Wiltshire, with long, open roads, wide views and gentle bends. The roads can be busy, especially the A4 and the main roads around Marlborough and Swindon, and the narrow lanes through the downs are often used by tractors and horse riders. The weather can be windy and exposed on the high ground. Marlborough, about nine kilometres away, is a handsome market town with a wide high street, fuel, shops and cafes. Avebury village has a cafe and shops run by the National Trust, which looks after the site, and the stones are at their most atmospheric early in the morning or at sunset, when the crowds have gone.
t.biglands house@54.9,-3.2:
Out on the Cumbrian shore of the Solway Firth, at the far western end of Hadrian's frontier, Biglands is a farmhouse name attached to the site of a small Roman milefortlet, one of the posts that carried the Wall's chain of defences down the coast once the stone curtain itself had stopped at Bowness. There is very little to see above ground; the fortlet was excavated and then returned to the grass. What you come for is the setting and the sense of standing at the edge of an empire, looking across a few kilometres of mud and water at Scotland.

The Solway is a strange, compelling landscape. Salt marsh stretches out for miles, cut by creeks that fill and drain with the tide, and the bore can come in surprisingly fast. Across the water Annan and the hills of Dumfriesshire look close enough to touch, which is exactly why the Romans watched this coast so closely: at low tide the firth could be waded by raiders who knew the fords. In winter tens of thousands of barnacle geese from Svalbard settle on the marshes, and the sky fills with noise at dusk.

Roads out here are narrow, flat and quiet, running behind the sea dyke between Bowness-on-Solway, Port Carlisle and Glasson. One stretch near Port Carlisle floods on the highest tides, so look at the water rather than trusting the tarmac; signs warn you, and they mean it. Expect gravel washed onto corners, the odd sheep and wind straight off the Irish Sea that leaves you leaning into the gusts. Visibility is long and the light changes by the minute, which makes it a lovely evening ride if the weather is kind.

Annan is the nearest real town as the crow flies, but there is no bridge across the firth, so by road your services are back towards Carlisle or Wigton, half an hour or so away. The villages have the occasional pub, and Bowness marks the start, or finish, of the Hadrian's Wall Path, so walkers will be the people you meet. Bring a layer: even in July it can feel like October on the marsh.
t.chesil@50.6,-2.6:
Twenty-nine kilometres of shingle, piled high and steep and running almost dead straight from West Bay to the Isle of Portland: Chesil Beach is one of the great natural oddities of the English coast. Behind it lies the Fleet, a long, shallow, brackish lagoon full of eelgrass and birds, and the whole system is part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site. The pebbles grade in size along the beach, small as peas at the western end and as big as potatoes towards Portland, so precisely that smugglers landing on dark nights were said to know where they were by the feel of the stones.

That smuggling past fed J. Meade Falkner's novel Moonfleet, set along this shore, and the old fishing communities still haul boats up the shingle in places. At Abbotsbury, at the western end of the Fleet, the swannery founded by Benedictine monks centuries ago still keeps a large colony of mute swans, and the stark chapel of St Catherine sits on its hill above the village. Ferrybridge, at the Portland end, is where most people first walk up onto the bank and hear that particular roar of waves dragging stones.

The B3157 between Weymouth, Abbotsbury and Bridport is the riding reason to be here, and it is one of the finest coast roads in southern England. West of Abbotsbury it climbs onto the downs and gives you the whole sweep of Chesil and Lyme Bay laid out below, with fast, open bends and some steep dips where the road crosses combes. It is popular, which means caravans in summer, plenty of cyclists and a firm police interest in speed. Midweek in spring or early autumn, with low sun over the sea, it is hard to beat.

Weymouth, eight kilometres away, has fuel, food and everything else; Bridport at the other end does too. Abbotsbury has tearooms and a pub and makes a civilised halfway halt. Swimming off Chesil is not for casual dips: the beach shelves very steeply and the undertow is notorious, so enjoy the water from the top of the bank. Sea mist can roll in quickly here even on bright days and turn the road damp and grey within minutes.
t.drumburgh roman fort and hadrian s wall:
The small Roman fort at Drumburgh sat on a low rise above the Solway marshes, guarding a stretch of Hadrian's Wall where the frontier ran along the edge of the firth towards its western end at Bowness. Nothing much survives of the fort itself, but its stones did not go far. Drumburgh Castle, a fortified farmhouse built in the sixteenth century by the Dacre family, is clearly made from reused Roman masonry, and you can still pick out dressed blocks and even the odd carved fragment set into its walls.

This was hard border country long after the legions left. The lands around the Solway were raided back and forth by the reiver families for centuries, which explains the bastle houses and fortified farms scattered across the flat landscape. A short ride east at Burgh by Sands, a monument on the marsh marks where Edward I, the Hammer of the Scots, died in 1307 while waiting to lead yet another army across the firth. The church at Burgh itself is built within the outline of another Roman fort and has a defensive tower for sheltering villagers.

The road through Drumburgh is a single lane across open, flat ground, more like a polder in the Netherlands than anything English. Glasson and Port Carlisle are just along the shore, and the road between them can be flooded at high tide, so check the tide if you are heading west. It is not a place for speed; it is a place for slow riding with the visor up, smelling salt and cut grass, watching curlews and lapwings lift off the marsh. In a westerly gale it is hard work, and after rain the verges collect mud from farm traffic.

Eastriggs and Annan show up as near neighbours on a map, but they are on the Scottish side with water in between. By road, Carlisle is your town, about twenty minutes east, with fuel, food and the castle and cathedral if you have time. A small village pub is the most you can hope for out here, and not every village has one, so carry water. If you are following the Wall Path, this flat stretch is where walkers tend to slow down and look out over the firth, and it rewards riders who do the same.
t.swarthy hill north tower 20b@54.7,-3.4:
Along the Cumbrian coast between Silloth and Maryport, the Roman frontier did not end when Hadrian's stone Wall reached Bowness. A chain of milefortlets and towers continued down the shore, watching the Solway for raiders arriving by boat, and Tower 20b near Swarthy Hill is one of them. It was a small stone watchtower, probably manned by a handful of soldiers, and what remains is a low outline in the turf above the beach. You come for the context and the view across the water rather than for the masonry.

That view is a fine one. Looking north-west across the firth you see the rounded bulk of Criffel above the Scottish shore, and on clear days the hills of Galloway stretch away beyond it. The beach below is a mix of shingle, sand and rock scars, with dunes and coastal grassland held together by marram and sea holly. Natterjack toads breed in a few spots along this coast, and the evening light out over the Irish Sea, with the Isle of Man sometimes visible, is reason enough to linger.

The B5300 runs along this coast from Silloth through Allonby to Maryport, and it is an easy, enjoyable road: mostly straight, open to the sea on one side, with gentle bends, a few village speed limits and wide verges where people park to walk the beach. Wind is the main hazard, often strong and gusty off the sea, and sand blows onto the road in places. On a sunny weekend Allonby fills up with day trippers and ice-cream queues, but on a weekday evening it can be almost empty.

Maryport, five kilometres south, is the place for fuel and food, and it repays an hour. The Romans had a substantial fort there called Alauna, and the Senhouse Roman Museum on the cliff above the harbour holds a remarkable collection of altars dedicated by commanders of the garrison, dug up from pits near the fort. The town itself grew in the eighteenth century as a coal and shipbuilding port and still has a handsome harbour. Allonby, closer to the tower, has a café or two and a few benches that face exactly the right way.
t.bowleaze cove to peveril point@50.6,-2.2:
This is where the geology lesson becomes a spectacle: Lulworth Cove, an almost perfect circle bitten out of soft clays behind a narrow gap in the harder limestone, and Durdle Door just to the west, an arch of Portland stone standing in clear green water. The Lulworth Crumple, where the rock layers have been bent nearly vertical by the same forces that raised the Alps, is visible at Stair Hole.

A large chunk of this coast is an army firing range, and that accident of history has kept it wild. The villagers of Tyneham were moved out in 1943 so the land could be used for training, and they never came back; the village survives as a quiet ghost settlement with its church and school preserved, open when the ranges are. The range roads and walks open mostly at weekends and in holiday periods, and red flags mean what they say. Further east, Corfe Castle stands broken on its hill, slighted by Parliament after the Civil War.

Riding here means small roads with big views. The lanes from Wool and Wareham to Lulworth climb over open chalk downs, with the steep descent into West Lulworth and the range road over to Kimmeridge and Steeple giving long views down to the sea. Expect narrow sections, hedges hiding bends, horse riders, tractors and, on sunny summer weekends, serious congestion around Lulworth and Corfe. Spring and autumn midweek are the sweet spots, ideally early morning before the car parks fill.

Wareham, nine kilometres away, is the nearest proper town with fuel, a supermarket and riverside pubs; Wool has a little more than the basics. Lulworth has cafés and pubs by the cove, and Corfe has tearooms aplenty in the shadow of the ruin. If you swim at Durdle Door or in the cove, the water is clean and cold and the beaches are steep, and the long staircase back up to the car park is a good reminder that motorcycle boots are not hiking boots.
t.gorseddau and prince of wales slate quar:
High above Porthmadog, in the empty upland between Cwm Pennant and Cwmystradllyn, two abandoned slate quarries sit like ruined castles on the hillside. Gorseddau and the Prince of Wales quarry are part of the Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales, which UNESCO listed in 2021, and they tell a story of big hopes and quick failure. Gorseddau in particular was developed in the 1850s with money and ambition, a tramway and a grand multi-storey mill at Ynys-y-Pandy whose roofless stone shell still looks like an abbey. The slate turned out to be poor, and within a couple of decades the whole enterprise had wound down.

What you find now are terraced galleries cut into the mountain, spoil heaps of blue-grey waste spilling down the slopes, the trackbeds of old tramways contouring across the hills and the remains of barracks where quarrymen lodged through the week. Sheep graze among it all. On a still day the only sounds are skylarks and the wind in the grass, and the reservoir of Llyn Cwmystradllyn lies dark below, backed by the bulk of Moel Hebog.

Getting there is half the fun. Narrow single-track lanes leave the A487 and A497 and wind up into the hills through gates and over cattle grids, with grass growing down the middle and walls close on both sides. They are slow, beautiful and demanding: blind bends, sudden steep pitches, loose stones and the occasional tractor coming the other way. Pull in where you can and let walkers' cars pass. The last stretch to the quarries themselves is on foot, so park considerately at the reservoir end.

Porthmadog, the nearest town, grew as the harbour from which slate went out to the world, and the Ffestiniog Railway still runs steam trains from its quay up to Blaenau Ffestiniog. It has fuel, cafes, chip shops and supermarkets. Criccieth's castle on its headland is a short ride west, and Portmeirion's Italianate fantasy village is just across the estuary. Weather in Snowdonia changes quickly; cloud can drop onto the hills in minutes, and the lanes stay greasy long after rain, so ride them with the patience they deserve.
t.brownrigg north tower 21b@54.7,-3.5:
Most people think Hadrian's Wall stops at the Solway, but the Roman frontier did not simply end at the water's edge. Beyond Bowness a chain of milefortlets and towers ran on down the Cumbrian coast, watching the sea and the hills of Scotland across the firth, and Brownrigg North, tower 21b in the archaeologists' numbering, was one of them. There is little to see on the ground now, often just a gentle swelling in a field, but stand here and look west and you understand why it was put there: the Solway opens out, and on a clear day the Galloway hills and the Isle of Man line the horizon.

The anchor of this coastal system was Maryport, four kilometres away, where a Roman fort called Alauna stood on the cliff above the harbour. An extraordinary group of Roman altars was dug up there in the nineteenth century, many of them now displayed in the Senhouse Roman Museum, which occupies an old naval battery overlooking the site. They were dedicated to Jupiter by successive commanders, and they are among the finest collections of their kind in Britain.

This is a different Cumbria from the Lake District tourist circuit, a coast of old mining and port towns, with Workington and Whitehaven to the south and the Solway marshes to the north. The A596 coast road is fast and fairly straight, with some lovely stretches where the sea is right beside you; smaller lanes inland towards Dearham and Cockermouth climb into green rolling country with views of the northern fells, Skiddaw dominant among them. Watch for agricultural traffic and mud, and in winter for salt spray on the coast road.

Maryport has fuel, shops, chippies and a harbour where you can sit and watch the tide, which rises and falls a long way here. Its Georgian streets climb up from the water, and the town was the birthplace of Thomas Ismay, founder of the White Star Line that later owned the Titanic. Sunsets over the Solway can be spectacular. When the westerlies are blowing, though, it can be properly wild, so check the forecast before you commit to the exposed stretches.
t.city of bath@51.4,-2.4:
Bath is one of the few whole cities on the UNESCO list, and it earns it twice over. Underneath lie the Roman baths of Aquae Sulis, built around the only natural hot springs in Britain, where water still comes up at around forty-six degrees and the great pool, with its later colonnade above, steams in the cold. On top sits the Georgian city that eighteenth-century society built when Bath became the place to see and be seen, in honey-coloured local limestone: the Circus, the sweep of the Royal Crescent, the shops on Pulteney Bridge over the Avon and the long elegant terraces climbing the hills.

Jane Austen lived here for a few years and used it in two of her novels, not always kindly, and the city still enjoys the connection. The abbey in the centre, with angels climbing ladders carved up its west front, is late Gothic and well worth a look inside for its fan vaulting.

As a riding destination, Bath is a city to walk, not to ride. It sits in a bowl of the Avon valley, and every road into it funnels traffic into a congested centre with one-way systems, buses and steep hills. Parking for motorbikes exists in town, but plan it before you arrive. The city introduced a clean air zone in 2021, aimed at commercial vehicles; private motorcycles are not charged, but check the current rules if you are on anything unusual. Arrive early or late and you will be happier.

The good news is everything around it. Within a few minutes you are into the southern Cotswolds, the Limpley Stoke valley with its canal and aqueducts, or out towards the Mendips, with lanes that twist through limestone villages and over steep wooded hills. Some are narrow and high-hedged, with gravel in the middle and tight blind corners, so take them gently. Fuel is easy on the main roads out of Bath; there are cafes on every corner in the city, a famous Sally Lunn bun if you want one, and the Thermae spa if you fancy floating in the hot water yourself.
t.bryneglwys slate quarry@52.6,-4.0:
High above the village of Abergynolwyn, in a side valley where the sheep outnumber everyone, the spoil heaps of Bryneglwys tell you that this quiet corner of southern Snowdonia was once an industrial place. Slate was cut here through the second half of the nineteenth century and into the twentieth, and the whole reason the little Talyllyn Railway exists is to carry it down the valley to the coast at Tywyn. The quarry finally closed just after the Second World War, and the railway, which should have died with it, was taken over by volunteers in 1951 and became the first preserved railway in the world. You can still walk up from the old incline at Nant Gwernol into the quarry workings, past roofless barracks and wheel pits, with streams running through all of it.

The riding around here is gentle in speed and big in scenery. The B4405 from Tywyn follows the Dysynni and then the Fathew valley up to Tal-y-llyn lake, a long ribbon of water under the steep southern face of Cadair Idris. The road is narrow, the stone walls are close and the sheep consider the tarmac theirs, so it rewards a calm pace rather than heroics. Beyond the lake you join the A487 and climb to the junction at Cross Foxes, then drop either to Dolgellau or south towards Machynlleth, and that stretch has real corners and real views. Off the main roads the lanes become single track with passing places and grass up the middle.

Near the mouth of the valley sit the ruins of Castell y Bere, built by Llywelyn the Great in the thirteenth century to guard this approach, and it is worth the short detour for the setting alone, on a rocky knoll with the Dysynni flats below. Further down, Craig yr Aderyn, Bird Rock, is one of the odd places in Britain where cormorants nest inland, a reminder that the sea once reached much further up this valley.

There is nothing at the quarry itself, so think ahead. Tywyn and Machynlleth both have fuel and shops, Barmouth too, and Aberystwyth is the nearest proper town if you need more. Abergynolwyn has a café and a pub, and the station at Tywyn has tea rooms for railway people. Pack waterproofs whatever the forecast says: Cadair Idris makes its own weather, and it usually makes rain.
You hear it before you understand it: water running in an iron trough thirty-eight metres above the River Dee, on stone piers so slender they look drawn rather than built. Thomas Telford and William Jessop finished the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct in 1805 to carry what is now the Llangollen Canal across the valley, and more than two centuries later narrowboats still glide over it, steered by people trying very hard not to look down. There is a towpath on one side with railings; on the other side there is only the edge of the trough and air. Walk across if you have a head for heights. It is one of the strangest and best ten minutes in Wales.

The aqueduct belongs to a whole engineered landscape. A few miles south, Chirk has its own aqueduct with a railway viaduct right alongside, and upstream the canal is fed from the Dee at the Horseshoe Falls, which is a curved weir rather than a waterfall but beautiful all the same. Telford also built the A5 through here, the London to Holyhead road, with gradients gentle enough for mail coaches, and you can feel his hand in the way it flows along the valley.

For riders the real magnet is a few miles up the valley at Llangollen. From the town the A542 climbs the Horseshoe Pass, a proper set of bends looping up a bare hillside to the café at the top, a well-known meeting place for bikers on any dry weekend. Beyond it the road drops towards Ruthin and the Clwydian hills. Alternatively the B5605 and the lanes around Ruabon and Rhosllanerchrugog take you through old coal country, where terraced villages and chapels sit on the slopes. In wet weather watch for slick slate chippings and farm mud; in summer the A5 through Llangollen can crawl behind caravans.

Trevor Basin, at the north end of the aqueduct, has parking, a café and a pub, and it is where you will start the walk across. Fuel is easy in Ruabon, Chirk and Llangollen, and Rhosllanerchrugog has the full range of shops.
