Llangollen itself is a good lunch town, with the Dee crashing over rocks right under the bridge and the ruins of Castell Dinas Brân on the hill above, a steep walk that pays you back with the whole valley at your feet.
t.beaumont motte castle and section of had:
Beaumont is one of those small places where history is stacked in layers, like books on a shelf. The little church of St Mary stands on a grassy mound that was once a Norman motte, a castle earthwork, and that mound in turn sits right on the line of Hadrian's Wall as it heads west from Carlisle towards the Solway. The builders of the motte used the Roman wall as a convenient quarry and foundation, and the church builders after them did the same. You will find no tall Roman masonry here, only the line itself, traced in field boundaries and the slight rise of the ground, and an awareness that you are standing on the edge of an empire.

West of Carlisle the wall was originally built of turf and later rebuilt in stone, and much of that stone has long since vanished into farm buildings across the parish. The countryside is flat and green, with the River Eden winding through its last loops before it reaches the estuary. A couple of miles on, at Burgh by Sands, a monument on the marsh marks where Edward I, the Hammer of the Scots, died in 1307 while waiting to cross into Scotland with yet another army. It is a lonely spot, open to the wind off the Solway, and strangely moving.

For riding, this is gentle country. The lanes from Carlisle out through Kirkandrews, Beaumont and Burgh are narrow, often hedged, sometimes muddy with tractor tracks, and they reward a slow, curious pace. Push further west towards Bowness-on-Solway, where the wall ended, and the road runs right across the salt marsh, with tide warning signs that you should take seriously: at high spring tides the sea covers the tarmac. The views across the firth to the hills of Scotland, with Criffel standing out, are the reason to go.

There is nothing in Beaumont itself beyond the church and a handful of houses. Carlisle is close, a real city with fuel, food and everything else, and it is worth an hour in its own right for the red sandstone castle and the cathedral. Gretna lies just across the border to the north if you fancy notching up Scotland. Bring a layer: the wind from the estuary can feel cold even on a sunny summer afternoon.
t.hadrian s wall between the field boundar:
Just outside Carlisle, among hedges and grazing fields, a short protected length of ground marks where Hadrian's Wall once ran between two farm boundaries. That is all the official name means, and the honest truth is that there is very little to see: a gentle bank, perhaps a slight ditch, the alignment of a hedge that follows the Roman line because nobody ever bothered to move it. What makes it worth a pause is the bigger picture. The wall here was heading for the crossing of the River Eden, where it met the fort of Stanwix on the north bank, the biggest fort on the entire frontier, home to an elite cavalry regiment a thousand strong.

Carlisle grew out of that military presence as Luguvalium, and through the centuries it remained a frontier town. The castle, begun under William II in the late eleventh century, was fought over by English and Scots for generations; Mary, Queen of Scots, was held there in 1568 after fleeing across the border. Later this whole region was the stamping ground of the Border Reivers, raiding families who stole cattle across a border that meant little to them. Tullie House museum in the city centre tells their story and the Roman one well, and it is a good place to dry off if the weather turns.

The River Eden gives this stretch its character. It meanders across a wide flood plain here, lined with willows and alders, and the meadows can lie under water after heavy rain in the Pennines. Herons work the shallows, and in winter big flocks of geese come in from the Solway. The light is soft and grey-green much of the year, and on a still evening the smell is of wet grass and river mud.

As a riding place it is a pause rather than a destination. The lanes are narrow and quiet, linking villages like Grinsdale and Kirkandrews-on-Eden, with occasional blind bends between hedges and the odd cow-churned patch. The fun roads lie further out: east along the Military Road, south into the Lake District, or north across the border into Dumfries and Galloway. Carlisle, a few kilometres away, has every service you could want, from fuel to a proper sit-down meal, so use the city as your base and treat this field as the quiet prologue.
t.beckfoot roman fort@54.8,-3.4:
Most people think Hadrian's Wall ended at Bowness-on-Solway, and in stone it did. But the Romans did not trust the shallow Solway Firth to keep raiders out, so they carried their defences on down the Cumbrian coast for many miles: a chain of small milefortlets and watchtowers, with proper forts at intervals, all the way to Maryport and beyond. Beckfoot is one of those forts, on a low bluff a few kilometres south of Silloth, looking straight across the water to Scotland. Above ground there is almost nothing, just a field with faint outlines, but aerial photos and excavations have shown the fort, its civilian settlement and its cemetery, and coastal erosion keeps nibbling at the remains.

What you do get is the landscape the Romans watched. The Solway coast is wide and open, with dunes, salt marsh and shingle, and the sky seems twice its usual size. On a clear day the granite bulk of Criffel stands up across the firth, and the sunsets over the Irish Sea are spectacular. Natterjack toads breed in the pools along this coast, and the marshes fill with waders and wildfowl in winter. The air smells of salt and seaweed, and there is almost always a breeze.

The B5300 runs along the coast from Silloth to Maryport, and it is a lovely, easy road: flat, with long views over the shore, occasional gentle bends and very little traffic out of season. Wind is the main hazard, strong crosswinds off the sea can catch you on exposed stretches, along with sand drifting across the tarmac after storms. Inland, the lanes through the Cumbrian plain towards Aspatria and Wigton are quiet and hedged, good for unwinding after the busier roads of the Lakes.

Silloth is a Victorian port town with a broad green, a cobbled main street and the big Carr's flour mill by the docks, and it has shops, cafés and fuel. Maryport, further south, is larger and home to the Senhouse Roman Museum, which holds a remarkable collection of altars dug up next to the fort of Alauna, and it is the place to see what these coastal garrisons actually left behind. Between the two there are small caravan parks and beach car parks, but not much else, so time your stops around the towns.
t.new swanage to studland bay@50.6,-1.9:
Between Swanage and Studland, the chalk of the Purbeck Hills meets the sea at the Foreland, and the white stacks of Old Harry Rocks stand off the headland like broken teeth. This is the eastern end of the Jurassic Coast, the World Heritage stretch of Dorset and East Devon that runs back through two hundred million years of geological history, and here the rocks are the youngest of the sequence, Cretaceous chalk. From Ballard Down above New Swanage, the views take in Swanage Bay, the Isle of Wight and the long sandy curve of Studland Bay.

Studland Bay is one of the finest beaches in southern England, backed by sand dunes and heathland managed by the National Trust, home to all six species of British reptile, including smooth snakes and sand lizards. Part of the beach is a naturist area. During the Second World War the bay was used for rehearsals for the D-Day landings, and a concrete bunker, Fort Henry, was built for Churchill, Eisenhower and others to watch the exercises.

The riding in Purbeck is pleasant but busy in summer. The road from Swanage to Studland climbs over the hills with views, and continues to the chain ferry at Sandbanks, which crosses the mouth of Poole Harbour in a few minutes and is a fun way to arrive or leave. Corfe Castle, a dramatic ruin on a hill in a gap in the Purbeck Hills, is a short ride inland. The roads are narrow and twisty in places, with tractors, cyclists and tourists.

Swanage has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat, and the Swanage Railway, a heritage steam line, runs to Corfe Castle and beyond. Studland has a pub and a café or two, and the National Trust has facilities at the beach. Fish and chips on the Swanage seafront is the classic end to a day in Purbeck.
t.portland harbour shore@50.6,-2.5:
Portland Harbour is one of the largest man made harbours in the world, enclosed by breakwaters built in the nineteenth century, partly by convict labour, from Portland stone quarried on the island above. For over a century it was a major Royal Navy base, and today it is a centre for sailing, windsurfing and kite surfing; the sailing events of the 2012 London Olympics were held here. The shore between Weymouth and Portland, with Chesil Beach stretching away to the west, is a fascinating place to explore.

The Isle of Portland, linked to the mainland by a narrow causeway and the end of Chesil Beach, is a block of limestone, famous for its stone, which was used to build St Paul's Cathedral, Buckingham Palace and many other buildings. The island has quarries, prisons, lighthouses and wild cliffs, and the views from the top over Chesil Beach and the harbour are spectacular. Chesil Beach itself, a shingle bank about eighteen miles long, has pebbles graded by size along its length, from pea sized at the west end to fist sized at Portland.

The riding here is a mix of town and coast. Weymouth is a busy seaside resort, with traffic in summer, and the road to Portland crosses the causeway and climbs steeply to the top of the island. The roads on Portland are narrow and twisty, with views on every side. The coast road west from Weymouth toward Abbotsbury and Bridport is one of the finest in Dorset, with views over Chesil Beach and the Fleet lagoon.

Weymouth has filling stations and supermarkets on its outskirts, and the old harbour area is lively, with pubs and restaurants. Portland has its own services. In the pubs, try local ales and seafood, especially crab and lobster from the Dorset coast. The weather here can be windy, which is great for sailors but less so for riders.
t.caradon mining district@50.5,-4.4:
Engine houses stand like chess pieces on the southern flank of Bodmin Moor, tall granite boxes with their chimneys still pointing at the sky, and around them the ground is scarred by spoil heaps, shafts and old tramway beds. This is the Caradon Mining District, around the village of Pensilva and the hill of Caradon, where copper was found in the 1830s and set off a boom that made it, for a few decades, one of the richest copper districts in Britain. It is one of the ten areas of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape World Heritage Site, listed in 2006.

The boom brought thousands of people, new villages like Minions and Pensilva, chapels and a railway, the Liskeard and Caradon line, which carried ore down to the canal and the port of Looe. When copper prices collapsed later in the century, the miners left, many for the mines of America, Australia and South Africa, taking Cornish engineering and the pasty with them. The moor took back what was left.

Up on the high ground around Minions the views are enormous, across Bodmin Moor to the north and down to the Tamar valley and Plymouth Sound on clear days. Bronze Age monuments sit among the mine ruins: the Hurlers, three stone circles, and the Cheesewring, a stack of granite slabs balanced on a tor above an old quarry. Ponies and sheep graze freely, and skylarks sing over the heather in spring.

The roads up here are narrow, unfenced in places and sometimes shared with livestock, with cattle grids, blind crests and very little room to pass. They are fun at a gentle pace, with long views and open moorland, but the weather can close in quickly with fog and rain sweeping across from the Atlantic. The lanes down to Liskeard and Callington are the classic Cornish type, sunk between high hedges, so take blind bends with care and expect tractors.

Pensilva is a village with a shop, and Minions has a tea room and a pub. For fuel, go to Liskeard, six kilometres away and a market town of over nine thousand people, or to Callington. A Cornish pasty from a proper baker in Liskeard is the obvious lunch.
t.rise how tower 25a@54.7,-3.5:
Hadrian's Wall does not simply stop at the Solway. Beyond Bowness, the Romans extended their frontier down the Cumbrian coast with a chain of milefortlets and towers, watching the shore against raiders crossing from what is now south-west Scotland. Rise How tower 25a is one of them, on the low cliffs just south of Maryport near Flimby, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. Little is visible above ground, but standing here and looking out over the water, you can see why they bothered.

On a clear day, the hills of Dumfries and Galloway, including Criffel, rise across the Solway Firth, and the Isle of Man floats on the horizon to the west. Behind you, inland, the fells of the Lake District crowd the skyline, with Skiddaw and the north-western fells closest. The coast itself is a mix of low cliffs, shingle beaches, dunes and the remains of old industry: coal mines, ironworks and harbours that once made this a busy coast.

Maryport, just north, was built in the eighteenth century as a coal port and named after the wife of the landowner who developed it. Before that, the Romans had a large fort here, Alauna, and the Senhouse Roman Museum, beside the fort site, has one of the finest collections of Roman altars in Britain, many found buried in pits near the fort. The town also has a maritime museum and a harbour with colourful boats.

The riding along this coast is a mixed bag. The A596 between Workington and Maryport is busy with traffic, but the minor roads along the coast and inland towards the Lake District are more fun, with bends, hills and views. A short ride east takes you into the Lakes, with famous passes like Honister, Newlands and Whinlatter, steep, narrow and spectacular, though busy in summer. The weather can be wild, with wind and rain sweeping in off the sea, so be prepared.

Maryport, under two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Workington, a few kilometres south, is a larger town with more options. Grab a bag of fish and chips and eat them on the harbour wall, watching the sun sink over the Solway; on a good evening, it is as fine a view as any in the north of England.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between the m6 mot:
On the eastern edge of Carlisle, where the M6 motorway sweeps north towards Scotland, the line of Hadrian's Wall crosses the fields and housing estates in a way that is barely visible. Yet the vallum, the great ditch the Romans dug south of the Wall, can still be traced here as a slight dip in the ground, and this stretch between the motorway and the outskirts of the city is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. It takes some imagination, but standing here you are on the line that marked the edge of the empire for nearly three hundred years.

Carlisle, just west, has been a border city for two thousand years. The Romans built a fort here, Luguvalium, which became an important town and supply base for the Wall. In the Middle Ages, the city changed hands several times between England and Scotland, and its castle, a massive red sandstone fortress, was besieged many times, most famously in the Jacobite rising of 1745, when Bonnie Prince Charlie's army captured it before retreating. Mary, Queen of Scots, was held prisoner there in 1568. The cathedral, one of the smallest in England, has a beautiful painted ceiling.

The Border Reivers, raiding families who terrorised the borderlands from the thirteenth to the seventeenth centuries, are a big part of local history. The Tullie House Museum in Carlisle tells their story, along with that of the Romans and the city itself. Names like Armstrong, Elliot and Graham are still common in the area, descendants of the reiving families.

The riding here is a mix of city and country. The roads into and out of Carlisle are busy, but heading east along the A69 or the Military Road takes you into the wild landscapes of the central Wall. South, the Eden valley offers quiet, scenic roads through red sandstone villages and farmland, with the Pennines rising to the east. North, the Scottish border is just a few miles away, with the rolling hills of Dumfries and Galloway beyond.

Carlisle, about three kilometres away, has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. Scotby, a small village nearby, has basic services. In Carlisle, look for a pub serving Cumberland sausage, a long, coiled pork sausage that is a local speciality, with mash and onion gravy, or stop by a bakery for a Cumbrian rum butter tart.
t.cardurnock milefortlet@54.9,-3.3:
The Cardurnock peninsula pokes out into the upper Solway Firth like a thumb, a flat, wind-scoured finger of farmland and salt marsh west of Bowness-on-Solway, with the tide sweeping in and out over the sands on three sides. Beyond the end of Hadrian's Wall, the Romans continued their defences down the coast with a chain of small forts and towers, and Cardurnock milefortlet was one of them, a small walled post with a handful of men keeping an eye on the fords and the open water. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site, though nothing much is visible now beyond the lie of the land.

What you will notice is the space. The Solway is one of the largest estuaries in Britain, and at low tide vast expanses of sand and mud are exposed, cut by channels that fill rapidly as the tide returns, which it does at a frightening speed. The salt marshes along the shore, grazed by cattle and sheep, are an important habitat for birds, and in winter tens of thousands of barnacle geese arrive from Svalbard to feed here, along with pink-footed geese, waders and ducks. Their calls and the sight of them lifting off the marshes at dawn are unforgettable.

Across the water, the hills of Dumfries and Galloway rise, with Criffel prominent, and on a clear day you can see the towns of Annan and the old Chapelcross nuclear power station, whose cooling towers were demolished in 2007. The remains of the Solway Junction Railway viaduct, which once crossed the firth to Scotland, can still be seen near Bowness.

The riding on the peninsula is peaceful and flat, with narrow lanes running along the shore and between farms, and little traffic. The roads can flood at very high tides, especially near Bowness and Port Carlisle, so check the tide tables and heed the warning signs. Strong winds are common, coming in off the sea. The landscape is stark and beautiful, with huge skies and changing light.

Silloth, about seven and a half kilometres away as the crow flies but further by road, has fuel and services. Annan, across the water in Scotland, is close in distance but not by road. Carlisle and Wigton are the main inland towns. The RSPB reserve at Campfield Marsh, nearby, is worth a visit for birdwatchers.

Silloth is a Victorian seaside town that never quite got the crowds it was built for, and it is all the better for that. Laid out in the 1850s as a port and resort at the end of a railway from Carlisle, it has wide cobbled streets, terraces of sandstone houses and a huge open green between the town and the sea, where people stroll, play and watch the sunsets over the Solway. On the dunes south of the town, near the famous golf course, the Romans built a chain of towers along the coast, and tower 12a was one of them, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The golf course itself is a classic links, laid out among the dunes and considered one of the best in England. The towers along the coast were part of a defensive system that extended Hadrian's Wall down the Cumbrian coast, watching for raiders from across the firth. Nothing remains to see of tower 12a, but the dunes and the views over the sea give a sense of what the soldiers would have seen.

Silloth is also known for Carr's flour mill, which has been grinding flour on the docks since the late nineteenth century, and the port still handles cargo ships. The sunsets here are famous, with the sun dropping behind the hills of Dumfries and Galloway across the water, painting the sky in reds and golds. Criffel, the hill opposite, is a landmark visible from much of the coast.

The riding around here is flat and coastal, with quiet roads along the shore and through farmland. Silloth, under two kilometres away, has fuel, shops, cafés and fish and chip shops. Wigton, about sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. Grab an ice cream and sit on the green, watching the ships come in and the sun go down over Scotland.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between the track:
Between Bowness-on-Solway and Drumburgh, the road follows the shore of the Solway Firth along a strip of land so flat and low that the highest tides cover it, and the line of Hadrian's Wall and its vallum runs just inland, through fields and past farms. This stretch, near Port Carlisle and Glasson, is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. Little is visible of the Wall itself, which was robbed for stone long ago, but the vallum and other earthworks can be traced in places by those with a keen eye.

It opened in 1823, but it was never a great success, and in the 1850s it was drained and converted into a railway, whose trains were later pulled by a horse in their final years. The remains of the canal basin and the harbour can still be seen, and the village is a peaceful place with a few houses and a pub.

Glasson Moss, inland from the shore, is one of the best-preserved lowland raised bogs in England, a national nature reserve with rare plants, insects and birds. The salt marshes along the shore are grazed by sheep and cattle and are home to thousands of waders and geese in winter. The views over the Solway to Scotland, with the hills of Dumfries and Galloway rising beyond, are beautiful, especially at sunset.

The riding here is gentle and peaceful, along narrow lanes beside the marshes, with little traffic. The road floods at high tides, with marker posts showing the depth, so check tide times and do not try to cross when the water is over the road. The landscape is flat and open, with huge skies and constantly changing light, and the wind can be strong.

Carlisle, about fifteen kilometres to the east, is the nearest city with all services. Wigton, to the south, is a small market town. Annan and Gretna, though close across the water, are a long way round by road. The pub in Port Carlisle and the one in Bowness are good stops for a pint and a meal.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between east side:
The Solway Firth, west of Carlisle, is a wide, shallow estuary where the Cumbrian plain opens out to the sea, and the marshes and farmland on its southern shore are the western end of Hadrian's Wall, with the Scottish hills visible on the far side. The land is low, wet and windy, with cattle in the fields and tall skies full of birds, and a visitor will find little that looks like Roman engineering until they look closely at the ground.

Hadrian's Wall was begun in about AD 122, in the reign of the emperor whose name it bears, and it ran for eighty Roman miles from the Tyne to the Solway. Beside it, to the south, the Romans dug the Vallum, a huge flat-bottomed ditch with a bank on each side, a feature found nowhere else on the empire's frontiers. Nobody is quite sure of its purpose, but it probably marked the southern edge of the military zone and controlled movement to and from the wall. On this stretch the earthworks are faint, softened by farming and time, but in good light you can pick out the ditch as a long hollow crossing the fields. Do not expect stone, because much of the wall here was built of turf and later rebuilt, and the farmers of the area took the rest for their buildings.

Nearby, at Burgh by Sands, King Edward I died of dysentery in July 1307, on his way to fight the Scots, and a monument stands on the marsh where he is said to have fallen. The Solway has some of the fastest tides in Britain, which rush in across the sands, so keep away from the shore unless you know the times.

The roads here are quiet and flat, with long straights and sharp, sudden bends between hedges, and the B5307 follows the line of the Wall through the villages. Gravel and mud from farm vehicles can be a hazard. Wind is strong off the firth, and rain comes in from the west, so waterproofs are sensible even in summer. Light in the evening is wonderful, with the hills of Galloway glowing across the water.

Carlisle, eight kilometres away, has everything: fuel, food and a castle, a cathedral and a good museum of Roman life. Gretna and Denton Holme have shops too. The best time is late spring or early autumn, when the marsh is full of geese.
t.written rock of gelt roman quarry inscri:
Beside the river Gelt, a small stream that runs through a wooded sandstone gorge east of Carlisle, a smooth face of rock bears an inscription cut by Roman soldiers some eighteen centuries ago. This is the Written Rock of Gelt. It marks the quarry where legionaries cut stone for the western part of Hadrian's Wall, and it records their work, with names and dates, in neat Latin letters that are still readable though weathered by the rain.

The quarrymen were from the legions, who did most of the heavy building of the Wall, and one inscription is dated to the early third century, when the emperor Septimius Severus was campaigning in Britain. They took the red sandstone from the gorge walls and carried it by cart to the nearby forts and the Wall itself. The quarry is hidden in the trees and not obvious from the road, so to see it you need to walk a short, sometimes muddy path, and take care near the water and the steep drop. The gorge is also an RSPB reserve with oak, ash and birch woods, and it is quiet and green, with dippers and wagtails on the stream and the sound of water in the rocks.

Brampton, three kilometres away, is the nearest town, a market town of four thousand people with a central octagonal moot hall and several cafes, and it has fuel. A little to the east, Lanercost Priory is a splendid ruined Augustinian house built partly with Roman stone from the Wall, where Edward I stayed for many months in 1306 and 1307, and its nave is still used as a parish church. Naworth Castle nearby is a fortified house with a great hall. The old border country gave rise to the reivers, families who raided across the line between England and Scotland until the early seventeenth century, and the castles and peel towers of this district remember them.

For riding, the lanes in this part of Cumbria are narrow and twisting, with high hedges, many blind bends and plenty of mud and gravel after rain, and the main A69 between Carlisle and Newcastle is a faster but duller option. The best days are in spring and autumn. In summer, farm traffic and tourists slow things down, and in winter ice lingers on the shaded corners. Carlisle, thirteen kilometres away, has all the services, and Brampton has a pleasant tea-room, so there is no pressure on time.

The river Sid is short, quick and small, rising in the hills of east Devon and running down the green valley past Sidbury and Sidford to the sea at Sidmouth, where it makes the shingle beach that the town grew around.

This is the Jurassic Coast, a stretch of the south coast of England from Exmouth to Studland that UNESCO inscribed in 2001 because the cliffs show almost two hundred million years of rock in sequence. At Sidmouth the cliffs are the red sandstones and mudstones of the Triassic, the oldest part of the coast, glowing brick-red in the afternoon sun, and as you ride east the colours move through the pale yellow of Lyme Regis to the chalk and limestone further on. Fossils are found at Lyme, and the Sid valley itself is unspectacular but wooded and unspoiled, with a pleasant quiet that suits a gentle ride.

Sidmouth is a Regency resort, with handsome cream-coloured terraces along the front, a lively folk festival every August, and a tradition of being a quiet place for retirement. It is also the home of the Donkey Sanctuary, a large charity that cares for rescued animals and is free to visit. The cliff paths on either side, over Peak Hill and Salcombe Hill, give dramatic views of the red cliffs and the sea.

The riding in this corner of Devon is charming and sometimes frustrating. The lanes are tiny, sunken and bordered by high banks and hedges, with blind corners, mud, gravel and farm machinery, and in summer long lines of cars and caravans fill the main roads. Early morning in May or September is best, when the verges are full of flowers and the air smells of grass. The coast road, the A3052, runs from Exeter to Lyme Regis and is a decent route when not crowded.

Sidmouth has about twelve thousand people, with several fuel stations, bakeries and tea-rooms, and a cream tea, with scones, clotted cream and jam, is a fixture of any stop. Colyton has a few shops, and Seaton, a bit further east, runs a tramway through the Axe valley, which makes a good diversion if the weather turns.
t.hadrian s wall between the dismantled ra:
The Solway Firth narrows at Bowness-on-Solway, a small village of whitewashed cottages on a low headland, and this is where Hadrian's Wall ended, or rather began, at its western end.

The Wall here was probably not of stone but of turf and timber, because there was no good quarry nearby, and it ended in the tidal marshes with a fort at Bowness, called Maia, to guard the crossing. At low tide, the sands can be waded, which is why the Romans placed milefortlets and watchtowers along the shore, and why this end of the frontier was always sensitive. The Wall Path, the long distance trail, ends here, and walkers often stop for a drink at the pub in the village. The dismantled railway mentioned in your label is the old Solway Junction Railway, which from 1869 carried iron ore across the firth on a viaduct nearly two kilometres long, joining Bowness to the Scottish side. It was damaged by ice floes and by traffic decline, closed in 1921 and was taken down in the 1930s, though the old embankment can still be traced across the fields.

The Solway coast is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, a landscape of salt marsh, mudflats and sand dunes, and in winter huge flocks of barnacle geese gather here, which is a wonderful sight at dawn and dusk. The tides are fast and dangerous and can cover the sands more quickly than a person can run, so stay on the marked paths and do not wander onto the flats.

The road along the shore, narrow and flat, is a pleasant ride when the weather is good, with long straights and gentle bends, though in winter it can flood at high tides and strong winds can make riding unpleasant. Cattle often graze unfenced beside the road, so keep your speed down. There is little in the way of services nearby, so fill the tank in Carlisle or in Annan, which has nearly nine thousand people and a few supermarkets and cafes. Eastriggs and Gretna have smaller shops. Spring and autumn are best for birds.

East of Carlisle, the Eden river bends through a broad red-sandstone valley, and the line of Hadrian's Wall once ran across it. Little of the wall is visible here, because stone was reused for houses and field walls over the centuries, but the course is known, and the Vallum, the great ditch and mounds on the south side, leaves faint marks in the fields. The sector between Baron's Close and the nearby farms runs through gentle pasture, with hedgerows, oak trees and cattle, and the memory of soldiers is carried by the land itself.

The Stanegate, a Roman road that predates the wall, runs close by. It linked the forts of the frontier before the wall was built, from Corbridge in the east to Carlisle, and the stretch near Crosby Lodge follows an ancient line. Hadrian's Wall, begun in AD 122, is part of the UNESCO listing Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and even where there is nothing to see, the place names carry the history: Stanwix, Walby, Crosby.

Scotby and Wetheral are the nearby villages, both comfortable, with pubs and village greens, and Wetheral has a famous railway viaduct that strides across the Eden. Carlisle, about seven kilometres away, is the main town, with a castle, a small cathedral, and all the fuel and supplies you need. The Lake District lies to the southwest, the Pennines to the southeast, and the Scottish border is a short ride north.

For riders, the lanes of the Eden valley are delightful. Narrow roads with high hedges climb gently and run beside the river, with the red stone and green fields in contrast, and traffic is light. Surfaces can be rough in winter after frost. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, and on a clear day you can see the North Pennines forming a blue line on the horizon. Farm vehicles are common, so take care at blind bends.

Hadrian's Wall did not stop at the sea. t.studley royal park including the ruins o:
Fountains Abbey is the largest monastic ruin in Britain, and it stands in a valley so green and quiet that it hardly seems real. In 1132, a group of Benedictine monks, dissatisfied with the lax life at York, left their abbey and sought a stricter rule, and with the help of the archbishop, they settled in this remote valley beside the river Skell. They became Cistercians, and over the next four centuries the abbey grew rich on sheep and wool, building a huge church, a vaulted cellarium, and a tower that still rises above the ruins. Henry VIII dissolved the abbey in 1539, and the roofs were stripped for lead.

Two centuries later, John Aislabie, a politician who had been disgraced in the South Sea Bubble, turned the valley next to it into a garden. Studley Royal, laid out from 1718, with straight canals, a crescent pond, temples, cascades and carefully framed views of the abbey, is one of the finest surviving water gardens in England, and his son William extended it. The abbey and the garden together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1986, and now cared for by the National Trust, with a deer park of fallow and red deer.

The nearby city of Ripon, about four kilometres away, has a small, atmospheric cathedral and a market square where a hornblower sounds a horn every evening at nine o'clock, a custom that goes back centuries. It has fuel and plenty of pubs and tea shops. Fountains is busy on summer weekends, so go early or late in the day. The grounds are large, and a visit takes a few hours.

The riding around is a joy. To the west lie Nidderdale and the Yorkshire Dales, with long climbs, open moorland, stone walls and hamlets, and to the east lies the flat Vale of York. Roads are often narrow, with cattle grids and sheep, and weekends bring plenty of fellow riders. Spring and autumn are most beautiful, and on misty mornings the ruins seem to float. A pot of tea and a scone in the courtyard is the proper ending.
t.saltaire@53.8,-1.8:
Titus Salt was a Bradford wool magnate who got tired of the smoke, the sickness and the squalor of the city, and in 1851 he began building a new mill and a new town beside the river Aire, a few miles north. Saltaire, his name joined to the river's, was a model community: tidy stone terraces of different sizes for different grades of worker, a hospital, a school, almshouses, a church, a park, and a huge Italianate mill with a campanile chimney. The mill opened in 1853 and was among the largest in the world. UNESCO listed the village in 2001 as an outstanding example of Victorian industrial planning.

Salt was a teetotaller, and the original village had no pub, an absence that was rather resented by some of the workers. The streets are named after members of his family, and the stone, honey-coloured and soot-darkened by now, gives the place a unity that few English towns have. Today the mill houses galleries, shops and a bookshop, and a large collection of paintings by David Hockney, who was born in Bradford, fills part of it. The Leeds and Liverpool Canal runs past, with narrowboats nosing along the towpath.

Baildon, the town on the hill just north, is a comfortable place with fuel, a handful of pubs and a moor on its doorstep, and Shipley is close. Bradford, a bigger city with a fine curry tradition, is a short ride away, and the curries of the district are the correct reward after a long ride. Saltaire has cafés and a good chip shop, and there is plenty of parking, though weekends fill it.

For riding, you are on the edge of the Yorkshire Dales and moors, and within minutes the lanes climb to open country. Ilkley Moor, with the Cow and Calf rocks, lies above, and the road across it is narrow, windy and exposed. Further on lie Wharfedale and Airedale, with stone villages and rolling dales. Winters can bring snow and ice to the high roads, and summers are mild and green. Morning light on the mill's golden stone is a lovely sight.
t.pasture house@54.9,-3.3:
The Solway Firth is one of Britain's great tidal estuaries, wide, shallow and quick. At low water, a vast expanse of sand and mud opens, and when the tide returns, it advances across the flats with astonishing speed. Pasture House lies on the English shore, on the Cardurnock peninsula, with the Scottish town of Annan visible across the water about six kilometres to the north. The Romans extended Hadrian's Wall defences down this coast, and Swarthy Hill milefortlet 21, on a neighbouring ride, is one of a chain of small forts that guarded against crossings.

The Bowness Common mosses, a few kilometres inland, are among the best-preserved raised bogs in England, rich in sphagnum, dragonflies and sundews. In winter, thousands of barnacle geese from Svalbard arrive to graze the marshes, and their calls carry over the water. A railway viaduct once crossed the firth here, the Solway Viaduct, opened in 1869 to carry iron ore between Cumberland and Scotland. It was battered by ice floes in the winter of 1881 and finally demolished in the 1930s, though its stumps are said to survive. Nothing of it can be crossed now, so to reach Annan you must drive around by Carlisle. Annan, with about nine thousand people, has fuel and shops, and Eastriggs is small.

The roads on the English side are quiet, flat and sometimes rough at the edges, with farm traffic and a few holiday visitors. Wind off the water can be fierce, and fog can roll in quickly. Check the tide tables if you go near the shore, because the flood is fast and dangerous. Spring and autumn are best for birds, and sunsets over the Solway, with the Scottish hills dark against the sky, are something to remember.
t.hadrian s wall and vallum between the fi:
Carlisle was a Roman town before it was an English one. Luguvalium grew beside the Eden, and just across the river at Stanwix stood the largest fort on Hadrian's Wall, home to a cavalry regiment of a thousand men. The wall itself ran along the north side of today's city, and though houses and roads cover it, its line can be traced by plaques and fragments, and the wall and its Vallum are part of the UNESCO listing. A stretch of the ditch and the foundations of milecastles are visible beyond the suburbs.

The medieval city was a border stronghold, and its red sandstone castle, begun in the eleventh century, saw sieges, raids and prisoners, among them Mary Queen of Scots in 1568. The cathedral, founded in the twelfth century, is one of the smaller English cathedrals, with a magnificent east window. Border reivers, the cattle-raiding families of the Anglo-Scottish frontier, terrorised the region in the sixteenth century, and their names still survive in local families and place names.

t.la falaise de bandiagara@14.4,-3.3:

t.sanchkou section of bei canal and nana c:

t.ravenglass roman fort@54.3,-3.4:

t.river axe@50.7,-3.0:

t.royal botanic gardens@51.5,-0.3:

t.cannon beach@45.9,-124.0:
Cannon Beach is known for a rock. t.aberdeen washington@47.0,-123.8:

t.forks@48.0,-124.4:

t.seattle pacific northwest@48.0,-121.0:
Beyond the map there is only forest. No bike can go there, and it is part of the appeal of the region that the surrounding tarmac skirts it.

The nearest rideable road runs along the Stevens Pass Highway, US 2, which crosses the Cascades from Everett to Leavenworth at about 1,240 metres. What you get instead are snow-streaked ridges at the end of a side valley, cold air pouring down from the high basins, and the cedar-and-resin smell that follows the rivers all the way down to the lowlands. t.crown point@45.5,-122.2:
Crown Point is a rock buttress rising about two hundred metres above the Columbia River, and the view from the top is among the great viewpoints of the Pacific Northwest. Its walls are carved stone, its dome is topped with copper, and inside there are marble floors, small exhibits and a modest cafe. Lancaster had been inspired by the mountain roads of Europe, and he built it with graceful stone bridges, masonry walls, tight bends and tunnels, taking care that the road would fit into the landscape. Parts of it were abandoned when the interstate was built along the river, and in recent decades sections have been restored, so the old road can be ridden again.

Wind at Crown Point is a real force, funnelled by the gorge, and the temperature at the top is often a handful of degrees cooler than at the river. Come early or late for the best light and the fewest people. Dress for weather, and bring a lens that can capture a very wide view.
t.ruby beach@47.7,-124.4:
Ruby Beach is where the Olympic Peninsula puts its raw side on show. t.horseshoe bay@49.4,-123.3:

t.porteau cove@49.6,-123.2:

t.multnomah falls@45.6,-122.1:

t.glacier washington@48.9,-121.9:
Glacier, Washington, is more a crossroads than a town: a handful of buildings, a general store, a ranger station and a bridge, in a damp green valley where the pavement turns decisively toward the mountains. t.heather meadows@48.9,-121.7:

t.hood river food@45.7,-121.5:

t.mount hood timberline@45.3,-121.7:

t.sandy@45.4,-122.3:
Sandy is a small city on the road between Portland and Mount Hood, and it does the job of a gateway very well. t.cardiff@51.5,-3.2:

t.liverpool@53.4,-3.0:

t.leeds@53.8,-1.5:

t.fes@34.0,-5.0:
Fes holds the largest car-free urban area in the world, or so it is often said, and walking through it for an hour makes the claim credible. The best view is from a terrace above, and you will be handed a sprig of mint to hold under your nose. The smell is strong. Do not take it personally.

The riding around Fes is the draw for motorcyclists. To the south, the road climbs into the Middle Atlas toward Ifrane, a town of alpine-style roofs and cedar forests that looks transplanted from Switzerland, and then on to Azrou, where Barbary macaques hang about the cedars. t.olympia@47.0,-122.9:
Washington's capital is a small, rather relaxed city at the very southern tip of Puget Sound, and it is where Highway 101 makes its last stand. t.village de songo@14.4,-3.7:
Songo stands on the edge of the Bandiagara escarpment in central Mali, the long sandstone cliff that is the heartland of the Dogon people. The Dogon moved to the cliffs long ago, displacing or absorbing an earlier people, the Tellem, whose small cliffside granaries and burial caves still dot the rock higher up.

I have to add a serious note. For some years, parts of central Mali, including Dogon country, have been affected by armed conflict and insecurity, and many governments advise against travel here. Anyone considering a visit must check the latest official advice and local conditions carefully, and should not go on the strength of an old guidebook. The road to the area, from Bandiagara, which is about eleven kilometres away, is usually a mix of tarmac and rough track, dusty in the dry season, and the climate is hot, with a rainy season from June to September when tracks turn to mud.

Respect is crucial: ask before photographing people, never touch sacred objects, and follow your guide's advice on where to walk. The silence in the evening, with the cliff turning red and children calling across the plain, is hard to forget.
t.fes el bali@34.1,-5.0:
Fès El Bali is the old walled city of Fez, founded at the end of the eighth century by Idris I and made a capital by his son Idris II, and it is often described as the largest car-free urban area in the world. The medina fills a bowl in the hills, with roofs stepping down toward the Fez river, and from the heights above it the whole place looks like a pile of sand-coloured dice.

Around it grew the madrasas, such as the Bou Inania with its carved cedar and zellij tilework, and the funduqs, the old merchants' inns with wooden galleries around a courtyard. Eat bastilla, the sweet-savoury pigeon pie, or a lamb tagine with prunes, and drink mint tea in a rooftop cafe as the call to prayer drifts over the roofs.
t.fes jedid@34.1,-5.0:
Fès Jedid, the New Fez, is a funny name for a district that is over seven hundred years old. The Marinid dynasty founded it in 1276 as a royal city beside the older medina, with its own walls, palace and mosque, and put the government and army there, leaving the old town to scholars and merchants. It remains a quieter quarter, where wide streets and gardens give relief from the crush of Fès El Bali.

The Royal Palace, Dar al-Makhzen, still serves the king and is closed to visitors, but its monumental gate is worth a visit all the same. Seven great brass doors, with enormous knockers, stand in a line before a patterned wall of green and blue tile. They are best photographed in early morning light, when the metal glows and the street is still empty. Behind them are gardens, courtyards and a palace used for official ceremonies.

The Mellah, the old Jewish quarter, lies within Fès Jedid, and it was created in the fifteenth century as a protected area for the community, close to the palace. Its houses have wooden balconies facing the street, unlike the inward-looking houses of the Muslim quarters, and there is a Jewish cemetery with whitewashed tombs and a restored synagogue, the Ibn Danan, now a museum. Fuel is in the new town, Ville Nouvelle, a few kilometres away. Spring is best, with green fields and mild air, and August is brutally hot, so go early and rest in the afternoon.
t.medina of fez@34.1,-5.0:
The tanneries are what everyone remembers. In the Medina of Fez, at the Chouara quarter, round stone vats stand in rows like a giant palette, filled with white lime, red, yellow and brown dyes, and men stand knee-deep in them soaking hides of goat, sheep and cow as their ancestors have done for centuries. Fez is more than leather. Coppersmiths hammer large pots in Place Seffarine, weavers work at looms, and carpenters carve cedar in tiny workshops, with guilds that go back to the Middle Ages. Finding your way is part of the experience. The medina has no real map in the mind, and the best advice is to choose a landmark, such as the Bab Boujloud gate or the Qarawiyyin mosque, and to accept that you will be lost. Ride in from the new town and leave the bike at a guarded lot, since the lanes cannot take a motorcycle. Traffic around the old city gates is thick, with petit taxis and carts. Roads leave toward the Middle Atlas, where cedar forests shelter Barbary macaques near Azrou, and toward Meknes. Fuel is easy in the new town. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with summer heat strong and winter nights cold.
t.duffy lake road@49.4,-122.9:
Anmore is a small village in the forested hills above Burrard Inlet, a short ride from Port Moody and the eastern edge of Vancouver's urban area, and the dot sits here because the Duffy Lake Road loop ends back in this part of the Lower Mainland. t.olympic peninsula@47.7,-121.9:
The Snoqualmie Valley, where Carnation sits, is a quiet pocket of dairy farms and berry fields in the western foothills of the Cascades, a short way east of Seattle's suburbs. t.beijing@39.9,116.4:
Beijing has been a capital, on and off, for most of the last eight hundred years, and the centre of the city still carries the weight of that. At its heart sits the Forbidden City, the vast palace complex from which Ming and Qing emperors ruled, with its red walls, yellow-tiled roofs and nine hundred or so buildings, and just south of it lies Tiananmen Square, one of the largest public squares in the world. The city's grid of boulevards and ring roads is laid out around this axis, and anyone who has looked at a map will see the logic.
