Traffic is heavy, the ring roads can be jammed at any hour, and signage is mostly in Chinese. If you travel here, the metro is cheap, clean and efficient, and taxis and ride-hailing apps are plentiful. The air can be hazy, particularly in winter, and the best weather is in spring and autumn.

Fuel and food are no issue in a city of this size. The hutongs, the old alleys around the Drum Tower and Houhai lake, are full of small restaurants, and Peking duck is of course the dish to try, carved at your table with crisp skin, pancakes and sweet bean sauce.

If you can, walk the lanes of the old city at dusk, when the lanterns come on and the cooking smells drift out of doorways.
t.old course of yellow river estuary@38.1,:
The Yellow River is the most restless big river on earth, and this is one of the places it used to leave the land. Over the centuries it has carried so much silt out of the loess plateau that it keeps building its own floor, rising above the plain, bursting its banks and changing course. In 1855 it broke out in Henan, gave up its long southern route to the Yellow Sea and swung north to the Bohai Gulf instead. The channel that ended here, on the low coast of Shandong, is one of the old mouths of that restless history, and the land around it is still being made by mud.

Do not expect mountains or corners. This is delta country: dead-flat, wide-skied, with raised embankments, drainage channels, reed beds, tamarisk scrub and salt-crusted flats that shimmer in the afternoon. The roads are straight and long, often with trucks serving the oil wells and chemical plants of the Dongying area, and the riding is about distance and light rather than technique. Early morning and the hour before sunset are the times to be here, when the reeds turn copper and the haze flattens out. Wind off the sea can be steady and tiring, and in summer the heat sits on the tarmac.

What makes the place worth the detour is the birdlife. The delta wetlands are a major stopover on the East Asian flyway, and the protected reserve here and at the present river mouth holds huge numbers of migrating and wintering waterbirds. Spring and autumn are the seasons to come, and on a good day the sky over the reed beds is busy with geese, cranes, gulls and waders. Cranes and storks are among the species the reserve is known for, though you will want binoculars and patience, not a motorbike engine, to see them.

The data for this point gives no named town nearby, which tells you how empty it feels, so plan fuel and water before you arrive. Fill up in a city on the way, and carry a little extra if you can, because filling stations thin out on the delta roads. Gates and access rules around protected land can change, and some tracks near the mouth are closed to vehicles, so treat the final approach as something to check locally. Come to look at a coastline that is still arriving, grain by grain, from the other side of a continent.
t.bellingham@48.8,-122.5:
Bellingham is the last substantial city before the Canadian border, a place of eighty-five thousand people on a sheltered bay in the north-west corner of Washington state. It is a university town, with a lively cafe and brewing scene, a revived waterfront, and the kind of outdoorsy, independent character you find in many Pacific Northwest cities. The old Fairhaven district, a Victorian district with brick buildings and bookshops, is a nice place to wander, and the ferry terminal for Alaska sits at its edge.

The mountain looms over everything. Mount Baker, a glacier-covered volcano of over ten thousand feet, stands to the east, and on clear days the white cone fills the horizon. It is one of the snowiest places on Earth, and in the winter of 1998 to 1999 the ski area on its flank set a world record for snowfall in a single season, with over a thousand inches. The Nooksack River runs down from its glaciers, and the valley below is full of dairy farms, berry fields and small towns.

The Mount Baker Highway begins here and runs about fifty-seven miles east, first across the flat farmland of the Nooksack valley and then, beyond the village of Glacier, climbing into deep forest of cedar, hemlock and Douglas fir. The road is well paved, with easy bends and a few tighter sections, and it follows the river through a gorge before ascending toward Heather Meadows. The final section is closed in winter, usually reopening in summer after the snow clears, so check conditions. Rain is frequent, even in summer, and cloud often covers the upper mountain, so be ready for wet roads.

Fuel and food are easy in Bellingham, and it is wise to fill up, because the services on the highway are limited to the villages of Deming, Maple Falls and Glacier. The Pacific Northwest is famous for coffee, and the city has many independent roasters, so a good cup is never far away. Spring and early summer bring waterfalls, and September and early October are often the best time, with stable weather and fewer visitors. Take a warm layer for the top, where the air is cool even in August.
t.artist point@48.8,-121.7:
The pavement ends at a car park on a ridge, and a short paved path leads to the best view in the North Cascades. Artist Point stands at around fifty-one hundred feet at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, and from the edge you look straight across a valley to Mount Shuksan, a jagged pyramid of dark rock and white ice, while the rounded, glaciated cone of Mount Baker sits close at hand to the west. Painters and photographers have been coming for a century, hence the name.

The road up is only open for part of the year. Heavy winter snow buries it, often deeply, and the last stretch is cleared in early summer, sometimes not until July, and shut again with the first big storm of autumn. Even in midsummer, snow patches survive beside the car park, and wildflowers bloom in a rush as soon as the ground thaws, with lupines, paintbrush and avalanche lilies making the meadows look painted. If you ride up in August or September you will probably have the best chance of clear weather.

The final miles climb through Heather Meadows, a high basin of subalpine meadow and small tarns, passing Picture Lake, where the mountain reflects in still water on a calm morning. The road is narrow, with steep drop-offs in places, sharp turns and a patchy surface after winter, so ride carefully, especially if mist or cloud rolls in. Temperatures can be twenty degrees lower than in the lowlands, and the wind can be sharp. Marmots whistle among the rocks, and mountain goats sometimes cross the high slopes.

A recreation pass is normally required for parking at trailheads and lots in the national forest, so check before you go. Short trails lead from the car park, including a gentle loop around the lookout and routes toward Table Mountain, but the weather is changeable and you should wear proper footwear. Fog can close in within minutes, so if the view is hidden, wait a while, because it often clears.
t.midelt@32.7,-4.7:
Midelt is a market town on a high, windy plain between two mountain ranges, at about 1,500 metres, and it feels like a place that exists in order to be passed through. The Middle Atlas lies to the north and the High Atlas to the south, with the great bulk of Jbel Ayachi, close to 3,750 metres, rising to the south-west, often snow-capped into spring. The town has about forty-five thousand people, a long main street of shops, cafés and mechanics, and a surrounding landscape of orchards, mines and open steppe.

It lies on the main road from Fez and the cedar forests of the north toward the Sahara, so many riders arrive here after crossing the Middle Atlas via Azrou and Ifrane, over a pass where in winter the snow can be deep. South of the town the road drops through the Ziz gorges toward Er-Rachidia and the desert oases. Between towns, the road is long and open, with wide views and sometimes strong wind, and the temperature swing between day and night is large, so pack layers.

Midelt is known for its apples, grown in the surrounding valleys, and for minerals: stalls along the road sell fossils, crystals and rocks from the mountains, some real and some carved to order, so look carefully before buying. The mines nearby have produced lead and other minerals for decades, and the area has a long history of Berber settlement. The town is also the starting point for the road east and then south into the high country toward Imilchil, for those who prefer something less travelled.

With a population this size, fuel, repairs and food are easy, and the town is the best place to stock up before the remote roads. Cafés on the main street serve tagines, grilled meat and mint tea, and hotels range from simple to comfortable. Winters are cold, with frost and snow common between November and March, so check conditions before setting out, and in summer the sun on the plateau is fierce. Starting early gives you the best light and the calmest air.
t.fez@34.0,-5.0:
Fez is the oldest of Morocco's imperial cities and it has been busy for well over a thousand years. The medina, Fès el-Bali, founded in the late eighth and early ninth centuries and listed by UNESCO, is a maze of thousands of alleys, many too narrow for anything but a donkey, and it is often described as the largest car-free urban area in the world. Inside are workshops, mosques, madrasas, fountains and markets, all packed so tightly that the sky is often a thin strip above your head.

At the centre sits the University of al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri, and regarded as one of the oldest continuously operating educational institutions in the world. The tanneries, where leather is still dyed in stone vats of red, yellow and white, are the sight everyone wants, and you can watch from a terrace above, with a sprig of mint under your nose against the smell. Metalworkers, weavers and ceramicists work in their own quarters, and the food is excellent: pastilla, a pigeon or chicken pie dusted with sugar and cinnamon, is the classic.

For the rider, Fez is both a place to leave the bike and a starting point. The medina is impossible on two wheels, so park securely in the newer city, and explore on foot with a guide if you want to avoid getting lost. From Fez, the road north to Chefchaouen climbs through the hills of the Rif foothills, with olive groves, villages and long views, and it is a ride of changing scenery, with tidy tarmac in some places and potholes in others. Traffic around the city is heavy, so leave early.

Fès has a population close to a million, so fuel, workshops, parts and every kind of food and lodging are easy to find, and the old town of Fès al Bali alone holds well over a hundred thousand people. Summers are hot and winters are cool and damp, so spring and autumn are best. Be polite but firm with unofficial guides, agree prices in advance, and keep valuables out of sight in the medina.
t.merzouga@31.1,-4.0:
The tarmac stops being the main attraction at Merzouga, because here the Sahara starts for real. Erg Chebbi, a wall of orange dunes more than a hundred metres high, rises out of the stony plain in the far south-east of Morocco, a short distance from the Algerian frontier, and the village sits right at its foot with a scatter of guesthouses, cafés and camel stables. In the early morning the sand has the colour of burnt sugar, and at sunset it turns the red of a hot stove.

The riding to get here is long, flat and hot, on the road through Erfoud and past the oasis town of Rissani, once the capital of the Tafilalet region and the cradle of the dynasty that still rules Morocco. Reçani, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town and the place where you should be thinking about your fuel gauge. Beyond it there is a surfaced road and a number of tracks into the dunes, and the tracks are where the problems begin: soft sand grabs a loaded motorbike without mercy, so be honest about your skills, ride with a partner, and do not wander off alone in the heat.

Wind is the main enemy. In spring a hot dry gust carrying fine sand can make visibility poor and fill your visor, and in midsummer the temperature is brutal, so the sensible months are autumn and spring, with the early morning the best hours. Nights in the desert can turn surprisingly cold. A few kilometres south lies the village of Khamlia, where the community of descendants of sub-Saharan musicians plays Gnawa rhythms with iron castanets and drums, and it is a rewarding evening if you can arrange it. Out on the flats, Dayet Srji, a lake that fills after rare rains, can draw flamingos.

Nearly everything here is arranged around visitors. You can take a sunrise camel trek, sleep in a tented camp, and eat bread baked in the sand, a kind of Berber pizza called madfouna stuffed with meat and onion. Fill the tank in Rissani or Erfoud before arriving, carry more water than seems sensible, and keep your phone charged. The ride on to the Todra Gorge to the north-west is a good way to leave, and it feels like the first sip of cool water.
t.historic columbia river highway point 3@:
Multnomah Falls drops about two hundred metres in two main tiers, and it is the most visited natural site in Oregon, which tells you what to expect from the car park. The classic stone lodge stands at the bottom, the arched footbridge spans the lower pool, and a path zigzags up to a viewing point above it. From a motorcycle seat you cannot see the whole thing at once, so the usual routine is to park, take off your jacket and walk the few minutes to the base.

Getting here is half the point. The old highway meanders past Latourell and Bridal Veil, each with its own waterfall, before reaching this one, and the road is at its most enjoyable on those stretches: tight, tree-lined, fenced by mossy stone walls and mostly shaded. Heavy rains can send rocks or branches onto the pavement, so keep an eye on the surface. The modern interstate runs just below, and motorcycles can drop onto it if time is short, but the old road is plainly the better ride.

The falls are fed by springs and snowmelt from Larch Mountain above, and the flow is strongest in winter and spring and weakest in late summer. Local legend, as told for generations, ties the falls to a Native American maiden who sacrificed herself for her people; whatever its origin, it is part of the place. The lodge and visitor services are right by the car park, with food and restrooms, though it gets busy at midday and long queues on summer weekends are normal.

Troutdale to the west and the gorge towns to the east are the reliable places to refill. Plan the day around the crowds if you can: arriving before nine or after late afternoon gives you the falls with room to breathe, and the cooler evening air in the gorge, with the mist rising off the lower tier, is the nicest time to be on foot here.
t.olympic peninsula loop point 3@48.0,-123:
West of Port Angeles the highway climbs into forest and the character of the ride changes. This stretch hugs the northern edge of the Olympic Mountains, and the road alternates between tall evergreens, small creek crossings and sudden glimpses of Lake Crescent, a deep and strikingly clear glacial lake whose water is a cold blue-green. The lake is only a short distance on, and it is among the best parts of the whole loop.

The riding here is a real pleasure. The road is two-lane, mostly well surfaced, and it follows the contours of the hills with long, rolling bends and a few tighter ones that need attention. Trees close over the road in places, and in the morning the light filters through the branches in a way that makes the tarmac patchy with shadow, which can hide a damp spot or a bit of loose gravel.

The Olympic Peninsula holds one of the largest remaining areas of temperate rainforest in the Northern Hemisphere on its western slopes, and the park contains glaciers, wild beaches and herds of Roosevelt elk. Here on the north side the forest is drier than the famous Hoh, but the scale of the trees is still impressive: old Douglas firs and western hemlocks thick enough that two people could not link arms around them.

Nature sets the schedule. The weather can change in minutes, and a morning of sunshine can become an afternoon of drizzle, so waterproofs belong in the pannier. Summer and early autumn are the best seasons, and the lake is calm at dawn. Pull over only at the signed turnouts, since the road has little shoulder and blind bends, and be respectful of the cyclists and campers who share it.
t.olympic peninsula loop point 4@48.1,-123:
Past Lake Crescent the road turns west and wanders on through country that feels properly remote. This section runs through the valley of the Sol Duc and the Soleduck River area, with thick forest, ferns, moss on the trunks and the occasional logged hillside showing where timber has been cut.

The road is where the pleasure lies. Highway 101 here is a classic two-lane mountain-edge highway with long straights broken by flowing curves and a few tighter turns where it follows a creek. Traffic thins out the further west you go, and on a weekday morning you can have sections almost to yourself. The surface is good for the most part, though the logging trucks wear grooves in places, and the shade means damp patches can hang around well into the day.

The Olympic Peninsula has a long Native American history, and the Quileute, Makah, Hoh and Klallam peoples have lived on this coast for thousands of years. Logging and fishing shaped the later settlement, and the timber industry still shapes the economy: small mills, log trucks and clear-cuts in various stages of regrowth mark the landscape. The tension between old-growth protection and logging was the defining political fight of the Pacific Northwest in the 1980s and 1990s, and you can read it in the scenery here, with protected forest on one side of a ridge and working timberland on the other.

Wildlife is the extra. Black-tailed deer step out at dawn and dusk, elk occasionally appear in meadows, and bald eagles hunt over the rivers. Slow down at those times of day, and watch the verge. The climate is mild but wet; even in summer a cold front can roll in from the Pacific, and temperatures drop quickly. A packable layer, a visor that shields rain, and a bit of patience for slow vehicles all make the ride better.
t.olympic peninsula loop point 6@47.7,-124:
South of Forks the highway bends away from the coast and runs on through rolling forest, passing the mouth of the Hoh and tracing the shore of the Pacific for stretches, with grey-green sea beyond the trees. This is remote country, and the nearest town is Forks, about twenty-seven kilometres back.

Riding here is calm and gently rhythmic. The road rolls through logged and regrowing forest, over small rivers, past occasional turnouts with views of the Pacific. The curves are mostly moderate and there is little traffic apart from logging trucks and the occasional camper van. It is a good place to settle into a steady pace and enjoy the landscape without stress, and on a dry day it is some of the easiest and most pleasant riding on the whole loop.

The coast here belongs in part to the Quinault and Quileute, and to the national park, whose Pacific strip runs for roughly seventy miles and is one of the wildest coastlines in the lower forty-eight. Beaches are strewn with driftwood the size of tree trunks, and tide pools shelter starfish and anemones. If you stop at a beach, check tide tables, because in places the tide can cut off headlands. The smell of salt, kelp and rain-soaked spruce is distinctive and gets into your gear.

Weather is the variable. Summer fog can drift in from the sea and cover the road for hours, while winter storms bring wind and heavy rain, and trees occasionally come down. Between June and September the odds are best, and the mornings can be foggy, clearing by noon. Bring a spare visor or an anti-fog insert. Further south the road leads to Lake Quinault and the Grays Harbor towns, where fuel is plentiful again, and Aberdeen, about an hour on, is the next substantial place for a proper meal and a bed.
Hardknott Pass tops out at about 393 metres, and the Romans got here first. Just below the summit on the Eskdale side stand the ruins of Mediobogdum, a fort built in the second century to guard the road from Ravenglass to Ambleside, and its stone walls, gateways and parade ground are laid out on a shelf with a view down the valley to the sea. Soldiers were posted here from as far away as Dalmatia, which makes the place feel even more remote. It is free to visit, and the walk from the road is short.

The road is the other attraction, and it asks for respect. Coming up from Eskdale the gradient reaches one in three on the hairpins, the surface is narrow and sometimes rough, and there are no barriers at the worst drops. The hairpins are tight enough that a loaded bike needs a firm hand, a low gear and a steady clutch, and stopping on the steepest part for a photograph is a bad idea. Wet leaves, gravel and sheep add to the challenge. In ice or snow, the pass is simply impassable, and signs warn drivers to turn back.

Come with a full tank and pack a flask. Mobile signal comes and goes. Brakes get a workout on the descent, and engine braking in first gear is better than riding the lever. If you meet a car on a narrow stretch, the usual courtesy applies: the vehicle going uphill generally has priority, as it is harder to restart.

The scenery is hard to beat. The pass runs over the shoulder of the high fells, with the great mass of Scafell and the crags of the Scafell range to the north, and on a clear day the Irish Sea shines in the west and the Isle of Man shows on the horizon. Herdwick sheep, hardy and grey, graze the verges. The wind blows constantly, and cloud can drop in minutes. A calm, clear morning in late spring or autumn is the best time to try it.
t.vancouver@49.2,-123.1:
Vancouver is one of those cities where the mountains feel close enough to touch from downtown. The North Shore peaks rise straight out of Burrard Inlet, the Lions Gate Bridge leaps across to them from Stanley Park, and on a clear day you can watch floatplanes take off over the harbour while snow still sits on the summits. It is a big, busy, expensive city, but for a rider it is above all a gateway: to the Sea-to-Sky Highway north, the Fraser Valley east, and, for these rides, the ferries across the Strait of Georgia to Vancouver Island.

The island rides begin with the boat. BC Ferries sails from Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver to Nanaimo's Departure Bay, and from Tsawwassen, south of the city, to Duke Point near Nanaimo and to Swartz Bay near Victoria. Motorcycles usually load first and get squeezed into corners of the car deck, which is one of the small pleasures of riding here, but summer weekends and long weekends are busy and booking ahead is wise. Once across, the road west to the Pacific Rim runs through Cathedral Grove's giant Douglas firs and over the mountains to Tofino and Ucluelet.

Getting out of the city itself takes patience. Traffic is dense, lights are frequent and the bridges choke at rush hour, so an early start pays off. The route to Horseshoe Bay along Marine Drive in West Vancouver is a pleasant way to leave, with glimpses of the water between big houses and cedars, and the Stanley Park causeway is short but memorable. Rain is part of the deal. The coast is green for a reason, and from October to April a wet day is more normal than not; summer is drier and often gloriously clear.

Before Europeans arrived, this was and is the territory of the Musqueam, Squamish and Tsleil-Waututh peoples, and you will see their art and names across the city, from the totem poles at Brockton Point in Stanley Park to the public art at the airport. The modern city grew around a sawmill settlement and the arrival of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the 1880s, with Gastown, the old core, now full of brick warehouses turned into bars and cafes.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere, and the city's food scene, especially its Asian restaurants, is a good reason to spend the last evening of a trip here. Fill up before the ferry, since prices on the island and especially out on the west coast tend to be higher.
t.richmond@49.2,-123.1:
Richmond is built on mud, and proud of it. The city occupies Lulu Island and neighbouring islands in the delta of the Fraser River, just south of Vancouver, land so flat and so low that much of it sits barely above sea level behind a ring of dykes. Vancouver's airport takes up Sea Island to the west, the North Shore mountains rise beyond the city skyline, and on a clear day Mount Baker floats above the delta to the southeast, a white volcano across the border in Washington.

Two Richmonds coexist. The centre is one of the most Asian cities in North America, with huge malls, Chinese restaurants, bubble tea shops and a summer night market that draws crowds from all over the region, and the food is a very good reason to stop. At the southwest corner of the island lies Steveston, an old fishing village with wooden docks, boats selling fish straight from the deck and the Gulf of Georgia Cannery, a national historic site that tells the story of the salmon canning industry and the Japanese Canadian fishermen who worked here before their internment during the Second World War.

The riding around Richmond is flat and urban, with traffic lights, busy roads and few curves, though the dyke roads by the river and the sea offer open views and the scent of salt and mud. Wind can blow strongly across the delta. The Mount Baker loop heads south across the border into Washington State. You will need a passport and the right documents for the bike, and waits at the crossings can be long at weekends. Once across, the Mount Baker Highway climbs east from Bellingham through forests along the Nooksack River toward the mountain, ending at Artist Point, usually open only in late summer when the snow has melted.

The weather is typical of the coast: mild, grey and wet from autumn to spring, and often bright and pleasant in summer. Fog sometimes hangs over the delta in the morning. In the mountains, snow can remain on the high roads until July.

Richmond has fuel, food and every service, and many locals cross the border to fill up in Washington, where fuel has often been cheaper. Keep receipts and know the duty-free limits if you bring anything back. Before or after the ride, a bowl of noodles in one of the city's many Asian restaurants is hard to beat.
t.near white center@47.5,-122.4:
Ferries are the quiet heart of this corner of Seattle. White Center, a modest, diverse neighbourhood, lies just inland, and Lincoln Park offers forest trails, beaches and views over the water.

Puget Sound is a complex inland sea carved by glaciers, with deep channels, islands and peninsulas, and its cold, nutrient-rich waters support orcas, seals, porpoises and salmon. On a clear day Mount Rainier rises huge and white to the southeast, a volcano so massive that it creates its own weather. The weather here is famously grey and drizzly from autumn to spring, but summers are often dry and sunny, with long evenings and clear skies.

The North Cascades Highway is one of the great rides of the Pacific Northwest. It leaves Interstate 5 near Burlington and heads east along the Skagit River, past the turquoise lakes of Diablo and Ross, which owe their colour to fine glacial flour, and climbs to Washington Pass, where granite spires rise above the road. The highway closes in winter because of snow and avalanche danger, usually from November until spring, so check the dates before you plan. Beyond Marblemount, services disappear for a long stretch until you descend to Mazama and Winthrop, so fill up before the climb.

Getting out of Seattle can be slow. Traffic on Interstate 5 and the city's bridges is heavy at rush hour and at weekends, and the West Seattle Bridge can be a bottleneck. Ferries can save time and offer a scenic alternative, though queues are long in summer. Riding in the rain is common, and the roads can be slippery with leaves and moss in the autumn.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy to find in West Seattle and White Center. For a pause before or after the ride, walk down to the water at Lincoln Park and watch the ferries come and go. With the islands, the mountains and the light on the Sound, it is a fine place to start or end any journey.
t.weedon beck@52.2,-1.1:
Roads, canals and railways all squeeze through the same gap at Weedon Bec, and that is the key to its story. The village lies in the gentle Northamptonshire countryside near Daventry, where the old Roman road of Watling Street, now the A5, the Grand Union Canal and the West Coast Main Line run side by side through a shallow valley. For centuries this has been a natural corridor between London and the northwest.

Weedon's most remarkable feature is hidden behind a high brick wall. During the Napoleonic Wars, when invasion seemed a real threat, the government built the Royal Ordnance Depot here, about as far from the coast as you can get in England, to store arms and gunpowder safely inland. A branch of the canal ran into the depot, through a portcullis gate, linking its storehouses to the national waterway network. Local legend says that the depot's pavilions were intended to house King George III and the government if Napoleon landed, though historians doubt it. The depot was used by the army until the twentieth century, and many of its buildings survive, some now home to businesses and shops.

The countryside around Weedon is rolling farmland, with hedges, small woods and villages built of the local ironstone, which gives the houses a warm brown and golden colour. The canal towpaths are pleasant for a walk, with narrowboats moored along the banks. Nearby, Althorp, the Spencer family estate where Diana, Princess of Wales, grew up and is buried, lies a few miles to the east.

For riders, the A5 is a fast but busy road, while the lanes around the villages are quieter and more interesting, with gentle curves, short climbs and views over the fields. The surface can be rough and muddy in places, especially after rain or the harvest, and the roads can be narrow. Silverstone, the home of the British Grand Prix, lies within easy reach to the south, and the Cotswolds begin further west, with their honey-coloured stone villages and winding roads.

Weedon Bec has a few shops and pubs, and Daventry, a few miles to the northwest, has supermarkets and fuel stations. A pint and a pie in a village pub is a classic English stop, though the drink-driving limit is strict, so keep it to soft drinks while you are riding.
t.stone@52.9,-2.2:
Narrowboats, breweries and a Georgian high street make Stone one of the more likeable market towns in Staffordshire. It stands on the River Trent and the Trent and Mersey Canal, which brought prosperity to the town when it opened in the late eighteenth century, with boatyards, warehouses and locks still lining the waterway today. The high street is lined with old coaching inns, independent shops and cafés, and the town has a relaxed, welcoming feel.

The canal is the heart of the place. Built under the guidance of the engineer James Brindley and backed by Josiah Wedgwood, the pottery manufacturer, it linked the Potteries to the ports of Liverpool and Hull, allowing fragile ceramics to be transported safely by water. Stone became a busy canal town and a brewing centre, and its water was prized for beer. Today the locks and towpaths are popular with walkers and boaters, and the canal-side pubs are a pleasant place for a break.

Stone is also linked to naval history: John Jervis, the admiral who became Earl St Vincent and was a mentor to Nelson, was born near the town. To the north, the Potteries towns around Stoke-on-Trent have a rich industrial heritage, and the Wedgwood factory and museum at Barlaston, a few miles away, tell the story of English ceramics. Trentham, just north, has large landscaped gardens and a monkey forest.

The riding from Stone is varied. The roads around the town are busy, with the A34 and the M6 nearby, but heading northeast you soon reach the Staffordshire Moorlands and the edge of the Peak District, where the A53 climbs past Leek toward the Roaches, a jagged gritstone ridge, and on to Buxton across open moorland. These are some of the best biking roads in England, with sweeping curves and wide views, but they are also heavily policed and often windy and wet. To the south, the lanes through the Staffordshire countryside lead toward Cannock Chase, a forested heath with quiet roads and wildlife.

Stone has cafés, pubs and restaurants on the high street, making it a good food stop, and fuel stations and supermarkets are easy to find on the edge of town. Oatcakes, a Staffordshire speciality that looks like a soft pancake and is usually filled with cheese and bacon, are the local breakfast, best eaten hot.
t.goring on the way back@51.5,-1.1:
The Goring Gap is one of the best bits of geography in southern England. Here the Thames, after wandering across the Oxfordshire plain, cuts straight through the chalk hills, with the Chilterns on one side and the North Wessex Downs on the other, and the valley narrows into a steep, wooded passage that feels almost Alpine by English standards. Goring is the village on the east bank, Streatley faces it on the west, and a bridge and a lock tie them together.

It is a place of old routes. The Ridgeway, a track used for thousands of years and often called Britain's oldest road, crosses the Thames here, and so does the Thames Path. The village has quietly gathered famous residents: Oscar Wilde spent a summer here in the 1890s and borrowed the name Goring for a character in An Ideal Husband, and George Michael lived in the village and died here in 2016, after which fans left flowers by his house for months.

The river is the reason for the stop. People do swim in the Thames around Goring and Streatley, mostly in the reaches upstream, where the water is slow and the banks are open, and on summer evenings you will see a few heads bobbing. Keep well away from the lock and weir, watch for boats, and know that after heavy rain the water can be fast and dirty. The roads around here are good and varied. Streatley Hill climbs steeply west out of the valley onto the downs with a fine view back over the river, and the roads beyond run across rolling open chalk country with long views and few hedges. Weekends bring cyclists and walkers, and the village itself gets busy on fine Sundays.

Goring has pubs, cafés and shops, and Pangbourne, a few kilometres downstream, is where Kenneth Grahame spent his last years, the author of The Wind in the Willows, a book that feels right on these banks. t.near croydon@51.4,-0.1:
Croydon is where the South Downs ride comes home to London, and it is honest about it: a big, busy town of glass office towers, flyovers, trams and shopping centres, sitting at the southern edge of the capital where the chalk hills of the North Downs fade into suburbs. It has a population larger than many British cities and its own strong identity, and for a rider it is the last stretch before the metropolis takes over.

It has a surprising history. Croydon Airport, a few kilometres south-west on the Purley Way, was London's main airport between the wars, the first in the world with a proper air-traffic control tower, and the departure point for many early flights to Europe and the Empire. Amy Johnson took off from here in 1930 on her solo flight to Australia. The old terminal building still stands, with a small museum, and it is a nice detour if you are interested in aviation. Croydon was also an ancient market town and the home of the Archbishops of Canterbury for centuries, whose old palace survives in the old town.

Getting here from the south means one of a few corridors. The A23 runs up through Coulsdon and Purley, and the A22 brings you in through Caterham and Whyteleafe, and both drop off the North Downs in a series of bends before turning into long suburban roads lined with shops and traffic lights. The downs themselves, just south of here, are still lovely, with steep lanes around Woldingham and Chaldon and views back over the Weald, so if time allows, a last loop up there before descending is a good farewell.

Urban riding is the end of the story. Expect buses, trams, busy junctions and drivers in a hurry, and the area is covered by the London Ultra Low Emission Zone, which applies to older motorcycles, so check your bike's status. Speed cameras are common on the main roads.

Everything practical is here: fuel, food from every cuisine, bike shops and dealers, and fast trains into central London. It is not a place to linger in your gear, but it is a perfectly good place to put the bike down, take a deep breath and remember that only a couple of hours ago you were looking at the sea from Beachy Head.
t.near berkhamsted on the way back@51.7,-0:
Berkhamsted lies in a narrow chalk valley cut through the Chilterns, with the Grand Union Canal, the River Bulbourne, the railway and the old main road all squeezed into the bottom together, and beech woods rising on both sides. It is a prosperous market town of around twenty thousand people, with a long high street of old coaching inns and shops, and it makes a fine last stop before the run back into the outskirts of London.

The castle is the history lesson. Only grassy earthworks and fragments of flint wall remain, but the moat is still there, and the site matters: after the Battle of Hastings in 1066, the English leaders came here to submit to William the Conqueror before he went on to be crowned in London. Later the castle passed through the hands of royal favourites and was the seat of the Black Prince. Graham Greene grew up in the town, where his father was headmaster of the school, and he wrote about the canal and the common in his memoirs.

A word of honesty about the water. This is not swimming country in the way the label might suggest: the canal is for boats and towpath strolls, not for a dip, and the Bulbourne is a small chalk stream. What the valley offers instead is cool shade and green, and on a warm evening the canal path, with narrowboats tied up and moorhens fussing in the reeds, is a calm place to sit for half an hour.

The riding around here is good in a very English way. Up on the ridge to the north, the Ashridge Estate is a great sweep of National Trust beech woods and commons, with the Bridgewater Monument rising above the trees and herds of fallow deer that wander across the lanes, especially at dawn and dusk. The roads twist through the woods with blind bends, steep dips and sometimes leaves and mud in autumn, and they are full of cyclists and walkers at weekends, so ride with patience. On a sunny late October afternoon, when the beeches turn copper and the light comes through sideways, it is as good as any woodland in the country.

Berkhamsted has fuel, pubs, cafés and everything else, and Chesham and Bovingdon are close if you need more. From here, the A41 is the quick way back towards the M25.
t.near kettering on the way back@52.4,-0.6:
Geddington, a stone village a few kilometres north-east of Kettering, owns one of the most moving monuments in England. In the middle of the village stands the Eleanor Cross, a tall, slender, triangular stone spire, put up in the 1290s by Edward I in memory of his wife, Eleanor of Castile. When she died in Lincolnshire, her body was carried to London, and at each place where the procession rested overnight the king raised a cross. Twelve were built; only three survive, and Geddington's is the best preserved of them.

Close by, the River Ise slides under a medieval stone bridge beside a shallow ford, and on a warm afternoon children paddle there while riders sit on the wall. That, honestly, is the extent of the water: the Ise is a small river, not a swimming spot, and the lakes in the area are fishing or nature reserves rather than places to swim. Come here for shade and stone rather than a plunge.

The landscape is the old Rockingham Forest, once a royal hunting ground stretching across this corner of Northamptonshire, now a patchwork of woods, rolling fields and villages built in golden-brown ironstone. Brigstock, a few kilometres north, has a Saxon church tower and a country park in old quarries. Just outside Geddington, Boughton House, the seat of the Dukes of Buccleuch, is often called the English Versailles, with its long French-style front and avenues of trees.

The roads are pleasant rather than thrilling. The lanes between villages rise and fall over gentle ridges, with long straights and the occasional tight bend at a church or a bridge, and the traffic is light outside the main roads. The A43 and A6116 are faster and busier, used by lorries heading to the industrial estates around Corby and Kettering. Watch for farm traffic and for mud on the lanes in autumn, and for deer in the woods at dusk.

Kettering, about six kilometres away, is the nearest big town, with fuel, supermarkets and everything else, and Geddington itself has a pub and a small shop. It is a lovely, quiet place to pause, and the sight of that thin grey cross in the sunlight, more than seven centuries after a king's grief put it there, stays with you on the road home.
t.sutton on the way back@52.1,-0.2:
Sutton is a tiny village in the east of Bedfordshire, close to Potton, and its fame rests on something wonderfully small: a ford and a medieval packhorse bridge. The road dips through a shallow stream at the bottom of the village, and beside it a narrow stone bridge, barely wide enough for a laden horse, carries walkers over the water as it has done since the Middle Ages. It is one of the few packhorse bridges left in this part of England.

The ford is a classic test of nerve and judgement for riders. Most of the year the water is shallow and the bottom firm, and you can splash through at walking pace with a grin, but after heavy rain it rises and runs fast, and the stones on the bed are slippery with weed. If in doubt, take the other road round. And yes, the label says swim, but that is too generous: the stream is for paddling feet on a hot day, not for swimming, and the nearest real water is elsewhere.

This is greensand country, a low ridge of sandy soil that runs across Bedfordshire, with pine woods, heath and old estates. Potton, on its edge, has long been a market-gardening town, famous for its vegetables, and its small square and old houses have an easy charm. Not far west, at Sandy, the RSPB has its headquarters in a heathland reserve, and at Old Warden the Shuttleworth Collection keeps vintage aircraft and cars, with flying displays in summer that are a real treat if you are an engineering enthusiast.

The roads are gentle and quiet. The lanes between Sutton, Potton and Gamlingay are narrow, with hedges and short bends and good surfaces, and the land is mostly flat, with long views across fields towards the Cambridgeshire border. Watch for tractors, especially in the harvest months, and for cyclists on the lanes around the villages. It is not a place for speed but for easy riding and a sense of the old countryside.

Potton has shops, a pub and a café or two, and for fuel and bigger services, Biggleswade is about six kilometres away, on the old Great North Road. Sutton itself has a pub and a church and very little else, which is exactly why it feels like a good place to stop.
t.brentford@51.5,-0.3:
Brentford is where the River Brent and the Grand Union Canal meet the Thames, on the western edge of London, and for centuries it was the first important crossing west of the capital. It is a busy, mixed place of new riverside apartments, old pubs, warehouses and roads, with Kew Gardens just across the water and Syon Park, the London home of the Dukes of Northumberland, next door.

It is a place with a long story. Julius Caesar may have crossed the Thames near here in 54 BC, according to local tradition, and in 1642, during the English Civil War, the Battle of Brentford was fought in its streets, as Royalist troops attacked the town on their way to London. In the nineteenth century the waterworks at Kew Bridge pumped water to West London with giant steam engines, and the old pumping station now houses the London Museum of Water and Steam, where some of those engines are still run on certain days. Brentford Football Club, after more than a century at Griffin Park, moved in 2020 to its new stadium beside the railway.

The finish here usually comes off the M4 or the A4 Great West Road, the road that carried traffic west from London and was lined in the 1920s and 30s with grand Art Deco factories, the so-called Golden Mile. Some of those buildings survive, others were lost. Coming from the New Forest or the south coast, you may instead come in through Richmond and over Kew Bridge, which is slower but far more pleasant.

The riding at this end is pure city. Expect heavy traffic at almost any time, frequent lights, buses and cyclists, and be ready for the Ultra Low Emission Zone and the many cameras that cover the main roads. In return, there are lovely river views from Kew Bridge, and the canal towpath and the riverside walk at Strand-on-the-Green, with its old pubs and cottages along the water, are pleasant places to walk off the ride.

Brentford has fuel, food, shops and everything else, and good train links to central London. Take a moment by the river at the point where the Brent flows into the Thames: the swans, the boats and the green of Kew on the other bank make a peaceful end to a long day.
t.richmond@51.5,-0.3:
From the top of Richmond Hill, the Thames bends below you through meadows and trees, and on a clear day you can see far across the river valley towards Windsor. This view is so admired that it was protected by an Act of Parliament in 1902, the only view in England with that honour, and painters like Turner and Reynolds came here to capture it. It is a fine place to end a long day, looking back towards the west where you have been.

Richmond has a royal past. Henry VII built a palace here and named the town after his earldom of Richmond in Yorkshire, and Elizabeth I died in that palace in 1603. Only a gatehouse and some old walls remain, close to the green, but the name stuck. Richmond Bridge, opened in 1777, is the oldest surviving bridge over the Thames in London, and the riverside below the hill, with its terraces and pubs, is one of the most pleasant spots in the city.

Richmond Park is the other big draw. It is the largest of London's royal parks, a huge area of grassland, ancient oaks and ponds, with herds of red and fallow deer roaming freely. Motorcycles are allowed on the park roads, but the speed limit is low, the roads close to traffic at night, and the deer and cyclists have right of way in all but name, so ride gently. In autumn, during the rutting season, the stags roar and clash, and it is wise to keep well away.

The ride in from Dorset usually comes along the M3 and A316, a straightforward run into the suburbs. The last stretch is urban, with traffic lights, roundabouts and plenty of cars, especially on weekend evenings when everyone is heading home. Watch for cameras and bus lanes, and if your bike is older, check the London emission rules.

Richmond has plenty of cafés, pubs and restaurants, fuel on the main roads and good train links into central London. Park up near the green or on the hill, take a short walk to the viewpoint and let the light settle over the river before you head into the city.
t.near ambleside@54.5,-2.9:
At 454 metres, the Kirkstone Pass is the highest pass in the Lake District that you can ride over, and the inn at the top, a squat stone building that has been serving travellers for centuries, claims to be one of the highest pubs in England. The pass gets its name from a large rock near the summit that looks a little like a church steeple, the kirk stone, and it is a natural stopping place where riders gather on summer weekends to admire the views and each other's bikes.

The road over the pass connects Ambleside and Windermere, to the south, with Patterdale and Ullswater, to the north, and it has been a route through the mountains since medieval times. The A592 is the main road, climbing from Windermere with long gentle bends, but the most famous part is the minor road from Ambleside, known as The Struggle, which climbs steeply out of the town with gradients of up to one in four and a series of tight bends. It is short but intense, and in wet or icy weather it demands respect.

From the summit the A592 descends north into a beautiful valley, past the small lake of Brothers Water and down to Patterdale and the southern end of Ullswater, with fells rising on both sides. The road narrows in spots, with stone walls close to the edge, and the surface can be uneven. Traffic is heavy in summer, especially at weekends, and sheep wander onto the road. In winter the pass can be closed by snow and ice, and even in summer conditions turn fast, with rain and mist sweeping over the summit.

The landscape here is classic Lake District: steep, rocky fells, green valleys, dry stone walls and lakes. It is the country that inspired Wordsworth and the other Romantic poets, and it remains one of the most popular areas for walking in Britain. The light here is always changing, and the views from the summit, on a clear day, are wonderful.

The inn at the top serves food and drink. For fuel, shops and other services, Ambleside, about five kilometres south, and Windermere, a little further, are the nearest towns. Patterdale and Glenridding, at the northern foot of the pass, have small shops and cafes.
t.near penrith@54.6,-2.9:
The northern shore of Ullswater, between Pooley Bridge and Glenridding, is one of the gentlest and most beautiful roads in the Lake District. The A592 runs along the water's edge, under old trees and past grassy shores, with the lake on one side and the wooded slopes of Gowbarrow Fell on the other, and at every bend there is a new view of the water and the fells at its southern end. Ullswater is the second-largest lake in the Lake District, long and winding, often called the most beautiful of them all.

The lake has strong literary connections. In April 1802, William Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy walked along this shore and saw a great mass of wild daffodils near the water at Glencoyne Bay. Dorothy described them in her journal, and William turned the memory into the poem known as I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, one of the most famous poems in the English language. In spring the daffodils still bloom along the shore. Nearby is Aira Force, a waterfall in a wooded ravine, with footpaths and bridges, one of the most visited waterfalls in the Lake District.

The Ullswater steamers, traditional boats that have carried passengers on the lake since the nineteenth century, run between Pooley Bridge, Howtown and Glenridding, and a trip on the water is a fine way to rest from the road. At Pooley Bridge, the old stone bridge over the River Eamont was swept away by floods in 2015 and replaced by a new steel bridge.

The road along the lake gets tight in parts, with stone walls and trees close to the edge, and it is busy in summer, with cars, buses and cyclists. Ride gently and enjoy the views. The tarmac is mostly sound. To the south, the road climbs to the Kirkstone Pass and over to Windermere, and to the north it leads to Penrith and the M6.

Pooley Bridge has a few cafes and shops, and Glenridding has more. Penrith, about twelve kilometres northeast, is the main town of the area, with fuel, supermarkets and all services. The lake is lovely in the early morning and the evening, when the water is still and the light is soft.
t.near glossop@53.4,-1.9:
The summit of the Snake Pass, at a little over 500 metres, is a bleak and beautiful place: a broad saddle of peat moorland between the high plateaus of Kinder Scout to the south and Bleaklow to the north, with heather, cotton grass and dark, eroded peat hags stretching away on both sides. The A57 crosses here on its way between Glossop and Sheffield, and the Pennine Way, Britain's oldest long-distance footpath, crosses the road at the top. On a clear day the view east down the valley of the Snake is wide and wild; on a bad day you can barely see the road.

The road was built in the early nineteenth century as a turnpike, engineered by Thomas Telford, and its name comes from the Snake Inn, further down the eastern side, which was named after the snake in the coat of arms of the Duke of Devonshire, the local landowner. For walkers, the moors around here have a famous history: in 1932, hundreds of people took part in a mass trespass on Kinder Scout to protest against the lack of public access to the moors, an event that helped lead to the creation of national parks and the right to roam in Britain.

The Snake Pass ranks among the most popular motorcycle roads in England, with long climbs, sweeping bends, tight corners and fine views. It is also one of the most dangerous: the road pinches down here and there, with steep drops, and the weather can be wild, with fog, rain, ice and snow, and the road is often closed in winter. Landslips have closed it at times. Traffic is heavy at weekends, and there are speed limits and enforcement. Ride carefully and respect the road.

The moors here are part of the Peak District National Park, the first national park in Britain, and they are home to grouse, curlews and mountain hares, which turn white in winter. The wreckage of several aircraft that crashed in fog lies on Bleaklow, a reminder of how treacherous the weather can be.

Glossop, about five kilometres west, has fuel, shops, cafes and pubs. To the east, the Ladybower Reservoir and the Hope Valley have more services. There is nothing at the summit itself, apart from a lay-by and the view.
t.near hope valley@53.4,-1.7:
Below the Snake Pass, on the eastern side, the A57 crosses the Ladybower Reservoir on a long viaduct, and in a few seconds you go from bare moorland to a scene that looks almost Alpine: dark water fingering into wooded valleys, steep slopes of conifers, and the stone walls of the dams further up the valley. Ladybower and its neighbours, Derwent and Howden, form a chain of reservoirs in the Upper Derwent Valley that supply water to the cities of the East Midlands, and on a calm morning their surfaces reflect the hills perfectly.

The reservoirs have a story. Ladybower was built during the 1930s and 1940s, and its rising water drowned two villages, Ashopton and Derwent, whose people were moved to new homes. The church spire of Derwent stood above the water for a few years before it was demolished, and in dry summers, when the level drops, the foundations of old houses and walls still appear on the exposed mud. Further up the valley, the Derwent Dam, with its castle-like towers, was used by the RAF in 1943 to practise for the famous Dambusters raid on the dams of the Ruhr, because its shape resembled the German targets. There is a small museum in the dam's west tower, and every so often a commemorative flypast.

The other thing that catches people's eyes are the two great overflow shafts, known locally as the plugholes, which swallow water from the reservoir when it is full, a hypnotic sight after heavy rain. The roads around the reservoirs are popular with cyclists and walkers, and in summer the valley can be busy.

The A57 here is a good road, with sweeping bends, gentle gradients and a decent surface, and the views over the water are lovely. Traffic is moderate, heavier at weekends. To the south, the A6013 runs past the reservoir toward Bamford and the Hope Valley, a pleasant valley with villages, pubs and the ruined Peveril Castle above Castleton, which also has caves you can explore underground.

Hathersage and Bamford, a few kilometres south, have shops, cafes and pubs, and Hathersage has fuel. Sheffield, about twenty kilometres east, is the nearest big city. There is a visitor centre at Fairholmes, up the valley beside the Derwent Dam, with a cafe and toilets, which is worth a halt.
t.macclesfield@53.3,-2.1:
Macclesfield is a market town at the foot of the Pennines, where the Cheshire plain runs into the first hills of the Peak District, and it built its prosperity on silk. From the eighteenth century the town was one of the main centres of silk production in Britain, with dozens of mills powered first by water and later by steam, and for a while it was known as the silk town. The industry has gone, but its traces remain in the tall mill buildings, the weavers' cottages with their wide top-floor windows to let in light for the looms, and the Silk Museum, where you can see the old machines at work.

The town has an old centre on a hill, with a market place, a church reached by a steep flight of steps known as the 108 Steps, and narrow streets of brick and stone buildings. It is also known, among music fans, as the hometown of Ian Curtis of Joy Division. Today Macclesfield is a busy commuter town for Manchester, with shops, pubs, cafes and restaurants, and a busy market.

For riders, the town is the western start of the A537, the road known as the Cat and Fiddle, which climbs east across the moors to Buxton. It ranks among the best-known motorcycle roads in England, and on a sunny weekend you will see plenty of bikes heading up the hill. The road begins with a steady climb out of the town, past fields and woods, and then onto the open moorland, with long bends, sharp corners and fine views back over the Cheshire plain. It has a reputation for accidents, and there are average speed cameras along its length.

Macclesfield has all services: fuel, shops, cafes, restaurants and accommodation. Prepare here for the ride over the moors, and come back for a pint afterwards. The countryside around it is attractive, with the Macclesfield Forest, a large area of woodland and reservoirs on the slopes above the town, and the canal, which winds through the hills to the south.

To the north, the villages of Prestbury and Bollington are pretty places, with pubs and cafes, and the White Nancy, a small round folly on a hill above Bollington, is a local landmark. On a clear day, the radio telescope at Jodrell Bank can be seen on the plain to the west.
t.near buxton@53.2,-2.0:
Near the summit of the A537, at about 515 metres, stands the Cat and Fiddle, a long stone building that was for years the second-highest pub in England and gave its name to one of the most famous and notorious motorcycle roads in Britain. The pub closed in 2015, then reopened as a distillery and shop, and it remains a landmark and a meeting place for riders, who gather in the car park on sunny weekends. Around it the moors stretch away in every direction, brown and purple with heather, with the Cheshire plain to the west and the hills of the Peak District to the east.

The Cat and Fiddle road runs from Macclesfield to Buxton, across the high moorland, and it is a superb ride, with long climbs, sweeping bends, tight corners and wide views. It has also been one of the most dangerous roads in Britain, with many serious accidents involving motorcycles, and in recent years average speed cameras have been installed along the whole route and the speed limit lowered. Ride with care, respect the limits and watch for the sharp corners near the top.

The weather on the moors can be harsh, with strong winds, rain, fog and snow in winter, and the road is sometimes closed by snow. Even in summer, the temperature at the top can be several degrees lower than in the towns below. The moorland here is part of the Peak District National Park, and it is home to red grouse, curlews and other birds, and in late summer the heather turns the hills purple.

Buxton, about six kilometres east, is a handsome spa town at over 300 metres, one of the highest market towns in England, known for its mineral water, which rises from a spring in the centre of the town and has been bottled and sold for centuries. The Romans used the springs, and in the eighteenth century the Dukes of Devonshire built the elegant Crescent and other buildings to turn Buxton into a fashionable resort. Today it has an opera house, a famous festival and attractive gardens.

Buxton has fuel stations, supermarkets and places to eat and sleep. Macclesfield, at the other end of the road, has all services too. The summit has the old building and its car park, which is where the bikes line up in rows on a sunny Sunday.
t.near llanddeusant@51.9,-3.7:
The top of the Black Mountain Pass, at 493 metres, is a wild spot on the A4069 between Brynamman and Llangadog, on the western edge of the Brecon Beacons, which in Welsh are now called Bannau Brycheiniog. The road crosses a high, open moorland of grass, bracken and limestone outcrops, with old quarries beside the road and wide views over the hills to the north and the valleys to the south. Sheep graze freely on both sides, and the only sounds are the wind and the occasional skylark.

The western range of the park is called the Black Mountain, Y Mynydd Du in Welsh, a long ridge of red sandstone with steep escarpments facing north. Hidden below those escarpments, a few kilometres from the pass near the hamlet of Llanddeusant, lies the lake of Llyn y Fan Fach, the setting for one of the best-loved Welsh legends: a young farmer fell in love with a fairy woman who rose from the lake, and she agreed to marry him on condition that he never struck her three times. When he did, she returned to the lake, taking her cattle with her, but her sons became the Physicians of Myddfai, famous healers of medieval Wales.

The road is among the finest motorcycle roads in Wales, with a series of tight hairpins on the southern side, known as the Brynamman side, long sweeping bends on the northern descent and spectacular views. It was used by television motoring shows and is popular with riders and drivers on summer weekends. The road narrows in spots, with no barriers, and sheep often stand on the road or lie on the warm tarmac. The sky can switch moods in minutes, with fog and rain on the summit, and in winter the road can be icy or closed by snow.

To the north the road descends through farmland to Llangadog in the Tywi valley, and to the west, on a limestone crag, stands Carreg Cennen Castle, one of the most dramatic castle ruins in Wales. The area is rich in history and legend, and the landscape is beautiful.

There are no services on the pass, apart from parking areas. Brynamman, about twelve kilometres south, has shops and fuel, and Llangadog to the north has a few services. Llandeilo, a little further, is a pretty market town with cafes.
t.brynamman@51.8,-3.9:
Brynamman is a former mining village at the head of the Amman valley, in the western corner of the South Wales coalfield, where the coal was anthracite, the hardest and purest kind. The village grew in the nineteenth century around collieries, ironworks and tinplate works, and it has the classic look of a Welsh valley community: terraces of stone houses climbing the hillsides, chapels with grand facades, a few shops and pubs, and the bare slopes of the Black Mountain rising behind. The mines have closed, but the community and its traditions remain.

This is a strongly Welsh-speaking area, and you will hear the language in the shops and on the streets. The chapels, the choirs and the rugby clubs were the heart of community life, and they still matter. The Amman valley also produced writers, poets and preachers, and the chapels of the area were famous for their music. If you have time, look at the details of the chapel buildings: their size and grandeur tell you how important they were.

For riders, Brynamman is the southern gateway to the Black Mountain Pass, the A4069, one of the best motorcycle roads in Wales. From the village the road climbs steeply north onto the moorland, with a series of tight hairpins and views back over the valley, before crossing the open summit and descending toward Llangadog in the Tywi valley. The road gets tight in parts, with no barriers and sheep on the road, and the weather can be wild on the summit. It is a superb ride, especially on a clear day, but it demands respect.

The valley itself has an interesting landscape, with the scars of mining slowly being healed by grass and trees, and the river running through the middle. The old railway lines have become cycle paths, and there are walks onto the hills. To the south, the valley widens toward Ammanford and the coast at Llanelli.

Brynamman has shops, a few cafes and pubs, and fuel in the area. Ammanford, a few kilometres down the valley, is the main town, with supermarkets and more services. Sort yourself out here before the climb, and come back down for a cup of tea afterwards.
t.near llangwm@53.1,-3.5:
The Denbigh Moors, Mynydd Hiraethog in Welsh, are a high, empty plateau of heather, grass and forestry in the north of Wales, between the Vale of Clwyd and the upper Conwy valley. It is a quiet, bleak and lovely landscape, with few people, wide skies and the reservoirs of Llyn Brenig and Llyn Alwen lying in the hollows, surrounded by conifers. The roads across the moors form the so-called Evo Triangle, named after a motoring magazine that used them for testing cars: the A543 from Pentrefoelas toward Denbigh, the B4501 past Llyn Brenig toward Cerrigydrudion, and the A5 back to Pentrefoelas. Together they make a loop of about thirty kilometres, with fast sweeping bends, sudden crests, tight corners and long straights across the moor, and it is among the most popular riding areas in Wales. Here the forest is thick and old, with Douglas fir, western red cedar and hemlock towering over the road, and the river below runs milky grey with silt ground off the Emmons Glacier, the largest glacier by area in the contiguous United States.

t.chinook pass scenic byway point 3@46.9,-:

t.near tieton@46.7,-120.7:

t.north cascades scenic highway point 2@48:
The first time you see Diablo Lake from the overlook on State Route 20, you will probably assume someone has tinted the photo. The water is an intense, milky turquoise, and it sits in a deep valley ringed by steep, forested slopes and jagged peaks streaked with snow and ice. The colour comes from glacial flour, fine rock dust ground by the glaciers above and carried down by streams. It reflects green and blue light, giving the lake its extraordinary hue.

t.north cascades scenic highway point 3@48:
Washington Pass, at 1,669 metres, is the high point of the North Cascades Highway, and the view from the overlook is one of the finest in the Pacific Northwest. t.north cascades scenic highway point 4@48:
Winthrop looks like a film set, and in a way it is. Here the valley narrows and the forest closes in, with towering Douglas firs and red cedars draped in moss, and the river rushes over boulders beside the road. Mount Baker itself is hidden for now, but you can feel it ahead.

t.mount baker highway point 3@48.9,-121.7:

t.sooke@48.4,-123.7:

t.lake cowichan@48.8,-124.1:

t.nanaimo@49.2,-123.9:

t.rainier@46.9,-122.7:
Despite the name, the town of Rainier is not on the mountain. t.near manchester@47.6,-122.5:
Across Puget Sound from Seattle, on the eastern shore of the Kitsap Peninsula, the little community of Manchester looks back at the city skyline from a beach of pebbles and driftwood.
