Some of the concrete gun emplacements and an old torpedo warehouse are still there, now surrounded by forest and used for picnics and events. There are trails through the woods and along the beach, and it is a pleasant spot for a walk at the end of the day.

A few kilometres south, Southworth is the terminal for the ferry to Vashon Island and Fauntleroy in West Seattle, and many people use it to commute to the city. To the west, Port Orchard is the main town of the area, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and across Sinclair Inlet lies Bremerton, home of the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard, where you can often see aircraft carriers and other naval ships moored.

The roads on the Kitsap Peninsula are generally quiet two-lane highways and country roads, winding through forests and along the shore, with occasional glimpses of the water. They can be wet and slippery under the trees, and deer are common, especially at dawn and dusk. As a finish point, Manchester is peaceful and pretty. If you are heading back to Seattle, the ferries are a fine way to end the day, with the city slowly growing larger as you cross the sound. Check schedules, as sailings are limited at certain times.
t.near richmond@49.2,-123.2:
The point lies on the western edge of Richmond, out where the city gives way to the mudflats and marshes of the Fraser River delta. Richmond is built almost entirely on flat delta land, protected by dykes from the river and the sea, and the western shore, along Sturgeon Bank, is a wide expanse of mud, eelgrass and tidal channels, important for migrating birds. On a clear day, the view across the Strait of Georgia to the mountains of Vancouver Island is wide and calming, and the sunsets are often spectacular.

At the south-western corner of Richmond lies Steveston, an old fishing village at the mouth of the Fraser, where boats still sell fresh fish and prawns directly from the dock. The Gulf of Georgia Cannery, once one of the largest salmon canneries in British Columbia, is now a national historic site and museum, telling the story of the fishing industry and the many Japanese Canadian, Chinese and Indigenous workers who made it run.

Richmond also has one of the most vibrant Asian food scenes in North America. The city has a large Chinese Canadian population, and its malls and restaurants serve some of the best dim sum, noodles and seafood outside Asia. In summer, the night markets are a lively, crowded experience with food stalls of every kind.

As a starting point for the Sunshine Coast ferry ride, Richmond is practical but requires a trip through Vancouver. The route north crosses the city, the Lions Gate Bridge or the Second Narrows, and then heads west along the North Shore to Horseshoe Bay, where ferries leave for Langdale on the Sunshine Coast. Traffic in the Vancouver area can be heavy, so allow plenty of time and leave early. Richmond has fuel and services everywhere. The weather on the coast is mild but often wet, especially from October to April, so good rain gear is essential.
t.near west end@49.3,-123.1:
Vancouver's West End is one of the densest neighbourhoods in North America, a grid of apartment towers and old wooden houses squeezed between downtown, Stanley Park and English Bay, and yet it feels oddly relaxed. People walk everywhere, the streets are lined with trees, and at the end of every road, it seems, there is water or mountains or both. As the finish of a ride, it is hard to beat for atmosphere.

Stanley Park, on the edge of the West End, is a vast area of forest on a peninsula jutting into the harbour, bigger than New York's Central Park, with huge cedars and firs, beaches and a seawall path that runs right around it. You can ride the park drive, a one-way road that loops through the forest with views of the harbour, the North Shore mountains and the Lions Gate Bridge, a graceful suspension bridge built in the 1930s that links the city to West Vancouver.

English Bay Beach, at the foot of Denman Street, is the place to be at sunset. Freighters anchored in the bay wait for their turn to enter the port, the sky turns orange and pink, and the beach fills with people sitting on logs and watching the light. In summer, an international fireworks competition is held here over several nights, attracting huge crowds.

The Mount Baker ride, which ends here, involves a border crossing into the United States and back, so remember your passport and be prepared for queues at the border, especially on weekends. Coming back into the city, traffic can be heavy, and the downtown streets are full of pedestrians, cyclists, buses and one-way systems. Parking is tight and expensive in the West End. There is fuel on the main arteries, though fewer stations in the central neighbourhoods than you might expect. Restaurants and cafés of every kind line Denman and Davie streets, so at least dinner will not be a problem.
t.mission@49.1,-122.3:
Mission takes its name from St. Mary's Mission, a Catholic mission and school founded in the nineteenth century by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate on the north bank of the Fraser River. The residential school that grew out of it is now remembered for its painful role in the history of Indigenous people in Canada. On a hill above the town stands Westminster Abbey, a Benedictine monastery whose modern church tower is visible from far away, and whose grounds offer peaceful views over the river valley.

Today Mission is a growing town in the Fraser Valley, about an hour east of Vancouver, and it serves as a practical fuel stop on the ride to Hope and the Fraser Canyon. The town has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, as well as Mission Raceway Park, a drag strip and road course that hosts motorcycle and car events. The bridge across the Fraser connects Mission to Abbotsford on the south bank.

The ride east from here follows Highway 7, the Lougheed Highway, along the north bank of the Fraser. It is a much more pleasant route than the busy Trans-Canada Highway on the south bank, with farmland, forests and views of the river and the mountains. The road passes through small communities and past the turnoff to Harrison Hot Springs, a resort town on a large lake, before reaching Hope at the mouth of the Fraser Canyon. The traffic is moderate, the curves gentle, and the mountains grow steadily closer.

North of Mission, Stave Lake and Hayward Lake, reservoirs for hydroelectric dams, are surrounded by forests and mountains, with quiet roads, picnic areas and trails. The Golden Ears, a distinctive twin-peaked mountain, rises to the west. Weather in the Fraser Valley is mild but often rainy, and in winter the outflow winds from the interior can bring cold, gusty conditions. Summer is the best time to ride, with long days and generally dry weather.
t.hope@49.4,-121.4:
Hope is where the Fraser River leaves the mountains. Upstream, the river roars through the narrow, steep-walled Fraser Canyon; downstream, it widens and slows across the flat, fertile valley towards Vancouver. The town sits at the junction, surrounded by forested peaks, and it has always been a crossroads: the Trans-Canada Highway heads north through the canyon, the Coquihalla Highway climbs north-east over the mountains to the interior, and the Crowsnest Highway runs east through Manning Park towards the Okanagan.

Film fans may recognise the town: in 1982, Hope stood in for the fictional town in the first Rambo film, First Blood, and the local tourist office will happily point you to the filming locations. The town is also known for its chainsaw carvings, wooden sculptures scattered through the streets. Just outside town, the Othello Tunnels, a series of old railway tunnels blasted through the granite of the Coquihalla Canyon for the Kettle Valley Railway, are now a walking trail, with the river rushing through the gorge beneath wooden bridges. It is one of the most impressive short walks in the province.

East of town on Highway 3, a vast scar on the mountainside marks the Hope Slide of 1965, one of the largest landslides in Canadian history, which buried the highway under tens of metres of rock. A viewpoint explains what happened. North of town, the Fraser Canyon road follows the river through tunnels and along cliffs, with the famous Hell's Gate, where the river squeezes through a narrow gap, about an hour away.

Hope has fuel, restaurants and motels, and it is the last large settlement before the mountain highways, so top up here without fail. The weather can change dramatically here. The coastal mountains catch a lot of rain, and the passes to the east can have snow from autumn to spring. Summer is the best time to ride, but even then, carry warm clothing for the higher roads, and check conditions before setting out on the Coquihalla or Highway 3.
t.salisbury@51.1,-1.8:
Approach Salisbury from almost any direction and you will see the spire first, a slender stone needle rising above the water meadows, the tallest church spire in Britain at around 123 metres. The cathedral beneath it was built with remarkable speed in the thirteenth century, which gives it an unusual unity of style, and it stands in the middle of a vast, peaceful lawn, the Cathedral Close, surrounded by elegant old houses. John Constable painted it from the meadows, and the view he chose is still there.

The cathedral's chapter house holds one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta, the charter of 1215 that limited the power of King John and became a cornerstone of English law. It is in remarkably good condition, and it is worth seeing. The city itself grew up in the thirteenth century when the bishop moved down from Old Sarum, an Iron Age hill fort a couple of kilometres north, whose ramparts and castle ruins are still visible.

Salisbury lies at the meeting of several rivers, the Avon, the Nadder, the Wylye and the Bourne, and the water meadows around the city are lush and green. To the north stretches Salisbury Plain, a vast chalk upland, much of it used by the army for training, with signs warning of tanks crossing and red flags flying when firing is in progress. Stonehenge, the most famous prehistoric monument in Europe, stands on the plain about fifteen kilometres north of the city.

The riding around Salisbury is a pleasant mix of open chalk downland, with long views and gentle curves, and narrow lanes through river valleys and villages. The main roads, like the A303 past Stonehenge, can be very busy, especially in summer, and slow. Salisbury has plenty of cafés, pubs and restaurants, as well as fuel and other services, though the city centre has a complicated one-way system and parking can be difficult. Park on the edge and walk in.
t.shaftesbury@51.0,-2.2:
Gold Hill is one of the most famous streets in England, and you have probably seen it without knowing its name: a steep, cobbled lane lined with old cottages, curving down from the top of the town, with the green fields of the Blackmore Vale spread out below. In 1973 it featured in a television advertisement for Hovis bread, directed by a young Ridley Scott, which became one of the best-loved adverts in British history. It is too steep and cobbled for bikes, so park in the town and walk down.

Shaftesbury sits on top of a greensand ridge, high above the surrounding countryside, and it is one of the oldest towns in Dorset. King Alfred the Great founded an abbey here in the late ninth century, with his daughter as its first abbess, and it became one of the richest nunneries in England, especially after the relics of the murdered King Edward the Martyr were brought here. Only the foundations survive, in a peaceful garden next to Gold Hill. Thomas Hardy called the town Shaston in his novels.

The views from Shaftesbury are wonderful, stretching over the Blackmore Vale to the west and Cranborne Chase to the east. Cranborne Chase is an area of rolling chalk downland, woods and valleys, once a royal hunting ground, and it has some of the best riding in southern England. The B3081 east of Shaftesbury climbs Zig Zag Hill, a short series of tight hairpin bends up the scarp of the downs, before continuing over the Chase through beautiful, quiet countryside.

The town has a good selection of cafés, pubs and restaurants, and the high street is lively, with independent shops. Fuel and other services are available. The lanes around Shaftesbury are narrow, often sunken between high hedges, with blind bends and steep gradients, and they can be muddy and slippery after rain. The weather can be changeable, and on top of the ridge the wind can be strong, but on a clear day the views make it all worthwhile.
t.basingstoke@51.3,-1.1:
Let us be honest about Basingstoke. It is a large, modern town on the M3, built up rapidly in the 1960s and 1970s as an overspill town for London, with a sprawl of housing estates, business parks and so many roundabouts that it is sometimes called Doughnut City. It is not a place anyone visits for its beauty. But it is very good at what riders need from it: fuel, food and a quick way back onto the road.

There is a little more depth to it if you look. Jane Austen was born and grew up in the village of Steventon, a few kilometres south-west, where her father was rector, and she attended balls in Basingstoke as a young woman. The town has a statue of her outside the Willis Museum. On the eastern edge of town, in the village of Old Basing, stand the ruins of Basing House, once one of the largest private houses in England, which was besieged for years during the Civil War and finally stormed and destroyed by Oliver Cromwell's troops in 1645.

The landscape around Basingstoke is part of the North Hampshire Downs, a gentle chalk upland with rolling fields, woods and small villages. The lanes to the west and south, towards Overton, Whitchurch and the Test valley, are quiet and pleasant, with gentle curves and little traffic. The River Test, one of the most famous chalk streams in the world for fly fishing, runs clear and cold through water meadows. Further south, the roads towards Stockbridge and Salisbury cross open downland with long views.

Basingstoke has fuel stations, supermarkets, fast food and every kind of service, all easily accessible from the ring road. The town centre is dominated by a large shopping centre, Festival Place, and is best avoided on a bike. The M3 and the A303 are the main routes west and can be busy, especially on Friday afternoons and summer weekends. Use Basingstoke for what it is good at, then head off into the countryside.
t.fairford@51.7,-1.8:
Fairford is a small, quiet town on the southern edge of the Cotswolds, built of honey-coloured stone along the River Coln, and it hides one of the great treasures of English medieval art. The parish church of St Mary has the only complete set of medieval stained glass windows to survive in any parish church in England: twenty-eight windows, made around 1500, telling the story of the Christian faith from the Creation to the Last Judgement. How they survived the iconoclasm of the Reformation and the Civil War is a mystery, but they did, and they are well worth twenty minutes of your time.

The town's other claim to fame is very different. Just south of Fairford lies RAF Fairford, a base used by the United States Air Force, and every July it hosts the Royal International Air Tattoo, one of the largest military air shows in the world, when the skies fill with jets and the roads fill with traffic. Outside that week, you might still hear the occasional roar of aircraft.

The landscape around Fairford is gentle and pastoral, with water meadows, stone villages and gravel pits, many now flooded and used as lakes for sailing and fishing in the Cotswold Water Park. A few kilometres east, Lechlade is the town where the Thames becomes navigable, and its riverside meadows are made for a short break. To the north, the roads climb into the Cotswold hills, with wide views, beautiful villages and quiet lanes, and further west lie the Welsh borders and the Brecon Beacons, the destination of the day.

As a fuel stop, Fairford is small, so options are limited; Cirencester and Swindon are the nearest large towns with plenty of choice. The town has a few pubs and cafés where you can get a coffee or a quick lunch. The roads around Fairford are flat and easy, with gentle curves, but the Cotswold lanes can be narrow and winding, with blind bends and stone walls close to the road. Watch for tractors, horses and cyclists.
t.brecon@51.9,-3.4:
Brecon is a small market town at the meeting of the Usk and the Honddu, in the shadow of the highest mountains in southern Britain. To the south rise the Brecon Beacons, now officially known by their Welsh name, Bannau Brycheiniog: a range of grassy, flat-topped sandstone summits with steep north-facing scarps, culminating in Pen y Fan, 886 metres high. On a clear day, the view of the mountains from the town is magnificent; on a wet day, which is often, they disappear into the clouds.

The town has a cathedral, a small, solid building on a hill above the river, and a long military tradition: the army has used the Beacons for training for generations, and you may see soldiers marching up the hills with heavy packs. The Monmouthshire and Brecon Canal ends here, and its towpath is good for a quiet half hour on foot. In August, Brecon hosts a well-known jazz festival.

For riders, Brecon is a gateway to some of the best roads in Britain. The A470 south through the Beacons, past the Storey Arms and down towards Merthyr Tydfil, is a fast, flowing road with long views over the mountains and reservoirs. To the west, the A4069 over the Black Mountain, between Llangadog and Brynamman, is a spectacular mountain road with hairpins and wide-open moorland that has featured on television as one of the best driving roads in Britain. To the north-east, the Gospel Pass, a single-track road from Hay-on-Wye over the Black Mountains, is the highest road in Wales.

The roads here demand respect. Sheep wander freely, cattle grids are common, and the weather can change in minutes, with rain, wind and fog sweeping in from the west. Mountain roads can be greasy and narrow, with sharp bends and steep drops. Brecon has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and pubs, and nobody will hurry you out of a café before or after the mountains. Welsh cakes and a cup of tea are a traditional and very welcome snack.
t.near arlington heights on the way back@4:
The North Fork of the Stillaguamish River flows west out of the Cascades here, through a wide valley of farmland and forests, past the small communities of Arlington Heights, Oso and Darrington, on its way to Puget Sound. You are in the hills above the valley, east of Arlington, and on a hot day on the way back from the North Cascades, the river and the small lakes in the area offer a chance to cool off.

The valley has a tragic recent history. In March 2014, a hillside above the river near Oso collapsed in one of the deadliest landslides in American history, burying a neighbourhood and killing forty-three people. The site is now a memorial, and State Route 530 passes right by it. It is a sobering place, and many travellers stop to pay their respects.

The North Cascades Highway, State Route 20, which the ride follows, ranks with the finest mountain roads in the United States, crossing the Cascades through the North Cascades National Park, with jagged peaks, glaciers and turquoise lakes like Diablo Lake. Washington Pass, at the top, has views of the granite spires of Liberty Bell Mountain. The highway is closed in winter, typically from November to April or May, because of avalanche danger.

Swimming in the rivers here is a serious business. The water comes straight from glaciers and snowfields, so it is cold even in midsummer, and the currents can be strong. Choose calm, shallow spots, and never swim alone. Some of the lakes in the foothills are warmer and calmer, with public access points. Arlington has fuel, supermarkets and fast food, and the valley has a few small stores and cafés. The roads are generally good, two-lane highways with gentle curves, but they can be busy with logging trucks and RVs.
t.riverbend@47.5,-121.8:
Fans of Twin Peaks will recognise the landscape. The television series was filmed partly in North Bend and nearby Snoqualmie, a few kilometres from the point, and the forests, the mountains and the misty river valley gave the show much of its brooding atmosphere. Mount Si, a steep, rocky peak, looms over the town, and a famous diner still serves cherry pie and coffee to pilgrims from all over the world.

Riverbend is a small residential community on the South Fork of the Snoqualmie River, just east of North Bend, at the foot of the Cascades. It is a place of houses scattered among tall firs and cedars, along the river, with mountains rising on all sides. For riders, it is a practical fuel stop, since North Bend has fuel stations, supermarkets and fast food, and it is the last town of any size before the long climb over Snoqualmie Pass on Interstate 90.

A short distance downstream, Snoqualmie Falls drops more than eighty metres over a rock ledge into a gorge, a powerful and beautiful sight, especially in spring, when the river is high with snowmelt. The falls are sacred to the Snoqualmie Tribe, and there is a viewing platform and a trail down to the base. The historic Salish Lodge sits at the top.

The ride to Leavenworth and Wenatchee crosses the Cascades, either over Snoqualmie Pass and Blewett Pass, or further north over Stevens Pass on US Highway 2. Both routes climb through dense forests to the crest of the mountains, and then descend into the drier, sunnier landscape of central Washington, with pine forests and sagebrush. The passes can have snow from autumn to spring, and the weather can change quickly, so check conditions before setting out. Interstate 90 is busy and fast, with heavy truck traffic, so the old roads and the smaller highways are more pleasant.
t.leavenworth@47.6,-120.7:
In the early 1960s, Leavenworth was a dying town. The railway had moved its operations elsewhere, the sawmill had closed, and the main street was full of empty shops. So the townspeople came up with a bold idea: they would remodel the whole town in the style of a Bavarian village, to attract tourists. It worked. Today Leavenworth pulls in visitors by the coachload from all over Washington, with half-timbered buildings, painted façades, beer halls, sausage shops and an Oktoberfest that draws huge crowds. It is gloriously kitsch, and it does not take itself too seriously.

The setting helps. Leavenworth sits at the mouth of the Tumwater Canyon, where the Wenatchee River comes tumbling out of the mountains, surrounded by steep, forested peaks that do look a little like the Alps. Icicle Creek, flowing into the river from the south, leads into a dramatic canyon popular with rock climbers, and beyond it lie the Enchantments, a high basin of granite peaks and lakes.

For a food stop, Leavenworth is perfect. The town is full of restaurants serving German food, from bratwurst and pretzels to schnitzel and strudel, as well as cafés, bakeries and breweries. The main street can be very crowded on summer weekends and during the festivals, so a weekday visit is more relaxed.

The ride into Leavenworth along US Highway 2, through the Tumwater Canyon, is beautiful, with the river roaring beside the road and steep, forested walls on either side. The road is good but busy, with tight bends in places. East of Leavenworth, the landscape becomes drier and more open, with orchards and sagebrush. Summers here are hot and dry, with occasional wildfire smoke, and winters are snowy, with the town transformed by Christmas lights. Fuel and services are available in town, and the drier air east of the crest usually means you can peel off a layer here that you needed on the pass.
t.wenatchee@47.4,-120.3:
Wenatchee calls itself the Apple Capital of the World, and the claim is not idle: the hills around the town, along the Columbia and Wenatchee rivers, are covered in orchards of apples, pears and cherries, irrigated with water from the rivers in an otherwise dry landscape. In spring, the orchards are a sea of blossom; in autumn, the trees are heavy with fruit, and the fruit stands along the roads sell crisp apples and fresh cider.

The town sits on the west bank of the Columbia, one of the great rivers of North America, where it flows through a broad valley lined with basalt cliffs, the remains of vast lava flows that covered this part of the continent millions of years ago. At the end of the last ice age, enormous floods from a glacial lake in Montana swept through the region, carving the cliffs and coulees that make the landscape so dramatic. A paved riverside trail loops along both banks of the Columbia.

Just north of town, Ohme Gardens is a remarkable alpine garden created on a rocky bluff above the river by a single family over decades, with pools, waterfalls and evergreens, and views over the valley. Further north, the Rocky Reach Dam has a visitor centre explaining the history of the river and the hydroelectric projects that transformed the region.

The riding around Wenatchee is varied and rewarding. To the south, US Highway 97 climbs over Blewett Pass through pine forests, with good curves and views. To the north, the roads along the Columbia towards Chelan follow the river through dramatic canyons. To the east, the plateau is open and dry, with long, straight roads through wheat fields. Wenatchee has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and a shady table there is welcome. Summers are hot, often over thirty-five degrees, so ride early and carry water.
t.point roberts@49.0,-123.1:
When the boundary between the United States and British North America was fixed along the 49th parallel in 1846, nobody seems to have noticed, or cared, that the line would cut off the tip of the Tsawwassen peninsula south of Vancouver. The result is Point Roberts, a small piece of Washington State, about thirteen square kilometres, that can only be reached by land by passing through Canada. To get there from the rest of the United States, you cross into Canada, ride about forty kilometres through British Columbia, and cross back into the US. Bring your passport, and expect four border crossings for a round trip.

The community is quiet and slightly surreal: a few streets of houses, a marina, a golf course, some shops and a lot of forest, with water on three sides. Many of the homes belong to Canadians who use them as holiday cottages, and the local economy depends heavily on visitors from the north. When the border was closed during the pandemic, Point Roberts was cut off from the outside world for well over a year, and the community struggled.

The views from the shore are wide and beautiful. From Lighthouse Marine Park, at the south-western tip, you look out over the Strait of Georgia to the Gulf Islands and Vancouver Island, and in summer, orcas are sometimes seen passing close to shore. The sunsets over the water are spectacular. Monument Park, at the north-western corner, marks the start of the land border, with a stone obelisk on the bluff.

Next door in Canada, Tsawwassen is the terminal for the BC Ferries to Victoria and the Gulf Islands, and you can watch the ferries come and go from the shore. The roads in Point Roberts are short and quiet, with little traffic, and they make a pleasant loop. There are a few fuel stations, a grocery store and some cafés. Border queues can be long on summer weekends.
t.birch bay@48.9,-122.7:
Birch Bay is a wide, shallow, crescent-shaped bay on the coast of Whatcom County, just south of the Canadian border, and at low tide the water retreats a long way, exposing vast flats of sand where children dig for clams and look for sand dollars. In summer, the incoming tide flows over the sun-warmed sand and the water becomes noticeably warmer than elsewhere in the area, making it one of the more pleasant places to swim in the chilly waters of the Salish Sea.

The town of Birch Bay is a laid-back resort community, with beach houses, holiday rentals, a few restaurants and ice cream shops along the shore road, and a state park with campsites, forest and beach at the southern end. On clear days, the view across the water stretches to the islands and the mountains of Vancouver Island, and Mount Baker rises to the east, a great white cone above the farmland.

A few kilometres north, in Blaine, the Peace Arch stands on the border between the United States and Canada, a white monument built in 1921 to celebrate the long peace between the two countries, in a park that straddles the border. The nearby Semiahmoo Spit is a long, narrow sandbar with a resort, a marina and views across Drayton Harbor.

For riders on the Sunshine Coast ferry ride, Birch Bay is a pleasant pause on the coastal route between the border and Bellingham. The roads here are quiet and flat, with views of the water, though the shore road can be busy in summer. Interstate 5 runs a few kilometres inland, carrying heavy traffic to and from Vancouver. Blaine and Birch Bay have fuel and food. If you are crossing the border, check the wait times, which can be long, especially on weekends and holidays, and have your documents ready.
t.sechelt@49.5,-123.8:
The Sunshine Coast is not an island, but it might as well be. Although it is part of the mainland of British Columbia, no road connects it to Vancouver; you have to take a ferry from Horseshoe Bay across Howe Sound to Langdale, and the forty-minute crossing, through a fjord of forested mountains, sets the tone for a place that feels removed from the rush of the city. Sechelt, the main town, sits on a narrow isthmus between the Strait of Georgia and the long, sheltered Sechelt Inlet.

Sechelt is the home of the shíshálh Nation, which in 1986 became the first Indigenous community in Canada to achieve self-government through federal legislation. The nation's cultural centre in town has exhibits about its history and traditions. The town itself is relaxed and friendly, with a waterfront promenade, galleries, cafés and restaurants, and it makes a good place for a meal at the end of a ride.

The Sunshine Coast Highway, Highway 101, runs along the coast from Langdale through Gibsons and Sechelt to Earls Cove, where another ferry crosses Jervis Inlet to the northern part of the coast. The road winds through forests and along the shore, with views of the water and the islands, and it is a pleasant, relaxed ride, though it can be busy in summer. Near Egmont, at the northern end of Sechelt Inlet, the Skookumchuck Narrows are a natural wonder, where the tidal currents create some of the fastest tidal rapids in the world, with whirlpools and standing waves. A walking trail through the forest leads to viewpoints.

Sechelt has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat, from fish and chips to more refined restaurants. The ferry schedule dictates the rhythm of travel on the coast, and in summer the ferries can be full, so reserve or arrive early. The weather is mild but often wet, though the coast lives up to its name more often than Vancouver does.
t.hook@51.3,-1.0:
Hook is a busy Hampshire village built around a crossroads and a railway station, and it exists for most riders as a convenient refuelling stop just off junction 5 of the M3. It is not a place of great charm, but the countryside around it is pleasant, with woods, commons and old villages, and there are a few surprises close by.

Odiham, a few kilometres south, is a handsome small town with Georgian houses and old inns. Nearby are the ruins of Odiham Castle, an octagonal keep built for King John, who is said to have ridden out from here to Runnymede to seal Magna Carta in 1215. The Basingstoke Canal passes close by, and its towpath is a quiet place to walk. RAF Odiham is home to the RAF's Chinook helicopters, and you will often hear them overhead.

Hartley Wintney, to the north-east, has a large village green, a cricket pitch and a row of antique shops. The commons around it are covered with heather and oak, and in late summer the heather turns purple.

The riding around Hook is a mix of fast A-roads and narrow country lanes. The A30 and A287 can be busy, but the lanes to the south and west are quiet, with tight bends, high hedges and occasional tractors. Watch for mud and gravel after rain, and for horses and cyclists on the narrow roads.

Fill the tank in Hook, which is quick and painless, then decide whether the day deserves more. If it does, Odiham's old coaching inns do a decent lunch, and the canal towpath behind the town is the quietest ten minutes in this corner of Hampshire.
t.near edgware@51.6,-0.3:
Most people know Edgware as the end of a Tube line, but riders know it for something older. The A5 that runs through it is Watling Street, the Roman road that ran from the Kent coast to the far side of Britain, and the long dead-straight run from here towards St Albans has the unmistakable stamp of legionary surveyors. The finish lies a little south, around Kingsbury and Queensbury, where north-west London becomes an endless spread of semis, shopping parades and busy junctions.

There is water close by, which is not what you expect. The Welsh Harp, officially the Brent Reservoir, was dug in the nineteenth century to feed the Regent's Canal, and it is now a nature reserve and sailing lake with herons, grebes and the odd cormorant, wedged between the North Circular and the houses. A short walk along its edge is the closest thing to countryside in this part of town.

For anyone mechanically minded, the RAF Museum at Colindale is a few minutes away, with hangars full of aircraft from the First World War to the jet age. Entry has traditionally been free, and it is a fine way to spend an hour if you finish early and the light is still good.

Coming back from the Peak District, the M1 delivers you straight into this, and the transition is brutal. The last few miles are all traffic lights, bus lanes, speed cameras and drivers looking for parking spaces. Filter carefully, watch for car doors and pedestrians stepping off the kerb, and remember that London's low emission zone covers this area; older bikes may need to check their status before riding in.

Fuel and food are easy, from big supermarkets to late-night takeaways. Edgware and Burnt Oak have plenty of cafés where you can sit with a tea and let the motorway hum fade from your ears.
t.wembley@51.6,-0.3:
The arch is what you see first, a white steel hoop rising over north-west London, visible from the North Circular, from Harrow, from the planes coming in to Heathrow. Wembley Stadium was rebuilt and reopened in 2007, replacing the old twin-towered stadium where England won the 1966 World Cup. The new one is bigger, slicker and less romantic, but on match nights the whole district still hums.

Wembley grew up around the stadium and the British Empire Exhibition of the 1920s, and much of the area is still shaped by those events. Wembley Park has been heavily redeveloped in recent years, with new apartment blocks, shops and restaurants around the stadium and the arena. On event days, traffic and parking restrictions are severe, so check the calendar before planning to finish here.

The ride into Wembley from the east is all about the A406 North Circular, one of London's busiest and most frustrating roads. Expect queues, speed cameras and frequent lane changes. Filtering is common, but take care around buses and lorries. The final approach through local roads is slow, with traffic lights, roundabouts and plenty of pedestrians.

Despite the urban sprawl, there are green corners. Fryent Country Park, to the north, is a surprising area of meadows and hedgerows on a hill with views over London. Barn Hill, at its heart, is a good place to watch the sunset over the stadium.

Wembley has every service you could want, with fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants on every main road. Ealing Road, to the south, is famous for its South Asian shops and restaurants, and a plate of food there is one of the best ways to end a long day in the saddle.
t.mitcham@51.4,-0.2:
Mitcham once smelled of lavender. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the fields here supplied much of London's lavender and herbs for perfumes and medicines, and the name still turns up on local street signs. Today it is a dense, busy South London district, but it has kept two large open spaces: Mitcham Common, a wide area of grass, scrub and ponds, and the old cricket green, where the game has been played for centuries, and which the locals will tell you is one of the oldest cricket grounds in the world.

For riders, Mitcham is a starting gate for the Surrey Hills. The A217 and A24 run south through Sutton and Epsom, and within half an hour you are climbing onto the North Downs. Box Hill, with its famous Zig Zag Road, is a classic destination, and the bikers' café at the foot of the hill has been a weekend meeting point for decades. On sunny Sundays, the car park fills with motorcycles of every type.

The ride out of Mitcham is slow at first, with traffic lights, buses and speed cameras, but it improves quickly once you pass Epsom. The downs offer narrow lanes, steep climbs and long views over the Weald, and the roads around Leith Hill and Coldharbour are among the best in the south-east. Watch out for cyclists, who are numerous in the Surrey Hills, and for police speed checks on popular routes.

Coming back, the return to Mitcham is often the hardest part of the day, with heavy traffic in the evening. Plan to arrive outside rush hour if you can.

Fuel and coffee are on every corner, so the only real decision is whether to pause on the green. If there is a match on, watch an over. Nobody has ever regretted ten minutes of village cricket before facing the A217.
t.near aldergrove on the way back@49.1,-12:
Mount Baker owns the skyline here. On a clear day the volcano rises white and enormous above the Fraser Valley, across the border in Washington State, and it seems much closer than it is. This stop lies in the farmland east of Aldergrove, between Langley and Abbotsford, a landscape of berry fields, dairy farms and horse paddocks, with the Fraser River to the north and the border just a few kilometres south.

The valley is one of the most productive farming areas in Canada. Abbotsford is known for its raspberries and blueberries, and in summer farm stands along the roads sell fresh fruit by the flat. The soil is rich alluvium, laid down by the Fraser over thousands of years, and the river still floods in wet years.

Across the river, on a hill above Mission, stands Westminster Abbey, a Benedictine monastery with a striking modern church and views over the valley. The monks welcome visitors to the church and grounds, and it is a peaceful place to stop.

The ride to Mount Baker crosses the border at Aldergrove or Sumas, and you will need a passport and the right documents for the United States. Queues can be long on weekends and holidays. Once across, the Mount Baker Highway climbs through forest to Artist Point, with views of glaciers and peaks, but the upper section is open only in late summer and early autumn, depending on snow.

Down in the valley the roads run on a grid, flat and quick, with the mountain sliding from one side of the visor to the other at every turn. Fill up in Aldergrove or Abbotsford before the border, and in July stop at any farm stand with a hand-painted sign. Berries eaten warm from the field taste of the whole valley.
t.near enfield town@51.6,-0.1:
The world's first cash machine was installed at a Barclays branch in Enfield in June 1967, and a blue plaque marks the spot. Enfield has another claim to fame for riders: the Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield Lock made the Lee-Enfield rifle, and the town's name passed to the Royal Enfield motorcycle company, whose bikes are still built today, though now in India. The factory site has since been redeveloped into housing around the old buildings.

This finish lies in the southern part of the borough, near Edmonton and Bush Hill Park, a district of terraced streets, parks and busy main roads. The Lee Valley, to the east, is a long green corridor of reservoirs, marshes and nature reserves, running north from London, and it is a surprising escape from the city.

Forty Hall, to the north, is a Jacobean manor house with gardens and a park, and Trent Park, nearby, has woods and lakes. The New River, an artificial waterway built in the early seventeenth century to bring fresh water to London, winds through Enfield, and its banks are lined with paths.

Coming back from Cambridge and the Fens, the final stretch follows the A10, a busy, fast road with speed cameras and heavy traffic. The roads into Enfield are congested at rush hour.

Fuel is plentiful along the A10. If you have a Royal Enfield in the garage, it is hard not to smile at the thought that you have just ridden it home, more or less, to the place its name came from.
t.arundel@50.9,-0.6:
Come over the downs from the north and Arundel appears all at once: a castle of grey towers and battlements on a ridge above the River Arun, a French Gothic cathedral beside it, and a steep little town tumbling down the slope to the bridge. It looks almost too much like a film set, and it has served as one more than once.

The castle has been the seat of the Dukes of Norfolk for most of the last five centuries. It was founded soon after the Norman Conquest, battered in the Civil War and largely rebuilt by the Victorians, which explains its slightly storybook perfection. The cathedral, built for the Catholic dukes in the late nineteenth century, is dedicated to Our Lady and St Philip Howard, an Elizabethan earl who died in the Tower for his faith. Below the town the Arun is tidal, brown and fast, and the wetland reserve on its banks fills with ducks, geese and waders in winter.

For riders the name that matters is Bury Hill. The A29 north of Arundel climbs the South Downs in a run of fast, open bends with views over the Arun valley, and on fine weekends the café at the top roundabout becomes an impromptu motorcycle show. Goodwood, a few miles west, adds the Festival of Speed and the Revival to the area's calendar, when every road nearby fills with machinery of every era and the traffic police are on full alert.

The A27 that skirts the town is notoriously congested, especially in summer, so plan to arrive early or late. Parking a bike in the narrow streets is usually manageable near the river.

Fuel is easiest towards Littlehampton or on the main roads. In town, the tea rooms and pubs on the High Street do a steady trade in walkers and bikers alike; take a table by the window and watch the castle change colour as the light goes.
t.wheatley@51.7,-1.1:
Wheatley sits on a hill just east of Oxford, where the A40 crosses the M40, and for most riders it is a quick pit stop: fuel, a sandwich, back on the road. The old village, though, deserves a minute. Its stone cottages climb a steep main street, and at the top stands a small octagonal stone lock-up, built in the nineteenth century to hold drunks and petty criminals overnight, a reminder of rougher days on the coaching road to London.

To the west, Shotover Hill rises between Wheatley and Oxford, a ridge of heath, woodland and sandy paths with views over the city's spires. It was once a royal forest, and highwaymen preyed on travellers on the old road across it. Today it is a country park, popular with walkers and dog owners.

The M40 heads east from here towards the Chilterns, and as it crosses the great chalk cutting at Stokenchurch, watch the sky. Red kites, reintroduced to the Chilterns in the 1990s after being wiped out in England, now wheel over the motorway in dozens, their forked tails twisting as they ride the wind. They are one of the great conservation successes in Britain, and they have become the emblem of the region.

The riding around Wheatley is a mix of fast A-roads and lanes through the Oxfordshire countryside. The lanes towards Thame and the Chilterns are narrow, winding and lined with hedges, with occasional steep climbs and blind bends. Watch for tractors, cyclists and horses.

Oxford, a few miles west, is a nightmare to ride into, with traffic restrictions, bus gates and one-way streets. Park on the edge of the city and walk if you want to see it. Back in Wheatley, the fuel station by the motorway junction is quick, and the village pubs serve decent food.
t.whittington@52.7,-1.8:
Three spires rise from the flat land south of the Trent, and they belong to Lichfield Cathedral, the only medieval cathedral in England to have kept all three. Whittington is a village a few miles east of it, with a church, a green, old pubs and a barracks that has housed soldiers since the 1880s. The Staffordshire Regiment's museum is there, with a reconstructed First World War trench that schoolchildren walk through in awed silence.

Lichfield itself is a handsome cathedral city, and it produced Samuel Johnson, the writer of the first great English dictionary, who was born in a house on the market square that is now a museum. Erasmus Darwin, grandfather of Charles and a remarkable scientist and poet in his own right, lived next to the cathedral close. The city is compact and easy to walk.

A few miles north, the National Memorial Arboretum at Alrewas is a vast, moving garden of memorials to the armed forces and the civilian services, with tens of thousands of trees planted in remembrance. It is free to enter and worth a quiet hour.

The canals meet near Whittington, where the Coventry Canal joins the Birmingham and Fazeley, and the towpaths make a peaceful walk among narrowboats and herons. Tamworth, to the south-east, has a Norman castle on a mound above the river, once a seat of the Mercian kings.

The riding is gentle Midlands fare, with A-roads, roundabouts and lanes through farmland. The A38 and A5 can be busy. Whittington itself has a pub or two; Lichfield, ten minutes away, covers fuel and food and has a market square ringed with cafés.
t.bury@53.6,-2.3:
Bury market is one of the most famous in the north of England, and its fame rests largely on a sausage. Black pudding, made from pig's blood, oatmeal and fat, has been sold here for generations, and the stalls in the market hall still serve it hot, sliced and with mustard, to queues of locals and visitors. It is the obvious food stop, and anyone who wrinkles their nose should try it before deciding.

Bury is a mill town at the edge of the Pennines, north of Manchester, built on cotton and wool. Sir Robert Peel, the prime minister who founded the modern police force and repealed the Corn Laws, was born nearby, and his statue stands in the town centre. On the hill above Ramsbottom, a few miles north, a stone tower built in his memory looks over the Irwell valley.

The East Lancashire Railway, a heritage line, runs steam and diesel trains from Bury up the Irwell valley to Rawtenstall, through old mill villages and green hills. On summer weekends, the smoke and whistles bring the valley back to life.

Riding north from Bury, the roads climb onto the moors of Rossendale and the West Pennines, with wide, empty landscapes, stone walls and reservoirs. The A56 and the roads over to Haslingden and Darwen are popular with bikers, with fast bends and big views. The weather can turn quickly, and the moors are often wet, windy and cold even in summer.

The market does not trade every day, so check before you plan lunch around it. If blood sausage is a step too far, the town also claims the simnel cake, a rich fruit cake with a marzipan layer once baked for Mothering Sunday. Either way, you will not leave hungry, and fuel stations ring the town centre.
t.etwall@52.9,-1.6:
Etwall is a quiet village in the south of Derbyshire, between Derby and the River Dove, with a church, almshouses and old brick houses. It sits on the edge of a district full of history, and a short ride in any direction brings something worth stopping for.

Repton, a few miles south, was the capital of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia, and its church has a crypt where Mercian kings were buried. In the winter of 873, a Viking army camped here, and archaeologists have found their defences and graves. The village is now known for its public school, founded in the sixteenth century.

Swarkestone Bridge, to the east, is a long medieval causeway across the Trent floodplain, and it marks the southernmost point reached by Bonnie Prince Charlie's Jacobite army in 1745, before it turned back to Scotland and defeat. A plaque records the moment.

Closer to Etwall, the Toyota factory at Burnaston builds cars on the site of an old airfield, and its huge sheds are visible from the A50. The A38 and A50 meet nearby, making this a convenient place to refuel on the way north.

Ignore the dual carriageways if you have time. The lanes west towards the Dove and Tutbury, where a ruined castle on a sandstone bluff once held Mary Queen of Scots, are quiet and gently bending, with red-brick farms and long views across the river meadows. Fill up before you leave the trunk roads, since the villages are small; Derby is the fallback if the local pumps disappoint.
t.hardingstone@52.2,-0.9:
Edward I, grieving for his queen, Eleanor of Castile, erected a stone cross at every place where her funeral procession stopped on its way from Lincoln to London in 1290. Twelve were built; three survive, and one of them stands by the roadside at Hardingstone, on the southern edge of Northampton. It is a slender Gothic monument of weathered stone, with statues of the queen looking out over the traffic, and it is more than seven centuries old.

Behind it, Delapré Abbey, a former nunnery turned country house, stands in a park. The Battle of Northampton, one of the bloodier clashes of the Wars of the Roses, was fought on the meadows nearby in 1460, and Henry VI was captured there. The abbey has been restored and is open to visitors, with gardens and a café.

Northampton is the capital of English shoemaking, and the industry still survives, with famous brands making boots and shoes by hand in the town. A museum displays thousands of shoes, from medieval leather to modern fashion.

Hardingstone itself is a village swallowed by the town, with old stone houses and a church. The M1 is close, at junction 15, and the A45 runs past. The riding around here is mostly about getting through the Northampton traffic and out into the countryside, where the lanes towards the Nene valley and the villages to the south are pleasant and quiet.

Fuel is quick to find on the ring roads. As for souvenirs, a pair of Northampton-made boots costs real money, but riders who own a pair tend to say the same thing: they outlast the bike.
t.near brent@51.5,-0.3:
The Hanger Lane gyratory has a fearsome reputation among London drivers, and this finish lies right next to it, between Ealing, Alperton and Park Royal. It is a sprawling roundabout system where the A40 Western Avenue meets the North Circular, with traffic lights, lanes and junctions that confuse even regulars. Keep your wits about you and know your exit before you arrive.

Ealing, to the south, likes to call itself the Queen of the Suburbs, a leafy district of Victorian houses, parks and a busy town centre. Its film studios are said to be the oldest continuously working studios in the world, and the Ealing comedies of the 1940s and 1950s made the name famous. Pitzhanger Manor, the country house that the architect John Soane designed for himself, has been beautifully restored and is open to visitors.

Park Royal, to the north-east, is one of the largest industrial estates in London, and for decades it was home to the Guinness brewery, which closed in 2005. The Grand Union Canal winds through it, and its towpath is a surprisingly peaceful route through the industrial landscape.

Coming back from the North Wessex Downs, the M4 or the A40 brings you into London, and the final stretch is a test of patience. Traffic is heavy, especially at rush hour, and the North Circular is often jammed.

Once off the gyratory, the world calms quickly. Ealing Green, with its old trees and the studio gates on one side, is a five-minute ride away and a far better place to end than a petrol forecourt, though there are plenty of those too.
t.kettering@52.4,-0.7:
Kettering grew rich on shoes, like its neighbours in Northamptonshire, and its streets of red-brick terraces and old factories still tell the story. Today it is a busy market town on the A14, a convenient fuel stop between the Midlands and East Anglia, and the countryside around it hides some remarkable buildings.

Boughton House, a few miles north, is the home of the Duke of Buccleuch, and its French-style facade has earned it the nickname of the English Versailles. It is full of art and furniture, and the parkland around it is beautiful. Rushton Triangular Lodge, to the north-west, is a strange little building, built in the 1590s by Thomas Tresham, a Catholic, as a symbol of the Holy Trinity. Everything about it is based on the number three: three sides, three floors, three windows on each side, and inscriptions of thirty-three letters.

Wicksteed Park, on the edge of Kettering, is one of the oldest amusement parks in Britain, opened in the 1920s by a local engineer who believed children should have places to play. Its playground equipment was famous across the country.

The riding around Kettering is a mix of fast A-roads and lanes through the old Rockingham Forest, with gentle hills, stone villages and quiet roads. The A14 is busy with lorries, and the junctions around the town can be congested.

On a long day towards the Black Mountains, this is a practical halt rather than a sightseeing one: fuel by the A14 junctions, a coffee, a look at the map. But if you are ahead of schedule, ten minutes at the Triangular Lodge will give you something to puzzle over for the next hundred miles.
t.wales@53.3,-1.3:
Yes, it really is called Wales, and no, it is nowhere near the Welsh border. This village sits in South Yorkshire, a few miles south-east of Sheffield, next to Kiveton Park, and the name probably comes from an Old English word for foreigners or Britons, the same root that gave the country its name. The joke never gets old for travellers, and the village sign is a favourite photo.

This was coal-mining country until the pits closed in the 1980s and 1990s, and the villages around grew up around the collieries, with rows of terraced houses for the miners. The landscape has since healed, with old spoil heaps turned into parks and woodland.

Rother Valley Country Park, to the west, is a large area of lakes and meadows created from old opencast mines, with watersports, walking paths and a café. Roche Abbey, to the north-east, is a ruined Cistercian monastery in a wooded valley, its grounds landscaped by Capability Brown in the eighteenth century. The ruins are atmospheric, with a stream running through them.

The M1 is close, at junction 31, and the A57 runs towards Worksop and the Dukeries, where Clumber Park and Sherwood Forest offer quiet roads through woodland. The riding around Wales is mostly about getting from one place to another, but the lanes to the south and east are pleasant.

As a food stop it is honest and unpretentious: a pub, a chippy or two, a café that does a proper breakfast. Eat well, take the photo by the sign, and head off knowing you have already been to Wales once today.
t.harlington on the way back@51.9,-0.5:
John Bunyan was arrested near Harlington in November 1660 for preaching without a licence, and he was taken to the manor house in the village to be questioned before being sent to Bedford jail, where he spent twelve years and began writing The Pilgrim's Progress. The house still stands, and an oak in the area, known as Bunyan's Oak, is said to be where he preached.

Harlington is a village at the foot of the Chiltern escarpment, south of Bedford, and the land rises sharply to the south, where the Sundon Hills and Sharpenhoe Clappers offer fine views over the Bedfordshire plain. The chalk grassland is rich in wildflowers and butterflies, and the beech woods on the Clappers are beautiful in autumn.

For a swim, the options are limited. The Marston Vale, to the north, has lakes created from old clay pits, used for brick-making, and some have watersports and beaches, but check whether swimming is allowed. The rivers around here are small and not suitable for bathing.

The riding is pleasant, with lanes climbing the escarpment and running through the villages. The M1 is close, and the A6 and A5 run north-south. Traffic can be heavy around Luton and Dunstable.

Flitwick, a few miles north, covers fuel. Then, if the evening is clear, ride up to the car park below Sharpenhoe Clappers and walk the ten minutes to the edge of the escarpment. The whole of Bedfordshire lies at your feet, which sounds less impressive than it looks.
t.near towcester on the way back@52.1,-1.1:
Silverstone is six kilometres away, and on Grand Prix weekend you will know it: the roads around Towcester clog with traffic, the sky fills with helicopters and the whole district hums with engines. On other days, this is quiet south Northamptonshire, a landscape of rolling fields, stone villages and woods, with the old Roman road of Watling Street running straight through Towcester.

The town was the Roman settlement of Lactodorum, a staging post on Watling Street, and later a coaching town, with old inns along its main street. Charles Dickens stayed at one of them and wrote it into The Pickwick Papers. Easton Neston, a grand house designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor, stands in parkland on the edge of the town.

East of Towcester, the Grand Union Canal passes through Stoke Bruerne, a canal village with a museum, a flight of locks and the southern portal of the Blisworth tunnel, one of the longest navigable canal tunnels in Britain. It is a lovely spot for a drink by the water, watching narrowboats work through the locks.

For a swim, there is little here. The canal is not for bathing, and the rivers are small. The honest answer is a pool in Towcester or Northampton.

The riding around Towcester is good, with lanes winding over the hills and through the villages, and the A43 and A5 offering faster routes. Traffic is heavy on race days and on summer weekends. Towcester covers fuel. On a quiet evening, though, make the short hop to Stoke Bruerne instead and sit by the top lock, where the only engines are narrowboat diesels chugging at walking pace.
t.morden@51.4,-0.2:
The Northern Line ends here, deep in suburban South London, and Morden is the place commuters come home to. It is a district of semi-detached houses, parks and shopping streets, built mostly in the 1920s and 1930s when the Tube arrived and turned fields into suburbs almost overnight.

There is a surprise hidden in the middle. Morden Hall Park, owned by the National Trust, is a green oasis on the River Wandle, with meadows, wetlands, a rose garden and old snuff mills where tobacco was once ground into powder. The river, which powered dozens of mills in its day, is now clean enough for trout, and the park is a peaceful place to walk.

Morden is also home to the Baitul Futuh mosque, one of the largest in Western Europe, built by the Ahmadiyya Muslim community, with a dome and minarets that stand out among the suburban roofs. It is open to visitors at certain times.

Coming back from the Chilterns and the Thames Valley, the final stretch takes you around the M25 and in through Kingston or Sutton. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, and the A24 into Morden is often congested. Watch for buses, cyclists and pedestrians.

There is fuel on the A24 and the London Road, and plenty of cafés near the station. But if you have half an hour, leave the bike by the park gates and follow the Wandle under the trees past the old mill wheels. It is about as far from the M25 as you can get while still technically being within earshot.
t.west end@49.3,-123.1:
The Lions Gate Bridge, a green suspension bridge spanning the First Narrows from Stanley Park to the North Shore, was built in the 1930s by the Guinness brewing family, who had bought land on the slopes of West Vancouver and needed a way to get buyers there. It is the gateway to the Sea-to-Sky Highway, and the West End, where this ride begins, lies at its southern end, a dense, leafy neighbourhood of apartment towers, old houses and tree-lined streets between downtown Vancouver and Stanley Park.

Stanley Park is one of the great urban parks of the world, a peninsula of old-growth forest, beaches and gardens almost surrounded by the sea, with a seawall path running around its edge. English Bay, on the West End's southern shore, has a sandy beach and a promenade, and the sunsets over the water are famous.

The Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 99, runs north from the bridge along Howe Sound, a fjord of steep mountains and dark water, to Squamish and Whistler. It was rebuilt for the 2010 Winter Olympics, with wider lanes and better curves, and it is one of the most spectacular rides in Canada. Along the way, the Britannia Mine Museum, Shannon Falls and the Stawamus Chief, a huge granite monolith popular with climbers, are worth a stop.

The highway is busy, especially on weekends, and speed enforcement is strict. Watch for rock falls, wet roads and sudden fog. The Lions Gate Bridge has a reversible centre lane and can be congested at rush hour.

Start with coffee on Denman Street, top up at a station on the way out, then take the causeway through Stanley Park, where the cedars close overhead for a few minutes before the bridge lifts you over the water and the Coast Mountains fill the visor. It is hard to think of a better first ten minutes for any ride.
t.near home@47.3,-122.9:
Home is a small community on the Key Peninsula, a long, wooded finger of land reaching into southern Puget Sound west of Tacoma. It has one of the stranger origin stories in the Pacific Northwest: in 1896 a handful of idealists founded an anarchist colony here on the shore of Von Geldern Cove, and for a couple of decades it attracted free thinkers, writers and the suspicious attention of the authorities. The colony faded, but the name stuck.

Today the place is quiet, almost hidden. The Key Peninsula Highway runs down the spine of the land through tall Douglas fir and cedar, with side roads dropping to small coves, oyster beds and boat ramps. It is not a technical road, but it rolls and curves pleasantly, with very little traffic, and the forest smells of resin and salt water after rain. On a clear day, the views back across the water take in Mount Rainier, impossibly large above the sound.

Weather is the main caution. From autumn to spring, damp is the default; moss and pine needles make shaded corners slick, and fog can sit in the hollows until late morning. Deer wander across the roads at dusk. Summer, by contrast, is often dry and gentle, the best time to explore these backroads.

Services on the peninsula are scattered and small, so do not count on finding fuel exactly where you want it. Gig Harbor and Purdy at the northern end of the peninsula are the reliable places to fill up and find coffee and food. From there, the route heads towards Hood Canal and the Olympic Peninsula, where distances get longer and the forest gets even deeper.
t.near lions bay@49.6,-123.2:
Above Lions Bay stand the two granite peaks that gave the village its name, The Lions, visible from much of Vancouver and known to the Squamish people as the Twin Sisters. The village itself clings to steep slopes above Howe Sound, a scatter of houses among cedars and firs, with a small beach and a marina far below. It is a residential community rather than a stop with services, but the setting is spectacular.

The road that brings you here is the Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 99, which runs from Horseshoe Bay to Squamish and Whistler. It was rebuilt and widened before the 2010 Winter Olympics, and the result is a fast, flowing road carved into the cliffs, with the fjord glittering on one side and rock walls on the other. The views across Howe Sound to the islands and the Coast Mountains are superb, especially in the morning light. A little further north, Porteau Cove offers a good place to pull over by the water.

The road demands respect. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends and holidays, with impatient drivers and lots of RVs. Rockfall and wet surfaces are a real risk, especially in the rainy months, when water streams across the road from the slopes. Speed enforcement is common, and the corners can tighten unexpectedly. In winter, snow and ice are possible, and the road is best left to cars.

Squamish, under the huge granite face of the Stawamus Chief, is a natural break point before continuing towards Whistler or Mount Baker on the cross-border loop.
t.nanaimo ferry from horseshoe bay@49.2,-1:
The crossing from Horseshoe Bay to Departure Bay is one of the classic openings of a Vancouver Island trip. The big BC Ferries ships leave from the little cove at the start of the Sea-to-Sky Highway and steam across the Strait of Georgia for about an hour and a half, past the islands of Howe Sound and out into open water, with the snowy Coast Mountains behind you and the long blue shape of the island ahead. On a clear day, it is a cruise in itself; in a winter gale, it is an adventure.

Motorcycles usually load first and are lashed down near the bow, so arrive early and follow the crew's instructions. Reservations are wise on summer weekends and holidays, when queues can mean missed sailings. Once aboard, head up to the deck to watch for seals, porpoises and, occasionally, orcas.

Nanaimo, where you land, is the island's second city. It began as a Hudson's Bay Company coal-mining post in the 1850s, and the wooden Bastion, a small fort built to protect the settlement, still stands by the harbour. The town is also the namesake of the Nanaimo bar, a rich no-bake dessert of chocolate, custard and coconut that you will find in every café and bakery.

From Departure Bay, the route heads north on Highway 19 before turning west on Highway 4 towards Port Alberni and the Pacific Rim. Nanaimo is well supplied with pumps, supermarkets and restaurants, so fill up before heading across the island. The harbour front is pleasant for a short walk and a coffee, a gentle way to shake off the crossing before the forests and mountains of the interior.
t.port alberni@49.2,-124.8:
Port Alberni sits at the head of the Alberni Inlet, a long, narrow fjord that reaches almost halfway across Vancouver Island from the west coast. This geography has shaped its history: it became a major centre for logging, sawmills and fishing, and the smell of the pulp mill has long been part of daily life. In 1964, the great Alaska earthquake sent a tsunami up the inlet, and the funnelling effect amplified the waves, which flooded parts of the town. Today, the waterfront has a harbour quay with shops, cafés and boat tours down the inlet.

The ride in from the east is one of the highlights of the island. Highway 4 passes through Cathedral Grove, in MacMillan Provincial Park, where ancient Douglas firs, some hundreds of years old, tower over the road. It is worth stopping to walk among the giants, but parking is tight and the road is busy, so be careful. Beyond, the highway climbs over the shoulder of Mount Arrowsmith before dropping steeply into the Alberni Valley, with tight bends and heavy truck traffic.

West of town, the road follows Sproat Lake, long home to giant Martin Mars water bombers that fought forest fires across the province, before heading into the mountains towards the Pacific coast. This next stretch is narrow, winding and remote, with few services and limited mobile coverage.

Port Alberni is therefore the last major service centre before Tofino and Ucluelet. It has fuel and food in abundance, so fill up, eat and check the bike before continuing. The weather can change dramatically between here and the coast, with rain and fog common, so pack your waterproofs on top.
t.near stanwood@48.3,-122.5:
Stanwood sits at the mouth of the Stillaguamish River, where it spreads into a delta of farmland and tidal marshes before reaching Puget Sound. The town was settled largely by Norwegian immigrants in the late nineteenth century, and the Scandinavian heritage still shows in local names and festivals. It is the gateway to Camano Island, connected to the mainland by a short bridge, and a pleasant stop on the way north.

The landscape around Stanwood is flat and open, with views across the farmland to the Cascades in the east and the Olympic Mountains across the water to the west. The fields are rich and productive, growing vegetables, berries and flowers. Further north, the Skagit Valley is famous for its tulip fields, which bloom in April and draw crowds. In winter, huge flocks of snow geese and trumpeter swans arrive from the Arctic, feeding in the fields and filling the air with their calls.

The roads here are mostly flat and straight, with gentle bends along rivers and sloughs. They are pleasant for a relaxed ride, but watch for farm machinery, slow traffic and wind on the open flats. From Stanwood, the route heads north and east towards the North Cascades Highway, State Route 20, one of the most spectacular mountain roads in the United States, which crosses the range through deep valleys and over high passes. It closes for the winter, usually from November to spring, so check the status before you go.

Stanwood has fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, making it a good place for a meal before heading into the mountains. Local bakeries offer Scandinavian pastries, a nod to the town's heritage.
t.near midhurst@51.0,-0.7:
Midhurst is one of the nicest market towns in the South Downs, and it sits on one of England's most loved biking roads. The A272 runs east and west across Sussex and Hampshire, through villages and woods and over little hills, and it has a cult following among riders who prefer charm to speed. Midhurst is a natural pause along it, with old coaching inns, timber-framed houses and a broad main street.

Just outside the town lie the ruins of Cowdray House, a great Tudor mansion visited by Henry VIII and Elizabeth, which burned down in 1793 and was never rebuilt. The roofless walls by the River Rother are hauntingly beautiful, and the surrounding parkland is famous for polo, with matches on summer weekends drawing a smart crowd. The writer H. G. Wells spent part of his youth in Midhurst, studying and teaching at the grammar school, and he wrote fondly of the town.

The landscape is classic southern England: the chalk ridge of the South Downs to the south, with long views from the top, and the wooded sandstone hills of the Weald to the north. Roads cross the Downs at points like Cocking and Duncton, with steep climbs and sharp bends. They are narrow, often lined with high hedges, and can be busy with cyclists, horses and tractors. Rain makes the chalk roads slippery, and mud from farm vehicles is common.

Midhurst has fuel, shops, pubs and cafés, as well as several good bakeries. A pub lunch in one of the old inns is a classic experience. Petworth, a few miles east on the A272, has a huge country house with a famous art collection and is equally worth a stop.
t.overton@51.2,-1.3:
The paper for Bank of England banknotes was made near Overton for centuries. The Portal family founded a mill on the River Test in the early eighteenth century, and their watermarked paper became the currency of the empire; the business, later part of De La Rue, still operates here. It is a curious claim to fame for a quiet Hampshire village of brick and flint houses, but it says much about the clear, fast chalk streams of this part of England.

The Test is one of the world's most famous chalk streams, rising just to the east of Overton and flowing south through Whitchurch, Stockbridge and Romsey to Southampton Water.
