The riding here is pleasant and unhurried. The roads follow the valleys and cross the chalk downs, with gentle curves, rolling hills and wide views. The B3400 through Overton and Whitchurch is a pretty route, and the roads north towards the Berkshire Downs and Watership Down, of rabbit novel fame, are quiet and scenic. Watch for tractors, horses and cyclists, and for mud and flint on the lanes.

Overton has a few pubs, cafés and shops, ideal for a lunch stop, while fuel is more easily found in Whitchurch or Basingstoke. A pint and a sandwich in a village pub, sitting by the river, is the essence of a ride in Hampshire. Northwards, the route eventually leads to the Peak District, a long ride away through the heart of England.
t.near snoqualmie@47.5,-121.8:
Snoqualmie sits in the foothills of the Cascades, about half an hour east of Seattle along Interstate 90. The town is best known for Snoqualmie Falls, where the Snoqualmie River drops about 270 feet into a misty gorge. The falls have long been sacred to the Snoqualmie Tribe, and today they draw visitors from around the world. Fans of the television series Twin Peaks will also recognise the area, as much of the show was filmed in and around Snoqualmie and North Bend.

As a start and fuel stop, Snoqualmie is well placed. You will find gas stations in town and in neighbouring North Bend, and it is a good idea to fill up before heading into the mountains, where services become scarce. The Northwest Railway Museum in the old Snoqualmie depot is a charming stop if you have time, with historic locomotives and carriages on display.

The riding from here can go several ways. I-90 climbs east to Snoqualmie Pass, the lowest of the major Cascade passes, while smaller roads wind north through the Snoqualmie Valley towards Fall City, Carnation and Duvall, with farmland, forests and river views. These valley roads are gentle and scenic, though traffic can be heavy on weekends, especially around the falls.

Weather in the Cascades foothills is famously changeable. Rain is common much of the year, and mist often hangs in the valleys. In winter, snow can affect the pass. Bring layers and rain gear, and enjoy the lush green forests that make this part of Washington so distinctive.
t.waller@47.2,-122.4:
Waller is an unincorporated community on the eastern side of Tacoma, in Pierce County, a semi-rural area of small farms, woodlots and scattered homes between the city and the Puyallup River valley. It is not a famous place, but it is a good example of the green, rolling country that surrounds the Puget Sound cities.

The Puyallup Valley, just east, is rich farmland that has been cultivated for generations. Daffodils, tulips and berries were once major crops, and the Puyallup Fair, held each September, is one of the largest in the state. On clear days, Mount Rainier dominates the skyline to the south-east, an enormous glaciated volcano that seems to float above the landscape.

Riding through Waller, you will find a mix of roads. Waller Road itself is a pleasant, gently curving route with trees on both sides, while nearby arterials can be busy with traffic heading to and from Tacoma, Puyallup and the surrounding suburbs. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, wet leaves in autumn and the occasional deer.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy to find in Tacoma, Puyallup and the surrounding towns. From here, the routes towards Mount Rainier and the Cascades open up, offering some of the best riding in the Pacific Northwest. Treat Waller as a pleasant passage, a quiet country interlude before the mountains.
t.near prairie ridge@47.1,-122.2:
Prairie Ridge is a residential community on a plateau above the Puyallup and White River valleys, south of Bonney Lake in Pierce County. The ridge rises above the surrounding lowlands, and on clear days the view of Mount Rainier is spectacular, the great volcano filling the south-eastern sky with its glaciers and snowfields.

The area sits close to State Route 410, the road that leads east through Buckley and Enumclaw towards Mount Rainier National Park and Chinook Pass. This is one of the classic rides of the region, climbing through dense forest into the Cascades, with the mountain appearing and disappearing between the trees. Chinook Pass is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to late spring, so check conditions before planning a crossing.

The roads around Prairie Ridge itself are suburban and semi-rural, with some gentle bends and climbs as you come up from the valley floor. Traffic can be heavy on SR 410 at commuter times and on summer weekends when visitors head to the park. Watch for deer, especially at dawn and dusk, and for logging trucks on the routes further east.

Services are available in Bonney Lake, Buckley and Enumclaw, including fuel, food and coffee. Enumclaw is a pleasant small town and a good place to stop before heading into the mountains, where options become limited. From the high ground here, the whole range of the Cascades seems to beckon.
t.near sequim@48.1,-123.1:
Sequim sits on the north side of the Olympic Peninsula, on a broad plain between the Olympic Mountains and the Strait of Juan de Fuca. It is famous for its climate: lying in the rain shadow of the Olympics, it receives far less rain than Seattle or the rainforests on the west side of the peninsula. That dry, sunny microclimate made it a farming centre, and today it is known for its lavender fields, which bloom in July and fill the air with fragrance.

The Dungeness Spit, just north of town, is one of the longest natural sand spits in the world, curving out into the strait with a lighthouse near its tip. The Dungeness National Wildlife Refuge protects the spit and its birdlife. Inland, the Olympic Mountains rise steeply, and Hurricane Ridge, reached from Port Angeles to the west, offers a famous mountain road climbing to alpine meadows with views across the range.

The riding around Sequim combines coastal roads, farmland and access to the mountains. US 101 is the main route, running through town and around the peninsula, and it can be busy in summer. Smaller roads lead to the coast and into the foothills, and the run towards Port Townsend or Port Angeles offers pleasant scenery. Watch for deer and elk on the roads.

Sequim has all services, including fuel, food and coffee. As a start and finish point, it is ideal: sunny, scenic and a gateway to the wild landscapes of the Olympic Peninsula.
t.near langley@49.1,-122.7:
Langley spreads across the Fraser Valley east of Vancouver, a mix of suburbs, horse farms, berry fields and wineries under a wide sky. It is not high in any alpine sense, but the gentle uplands here lift you just enough to see the Coast Mountains to the north and, on a clear day, the white cone of Mount Baker floating across the border to the south-east.

The history is bigger than the landscape suggests. Fort Langley, on the Fraser River at the north end of the township, was a Hudson's Bay Company trading post, and in 1858 it was where the Colony of British Columbia was proclaimed. The reconstructed fort is now a national historic site, and the village around it has kept a pleasant small-town main street with cafés and antique shops.

For a hot day, there is water nearby. The Fraser itself is fast, cold and silty and not a place to swim, but lakes and pools in the wider valley draw locals in summer, and the river parks along the banks are good for a shaded rest. Check local signage before getting in anywhere; currents and water quality vary.

The roads here are rural grids with the occasional diagonal, mostly flat and straight with good surfaces, interrupted by roundabouts and the odd tractor. Glover Road and the routes towards Fort Langley have a pleasing country feel. Traffic around the Highway 1 interchanges can be heavy. Fuel and food are plentiful throughout Langley, so there is no need to plan ahead; just enjoy the farmland and the mountain views.
t.near pitt meadows@49.2,-122.7:
Pitt Meadows lies on the flat delta land where the Pitt River meets the Fraser, east of Vancouver. Dykes hold back the rivers, and behind them stretch blueberry and cranberry fields, wetlands and farmland, with the steep, forested peaks of the Golden Ears rising dramatically to the north. On a clear evening, with the sun catching the mountains and the fields glowing, it is a beautiful place to end a ride.

The dykes are a defining feature. Built to protect the low-lying land from flooding, they now carry walking and cycling trails and offer elevated views over the river and the farmland. The Pitt-Addington Marsh to the north is a haven for birds, including sandhill cranes and bald eagles. Pitt Lake, one of the largest tidal freshwater lakes in North America, lies just beyond.

For a swim, the options are nearby rather than right here. Golden Ears Provincial Park, reached through Maple Ridge, has Alouette Lake with beaches and picnic areas that are very popular in summer. The water is cold but refreshing after a hot day on the bike. Arrive early on weekends, as parking can fill up.

The roads around Pitt Meadows are flat and open, with long straights between the fields and some pleasant river-side stretches. Watch for farm vehicles and strong winds off the river. Fuel and food are available in Pitt Meadows and Maple Ridge, and the Lougheed Highway provides a quick route back towards Vancouver.
t.walnut grove@49.2,-122.6:
Walnut Grove is a suburban neighbourhood in the north-west of the Township of Langley, close to where Highway 1 crosses the Fraser Valley. It is a tidy, residential place with shopping centres, parks and easy access to the freeway, making it a convenient start and fuel stop for rides heading out of the Vancouver area.

The Golden Ears Bridge, opened in 2009, connects Langley with Maple Ridge and Pitt Meadows across the Fraser River just to the north. Nearby, the historic village of Fort Langley offers a charming detour, with the reconstructed Hudson's Bay Company fort and a lively main street.

The riding out of Walnut Grove depends on your direction. Highway 1 heads east up the Fraser Valley towards Abbotsford and Hope, gateway to the mountain roads of the interior. To the west lies the city and the ferry terminals for the Sunshine Coast and Vancouver Island. Local roads are mostly flat and well maintained, but traffic can be heavy, especially at rush hour.

Fuel, coffee and food are abundant in Walnut Grove, with several service stations near the highway interchanges. It is a good place to meet a group, top up and grab a quick bite before setting off. The ferry ride to the Sunshine Coast, a short drive away, is a wonderful way to start a coastal adventure.
t.near squamish@49.7,-123.0:
Squamish sits at the head of Howe Sound, about an hour north of Vancouver along the Sea-to-Sky Highway, and the first thing that hits you is the Stawamus Chief. This massive granite monolith rises sheer above the town and the highway, one of the largest granite formations in the world, and on any fine day you will see climbers inching up its faces.

The Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 99, is the reason many riders come here. It runs along the steep eastern shore of Howe Sound from Horseshoe Bay, with the fjord glittering below and mountains plunging into the water. The road was extensively upgraded for the 2010 Winter Olympics and now offers smooth, flowing curves with spectacular views. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends and during ski season, and speed enforcement is common.

Around Squamish, there is plenty to see. Shannon Falls, just south of town, drops in a series of cascades from the cliffs above. The Sea to Sky Gondola carries visitors up to a viewing platform with panoramic views over the sound. The Squamish Spit is a famous windsurfing and kiteboarding spot, thanks to the strong winds that funnel up the sound in the afternoons. In winter, bald eagles gather in large numbers along the Squamish River to feed on salmon.

Squamish has full services, including fuel, food and coffee. As a start and finish, it is ideal, offering a stunning setting and easy access to the mountains, the sea and the road north to Whistler and beyond.
t.near anmore@49.4,-122.9:
Anmore is a small, wooded village in the hills above Port Moody, just east of Indian Arm, the steep fjord that runs north off Burrard Inlet. It is a quiet, semi-rural place, with large lots, forest and a strong sense of being on the edge of the wilderness, despite being only half an hour from downtown Vancouver.

The area's main attractions are its lakes. Buntzen Lake, a reservoir surrounded by forest and mountains, is a popular spot for swimming, paddling and hiking. Sasamat Lake, in Belcarra Regional Park, is one of the warmest lakes in the region in summer, with a floating dock and beaches. Both can get very busy on hot weekends, so arrive early.

The roads around Anmore are narrow and winding, climbing through forest from Port Moody. They are pleasant to ride, but watch for cyclists, pedestrians and wildlife, including bears, which are common in the area. Surfaces can be damp and slippery under the trees, especially in the wet months.

These towns also offer plenty of food and coffee options. From here, the route north towards the Sea-to-Sky Highway and the Duffey Lake Road offers some of the finest riding in British Columbia.

It is worth lingering a moment on Indian Arm itself if you get a glimpse of it. The fjord cuts deep into the Coast Mountains, its walls rising almost straight from the water, and for much of its length there is no road at all; boats and floatplanes reach the cabins along its shore. Standing among the cedars and firs above Port Moody, with the smell of wet bark and the sound of nothing much, it is hard to believe a city of millions lies just over the hill.
t.near buckingham@52.0,-1.0:
Buckingham is a small, handsome market town in the north of the county that bears its name, wrapped in a loop of the river Great Ouse. Its centre is a pleasing jumble of Georgian brick, coaching inns and a castellated old gaol that now houses a little museum. The town also has the distinction of being home to the University of Buckingham, the first independent university in Britain, founded in the 1970s.

A few miles north, the landscape garden at Stowe is one of the great achievements of English garden design. Over the eighteenth century, the Temple family turned their estate into a political and philosophical manifesto in stone and greenery, with dozens of temples, monuments and bridges set among lakes and lawns. A young Lancelot Brown worked here as head gardener before he became Capability Brown. The house itself is now a school.

For riders, there is another lure: Silverstone, home of the British Grand Prix and the British round of MotoGP for many years, lies just over the border into Northamptonshire, a short hop north-west. Even when nothing is on, it is hard to ride past the signs without a twitch of the right wrist. Keep it for the track; the A43 is well policed.

The roads around Buckingham are classic English shire riding: hedgerows, gentle hills, honey-stone and brick villages, and B-roads that wriggle unpredictably between them. Surfaces vary from smooth to dreadful, and mud from farm traffic is common after rain. The town has fuel, cafés, pubs and a supermarket, and makes a calm, attractive place to begin or end a long day towards Dorset.
t.near marlow@51.6,-0.8:
Marlow has one of the prettiest Thames frontages anywhere, and the white suspension bridge is the reason. It was designed by William Tierney Clark and opened in the early 1830s, and Clark went on to design the Széchenyi Chain Bridge in Budapest, a much larger cousin built on similar lines. Stand by the river on a summer evening, with the church spire behind the bridge and rowers sliding past, and it is hard to imagine a more English scene.

The town has literary connections, too. Mary Shelley finished Frankenstein while living in Marlow with Percy Bysshe Shelley, who wrote poetry while drifting on the river. Jerome K. Jerome, author of Three Men in a Boat, also spent time here. Today Marlow is affluent and lively, with a high street full of independent shops, cafés, pubs and restaurants, which makes it an excellent food stop.

The riding around Marlow is a mix of river valley and Chiltern hills. The A4155 runs along the Thames towards Henley, a lovely road with views over the water, though often busy. To the north, narrow lanes climb steeply into the Chilterns through beech woods, with tight bends, blind crests and sudden views. Red kites, reintroduced to the Chilterns in the 1990s, are everywhere, wheeling overhead with their forked tails.

Traffic can be heavy, especially at weekends, and parking in the town centre is tight. Fuel is available on the edges of town. As a start and finish, Marlow offers plenty of places to eat and drink, from riverside pubs to cafés and smart restaurants.
t.near blewbury@51.5,-1.2:
Blewbury is a village of thatched cottages, chalk streams and old cob walls at the foot of the Berkshire Downs, south of Didcot. It has the slightly enchanted feel of a place that has been left alone, and it is no surprise that Kenneth Grahame chose to live here in the years after he wrote The Wind in the Willows. Wander the lanes and you could easily imagine Ratty and Mole somewhere among the willows by the stream.

Above the village, the downs rise in long, smooth curves of grass and arable, crossed by the Ridgeway, an ancient track used for thousands of years, said to be one of the oldest roads in Britain. Racehorses train on the gallops of the downs, and on an early morning you may see strings of them cantering along the ridges. The views from the top stretch over the Thames valley towards the Chilterns.

For riders, the roads around Blewbury are a delight. The A417 runs along the foot of the downs through a string of pretty villages, while the minor roads climb onto the downs with long, open views and fast, flowing curves. Surfaces vary, and some lanes are very narrow, with high banks and blind bends. Watch for horses, cyclists and farm traffic.

As a start and finish, Blewbury is peaceful, though services are limited in the village itself. Fuel and food are available in Didcot and Wantage nearby. For a photo, the downs above the village offer sweeping views, especially in the early morning or late evening light.
t.near dunstable@51.8,-0.5:
Dunstable sits where Watling Street, the old Roman road from London to the north-west, cuts through the chalk of the Chiltern Hills, and the town has been a stopping place for travellers for nearly two thousand years. Henry the First founded a priory here in the twelfth century, and its great church still stands, though much reduced. Today the town is busy and practical, with plenty of service stations and supermarkets.

Just south-west of town, the Dunstable Downs rise to the highest point in Bedfordshire, a long chalk escarpment with views over the Vale of Aylesbury. The London Gliding Club operates from the foot of the downs, and on a good day the sky is full of gliders riding the updraughts along the ridge. Kite flyers and walkers gather on the top, and the visitor centre has a café.

A little further south, at Whipsnade, a huge white lion is cut into the chalk hillside below the zoo, visible for miles. Nearby, the Whipsnade Tree Cathedral is a remarkable memorial garden planted in the shape of a cathedral after the First World War.

As a start and fuel stop, Dunstable is convenient, with easy access to the M1 and the A5. From here, the roads north towards the Peak District or west into the Chilterns are open. The lanes over the downs and through the Chiltern villages are narrow and winding, with plenty of bends and some steep climbs. Traffic can be heavy around the town, especially at rush hour.
t.near amersham@51.6,-0.6:
Amersham is two towns in one. Up on the hill is the modern town, built around the station at the end of the Metropolitan line in the early twentieth century, the heart of what was marketed as Metro-land. Down in the valley of the Misbourne is Old Amersham, a beautiful street of coaching inns, timber-framed houses and Georgian façades, with a seventeenth-century market hall on its arches. The contrast is striking.

The town has a darker history, too. In the sixteenth century, several local people were burned at the stake for their Lollard beliefs, and a memorial on the hillside above the old town remembers them. Today, the town is prosperous and peaceful, surrounded by the Chiltern Hills, a designated area of outstanding natural beauty.

As a start and fuel stop, Amersham is practical. There are service stations on the main roads and plenty of cafés and shops in both parts of the town. From here, the roads lead into the Chilterns, with narrow lanes winding through beech woods, past flint cottages and over steep hills. The A413 and A404 are the main routes, but the minor roads are more interesting, if slower.

Traffic can be heavy around Amersham, especially at rush hour, and the lanes are narrow, with blind bends and steep gradients. Watch for cyclists, horses and walkers. The beech woods are beautiful in spring, when bluebells carpet the ground, and in autumn, when the leaves turn gold.
t.near henley on thames@51.6,-0.9:
Every summer since 1839, rowers have raced up a straight stretch of the Thames at Henley, and the Royal Regatta has become one of the fixtures of the English social season, with blazers, boaters, Pimm's and picnics on the riverbank. The rest of the year, Henley is a handsome market town on the river, with a fine bridge, old inns and the River and Rowing Museum, which tells the story of the Thames and the sport.

The high ground around Henley is the southern end of the Chiltern Hills. West of town, the land rises steeply through beech woods towards Nettlebed and the Oxfordshire plateau, and to the east, Remenham Hill climbs out of the valley on the road towards Maidenhead. From the tops, you look down over the Thames valley, with the river winding between meadows and wooded slopes.

For riders, the roads around Henley are among the best in the Home Counties. The A4130 climbs west through Fair Mile, a broad avenue of trees, and on towards Nettlebed and Wallingford, with flowing bends and good views. The minor roads through the Chiltern villages, like Hambleden, Turville and Fingest, are narrow and twisting, with steep hills and beautiful scenery. Turville, with its windmill on the hill above, appeared in many films and television series.

Traffic can be heavy, especially during the Regatta, and the lanes are narrow, with blind bends. Fuel and food are available in Henley. As a high point, the Chiltern escarpment offers sweeping views over the Thames valley.
t.near milford@51.2,-0.7:
Milford is a village just south of Godalming in Surrey, on the old road from London to Portsmouth. The A3 runs past it, climbing south towards Hindhead and the Devil's Punch Bowl, a huge natural hollow in the sandstone hills, and that climb is the reason this is a high point on the ride.

For decades, the A3 squeezed through Hindhead and along the rim of the Punch Bowl, a notorious bottleneck. In 2011, a tunnel was opened beneath the hill, and the old road was removed and returned to heathland. Now you can walk along the rim of the Punch Bowl in peace, with views across the heath and woodland to the South Downs on a clear day. Gibbet Hill, nearby, is one of the highest points in Surrey, named for the gallows where highwaymen and murderers were once hanged.

The countryside around Milford is a mix of heath, woodland and farmland, with sandy soils and pine trees. Witley Common and Thursley National Nature Reserve are among the best heathland reserves in southern England, home to rare birds, reptiles and dragonflies. The villages are pretty, with old cottages and churches.

For riders, the roads here are part of the Surrey Hills, a popular riding area. The lanes are narrow and twisting, with steep hills and blind bends, and the A-roads are faster, with long, open bends. Traffic can be heavy, especially at weekends, and speed limits are strictly enforced. Fuel and food are available in Milford and Godalming. As a start and finish, Milford offers easy access to the hills.
t.cayuse pass@46.9,-121.5:
Cayuse Pass sits at about 1,430 metres on the eastern flank of Mount Rainier, and its main job is to be a junction. State Route 123 comes up from the south along the Ohanapecosh side, State Route 410 arrives from the north out of the Greenwater valley, and just beyond the crest the road keeps climbing east toward the higher Chinook Pass. You arrive through old-growth forest, Douglas fir and western hemlock so tall that the road feels like a tunnel, and then the trees thin and you are standing in subalpine meadow with the mountain somewhere above you, usually in cloud.

The riding here is the sort that does not need to be fast. The corners are long and open, the asphalt in the national park is generally kept in decent shape, and the speed limits are low and enforced by rangers who have seen every kind of motorcycle. Traffic is the real variable. On a July weekend the lay-bys fill with cars and the pace drops to that of the slowest camper van, so go early in the morning or on a weekday, or come in September when the huckleberry bushes turn red and the crowds have gone back to school.

Timing matters more than usual, because this is a seasonal road. Snow in this part of the Cascades is measured in metres, and both 123 and 410 over the passes are closed through the winter, usually reopening late spring and sometimes not until the plough crews have fought through a heavy year. Check the state road reports before you plan a loop around it. The weather can turn in an hour: you can leave the lowlands in sun and meet fog and four degrees at the pass.

Rainier itself is a volcano, around 4,400 metres high, and the most heavily glaciated peak in the lower forty-eight. You will mostly see it as a vast white shape appearing and vanishing between the clouds, and that is part of the pleasure. Do not count on the pass for anything but views: arrive with a full tank, filled in Enumclaw to the north or Packwood to the south. Bring a layer more than you think you need, and watch the margins of the road at dusk, because deer and the occasional black bear use the same clearings you do.
t.mount rainier@46.9,-121.5:
Everyone who rides around here is really riding around one object. Mount Rainier is a stratovolcano of roughly 4,400 metres that rises out of the Cascade foothills with nothing of comparable size near it, which is why it dominates the sky from Seattle on a clear day and why, from up close, it seems to have its own weather. Locals call it simply the mountain, and they say it with the tone people use for a moody relative.

The road system on the park's eastern and northeastern side is built for looking. It climbs through dense forest of fir and cedar, breaks out into meadows, then tucks back under the trees, so the mountain appears in short surprises rather than one long reveal. Corners are broad and easy, the gradients are gentle, and the surface is usually fine. What costs time is not the road but the stops, because the viewpoints are good enough that you will make more of them than you planned. Riding it in the cool early hours gives you empty tarmac and low light on the glaciers.

Tintagel has been selling King Arthur for a long time. Archaeologists have since found that the site was an important trading post in the fifth and sixth centuries, when imported Mediterranean pottery and glass came in by sea, so something notable did happen here, but whether it involved a king named Arthur is another matter.
